title: accrued YieldDistributor rewards are permanently stranded once the asset leaves `ENABLED`, because `iClaim` is the only exit and it hard-reverts on any other status
summary: The YieldDistributor is a smart contract that accumulates rewards for NFTs and holds the token balance on its own address. However, there is a bug in the contract that causes the rewards to become locked and unrecoverable if the asset status changes from ENABLED to DISABLED or EMERGENCY_STOP. This means that once the status changes, NFT owners cannot claim their rewards, the treasury sweep does not include the rewards, and there is no other way to access them. The bug also affects other functions such as iWithdraw and ess_withdraw. To fix this issue, the isActive() precondition in iClaim should be relaxed so that NFT owners can still claim their rewards even after the asset status changes. Alternatively, a treasury-only sweep should be added to the YieldDistributor under EMERGENCY_STOP to ensure that the rewards are not permanently locked in the contract. The bug has been fixed in the latest commits and has been verified by Cyfrin.

title: `STBL_ESS_Wrapper1` exposes no call paths to `WithdrawExpired`, `distributeYield`, or `WithdrawFees` — three isWrapper-gated admin functions are permanently unreachable, freezing expired LT assets, blocking yield distribution, and stranding protocol fees
summary:
The bug report describes an issue with three administrative functions in the STBL_XLayer_Asset_Issuer and STBL_XLayer_Asset_Vault contracts. These functions are gated by the "isWrapper" modifier, which means that only the authorized wrapper contract can call them. However, there is no function in either the abstract STBL_ESS_Wrapper1 or the concrete STBL_XLayer_Wrapper that calls these functions. This means that any external account trying to call these functions will be blocked by the "isWrapper" modifier, as there is no external caller that is the wrapper.

This bug has several consequences. Firstly, the "WithdrawExpired" function is permanently blocked, meaning that lock-time assets cannot be reclaimed from the vault once their lock duration has elapsed. This affects any deposit with a lock duration that has expired. Secondly, the "distributeYield" function is also permanently blocked, meaning that yield from asset appreciation is never distributed to NFT holders. This means that NFT holders entitled to yield from asset appreciation will receive nothing, regardless of how much value the underlying asset accrues. Lastly, the "WithdrawFees" function is also permanently blocked, meaning that accumulated protocol fees are locked in the vault and cannot be retrieved by the treasury. The longer the vault operates, the larger the stranded balance grows.

The recommended solution is to add pass-through functions to the STBL_ESS_Wrapper1 or the concrete wrapper for each missing operation. These functions should be gated by an appropriate access-control check and exposed through their respective interfaces. This will allow the wrapper to dispatch these functions correctly.

The bug has been fixed in commit [afc1f16](https://github.com/USD-Pi-Protocol/stbl-contracts-evm-ess-common/commit/afc1f164f3b3ffcb06e0eff5f84cb9bfa3098173) and has been verified by Cyfrin. The fix includes adding external pass-through functions for "distributeYield" and "withdrawFees" on STBL_XLayer_Wrapper, as well as delegating to internal helpers that iterate over all configured asset vaults and call the corresponding isWrapper-gated functions on each. The "WithdrawExpired" function is not applicable in this deployment as the system exclusively uses PT asset types.

title: `STBL_ESS_NFT_Vault1::_Vault_mergeLot` skips yield claim before NFT burn, permanently stranding accrued rewards in the `YieldDistributor`
summary: The bug report describes an issue with the `mergeLot` function in the STBL_ESS_NFT_Vault1 smart contract. This function merges two NFT pairs without first claiming any accrued yield on the NFTs. This results in the yield being permanently locked in the YieldDistributor contract, making it impossible to retrieve. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate the impact of this bug. The recommended mitigation is to call the `_Vault_claimYield` function before merging the NFTs. This bug has been fixed in the latest commit.

title: `STBL_Redemption_Core::iRedeem` burns the wrong split slice, causing an internal amount mismatch and DoS-ing `redeem` for `_amt < poolSVN/2`
summary: The bug report is about an internal inconsistency in the iRedeem contract, specifically in the `split` function and `withdraw` function, which leads to a mismatch between the amount of tokens being burned and the amount being collected from the redeemer. This causes the function to fail when the input amount is less than half of the total pool value. The report includes a proof of concept test and suggests a change to align the burned amount with the user input amount. The bug has been fixed in the latest version of the contract.

title: LP yield permanently orphaned in `STBL_Redemption_Core::iWithdraw` and `STBL_Redemption_Core::iRedeem` due to missing `iClaimYield` before pool NFT split
summary:
The bug report describes an issue with the `STBL_Redemption_Core` contract. The contract holds a single NFT (`NFTID`) that represents all LP deposits and accrues yield continuously. The yield can be claimed by calling `YieldDistributor.claim(NFTID)` and increasing the internal `rewardIndex`, which is the only way for yield to reach LP shareholders.

However, the functions `iWithdraw` and `iRedeem` do not call `iClaimYield` before calling `spliter.split(NFTID, _amt)`. This results in the old `NFTID` being burned and two new NFTs being minted, without capturing the pending yield into the pool's `rewardIndex`. This means that the unclaimed yield is stranded and can never be accessed again.

The impact of this bug is that every call to `STBL_Redemption::withdraw` or `STBL_Redemption::redeem` is affected, resulting in permanent loss of yield for LPs. The bug has been fixed by calling `iClaimYield` at the top of the `iWithdraw` and `iRedeem` functions, before the `spliter.split` call. This ensures that all pending yield is captured into the pool's `rewardIndex` before the old NFT is burned and replaced.

title: Pending LP yield permanently destroyed in `STBL_Redemption_Core::iDeposit` due to missing call to `STBL_Redemption_Core::iClaimYield` before pool NFT is merged and burned
summary: The bug report discusses an issue with the `STBL_Redemption_Core` protocol. This protocol has a liquidity pool where users deposit YLD NFTs and earn yield from an external `YieldDistributor`. However, there is a bug in the code that causes all pending yield to be destroyed whenever a new user makes a deposit. This happens because the code does not properly handle the merging and burning of NFTs, resulting in the loss of all accrued yield for existing LPs. The impact of this bug is significant, as it affects all new deposits and can be triggered by anyone. A suggested solution is to call `STBL_Redemption_Core::iClaimYield` at the start of the `iDeposit` function, before updating state and merging NFTs. This has been fixed in the latest commit, and the fix has been verified by Cyfrin.

title: Missing `assetID` validation in `STBL_Redemption_Core::iDeposit` first-deposit path allows wrong-asset NFT to permanently brick the redemption pool
summary: The bug report describes a problem with the `STBL_Redemption_Core` contract, which is responsible for managing a pool of NFTs. The contract has a function called `iDeposit` which is used to deposit NFTs into the pool. However, the function does not check the `assetID` of the incoming NFT, which can lead to a wrong-asset NFT being deposited into the pool. This can cause several issues, including a permanent denial of service for all future deposits, incorrect distribution of rewards, and incorrect redemption of NFTs. The bug can be exploited by anyone who holds a YLD NFT for an asset other than the pool's `AssetID`. A proof of concept is provided to demonstrate how the bug can be exploited. The recommended mitigation is to add an `assetID` check in the `iDeposit` function to prevent wrong-asset NFTs from being deposited into the pool. The bug has been fixed in the latest version of the contract.

title: Yield permanently locked in `STBL_XLayer_NFT_Vault` via permissionless `YieldDistributor::claim` defeating balance-delta measurement in `_Vault_claimYield`
summary: The bug report describes a flaw in the `STBL_XLayer_NFT_Vault` contract that allows any external actor to call the `STBL_XLayer_Asset_YieldDistributor` contract's `claim()` function without any access control. This results in the rewards being sent to the vault (the ERC-721 owner of the NFT) and permanently locked in the vault, making it impossible for the legitimate `claimYield()` function to collect the yield rewards. The bug can be exploited by an attacker by calling the `fetchLotCounter()` and `fetchLotDetails()` functions to enumerate the NFT IDs held in the vault and then calling the `claim()` function on the distributor for each NFT ID. The impact of the bug is that the yield is permanently locked in the vault and cannot be recovered. The bug has been fixed in the `STBL_XLayer_Asset_YieldDistributor` contract by restricting the `claim()` function to only be called by the `nftVault` and adding a sweep phase in the vault's `_Vault_claimYield` override to transfer any stranded tokens before the balance-delta logic executes.

title: `STBL_Redemption_Core::iDeposit` mints LP shares 1:1 instead of at the current pool rate, diluting new LPs into existing ones whenever the pool is off-peg
summary: The bug report describes an issue with a pool that causes new deposits to be undervalued and transfer value to existing LPs. The problem occurs because the pool does not mint new shares at the current rate, causing the per-share value to decrease over time. This results in new deposits being worth less than what the depositor paid and the difference being transferred to existing LPs. The impact of this bug is that the pool is off-peg, meaning its value is lower than the total supply of shares. This can happen repeatedly and cannot be fixed by an administrator. The bug has been fixed in the code and verified by a third-party.

title: Full redemption pool drain via inverted split-piece assignment in `STBL_Redemption_Core.iWithdraw`
summary: The STBL_Redemption_Core contract, which manages the STBL redemption pool, has a bug that allows an attacker to drain the entire pool with just a 1-unit withdrawal request. This is due to an inversion in the code that assigns the split pieces, causing the pool to retain only 1 unit while the attacker receives a large remainder. This permanently locks all LPs and causes a total and irreversible loss. A proof of concept has been provided and a recommended mitigation is to swap the A/B assignment in the code. The bug has been fixed in the latest commit.

title: [H-03] Global epoch index corruption from `subtractFromEpochEndLocked` without check
summary: The report talks about a bug in the code that can be exploited by a single user to remove an epoch from the global index, even when other users still have non-zero locked balances at the same epoch. This can cause issues with global accounting, voting power, and other mechanisms that rely on global checkpoints. The bug can be triggered through standard flows such as extending a lock, withdrawing a specific lock, or emergency withdrawing all. The report recommends only removing an epoch from the global index when the updated total locked amount is zero, to prevent cross-user corruption of the index.

title: [H-02] Duplicate deduction of expired locks at epoch boundary
summary: The bug report is about a function called `_decayBias` that calculates voting power decay, which is used by the `LockManager` to reduce the amount of voting power a user has over time. The bug occurs when a checkpoint is recorded exactly at an epoch boundary, causing the function to reprocess the same boundary and deduct the user's voting power twice. This can lead to an artificially inflated voting power for the user, and in extreme cases, can even result in non-decaying voting power. The recommendation is to either zero out the mapping value when an epoch is processed, or to skip the deduction entirely when the duration is equal to 0. This will prevent the bug from occurring and ensure that the voting power is calculated correctly.

title: [H-01] LastProcessedDistributionIndex can skip unfinished older distributions
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `_updateReward()` function in a smart contract. The function is responsible for advancing a cursor, `lastProcessedDistributionIndex`, by the number of fully completed distributions in a scanned window. However, the function does not take into account the size of the contiguous completed prefix, leading to potential errors in distribution completion and loss of rewards for users. The report recommends only advancing the cursor by the length of the contiguous completed prefix, and ensuring that all distributions before the cursor are fully processed for the user. This issue can occur when distributions have different lengths and can result in permanent reward skipping and loss for users.

title: [H-08] Access control missing on fee functions enables misuse
description:
_Resolved_

## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

The `FeeCollector` contract exposes critical functions — namely `claimCollectorRewards` and `claimNFTUnderlying` — which are callable by anyone without any form of access control or role restrictions. This creates severe opportunities for malicious actors to disrupt the protocol’s revenue accounting and fee distribution logic by front-running or deliberately misusing these functions.

#### Unrestricted `claimCollectorRewards`

The `claimCollectorRewards` function is intended to pull rewards from whitelisted `target` contracts (like LendingPools or Vaults) and allocate them according to the specified `feeType`. However, it is fully permissionless:

```solidity
function claimCollectorRewards(address token, address target, bytes32 feeType) 
    external nonReentrant whenNotPaused returns (bool) {
```

This means **any external user can invoke reward claims at any time**, specifying arbitrary valid `feeType` values. Since different `feeTypes` dictate distinct distribution percentages (e.g., 50% Treasury / 50% veRAAC for `VAULT_YIELD_FEE` vs. 90% Treasury / 10% Burn for `NFT_ROYALTY_FEE`), an attacker can front-run legitimate reward distributions to force allocations under less favorable splits.

Example scenario:

* The protocol intends to claim and distribute `VAULT_YIELD_FEE` rewards (50/50 split).
* An attacker front-runs this by calling `claimCollectorRewards` with the same target and token, but sets `feeType` to `NFT_ROYALTY_FEE`.
* Funds get allocated with a different distribution ratio, undermining the intended protocol economics.

This was originally highlighted in findings \[H-11] and \[M-32].

#### Unrestricted `claimNFTUnderlying`

Similarly, the `claimNFTUnderlying` function, used to extract crvUSD (or other tokens) paid for NFT minting, also lacks any access control:

```solidity
function claimNFTUnderlying(address token, address target, uint256 amount, bytes32 feeType) 
    external nonReentrant whenNotPaused returns (bool) {
```

This allows any actor to trigger withdrawals from whitelisted NFT targets, specifying any `feeType` to misallocate collected fees.

**Example:**

* `RAAC_CORP` has 100,000 crvUSD of minting fees meant for its revenue pool.
* An attacker front-runs with `claimNFTUnderlying`, setting the `feeType` to `ROYALTY_FEE` (which distributes to veRAAC holders).
* The funds are now accounted under the wrong `feeType`, resulting in unintended beneficiaries receiving the funds.

**Impact:**

* **Direct manipulation of protocol fee flows**, bypassing governance or operator-controlled scheduling of fee distributions.
* **Permanent misallocation of revenue**, undermining investor and treasury interests.
* **Potential front-running attacks**, exploiting predictable distribution calls queued by protocol operators.

## Recommendation

**Implement robust access control on critical functions:**

* Restrict `claimCollectorRewards` and `claimNFTUnderlying` to be callable only by an authorized admin or operator role (e.g., using `onlyOwner` or RBAC pattern).
* This ensures that fee claiming and distribution can only be triggered by trusted actors under the protocol’s controlled schedule, preventing manipulation of `feeType` allocations and front-running of legitimate distributions.
summary: This bug report discusses a problem with the `FeeCollector` contract in a protocol. The contract has two functions, `claimCollectorRewards` and `claimNFTUnderlying`, which can be called by anyone without any restrictions. This means that malicious actors can disrupt the protocol's revenue and fee distribution by manipulating these functions. The report suggests implementing access control for these functions to prevent unauthorized use and manipulation. This will ensure that only trusted actors can trigger fee claiming and distribution, preventing potential attacks and manipulation of fee allocations.

title: [H-07] Incorrect `RToken` scaling inflates supply and breaks reserves
description:
_Resolved_

## Severity

**Impact:** Medium  

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `RToken` contract incorrectly manages the aggregation of total deposits and interest index scaling. During `mint`, it directly adds the user’s deposit `amount` to `_rawTotalDeposits`. However, this `amount` is already adjusted by the current `liquidityIndex`, reflecting interest accrued up to that point.

When `totalSupply()` later multiplies `_rawTotalDeposits` by the current `liquidityIndex`, it applies the interest index a second time. This results in the total supply being overstated, disrupting accurate reserve and utilization calculations. It also breaks functions like `calculateDustAmount()`, causing it to return zero or incorrect values even when excess funds (dust) exist.

Similarly, in the `burn` function, the contract reduces `_rawTotalDeposits` by the full withdrawal `amount`, which includes accumulated interest. This causes `_rawTotalDeposits` to decrease faster than intended, underreporting the actual deposited principal.

### Example scenario

1. User deposits `100` when `liquidityIndex = 1.0`.
   ```
   _rawTotalDeposits = 100
   totalSupply = 100 * 1.0 = 100
   ```

2. The index grows to `1.05` from accrued yield.
   ```
   totalSupply = 100 * 1.05 = 105
   ```

3. Another user deposits `50` when `liquidityIndex = 1.05`.
   ```
   _rawTotalDeposits += 50 = 150
   totalSupply = 150 * 1.05 = 157.5
   ```
   However, the true combined supply should be:
   ```
   (100 * 1.05) + (50 * 1.05 / 1.05) = 105 + 50 = 155
   ```

This demonstrates how the protocol overstates the actual total deposits due to applying the interest index twice.

## Recommendations

Instead of adding amounts that already include the current `liquidityIndex`, track scaled principal balances by dividing by the index at the time of the mint or burn operation. Then apply the index only once inside `totalSupply()`.

```
uint256 scaledAmount = amount.rayDiv(liquidityIndex);
_scaledTotalDeposits += scaledAmount;

function totalSupply() public view returns (uint256) {
    return _scaledTotalDeposits.rayMul(ILendingPool(_lendingPool).getNormalizedIncome());
}
```

When burning (withdrawing), apply the same inverse scaling to ensure symmetry:

```
_scaledTotalDeposits -= amount.rayDiv(liquidityIndex);
```

This approach ensures that interest is applied exactly once, maintaining accurate total supply reporting, utilization metrics, and reserve calculations.
summary: The `RToken` contract has a bug that affects how it calculates the total deposits and interest index scaling. This is causing the total supply to be overstated, which is disrupting accurate reserve and utilization calculations. The bug also affects the `calculateDustAmount()` function, causing it to return incorrect values. To fix this issue, the contract should track scaled principal balances and apply the interest index only once inside the `totalSupply()` function. The same approach should be used when withdrawing funds to ensure accurate calculations.

title: [H-06] Liquidation failure due to incorrect interface signature
summary: The `LiquidationSwap` contract has a bug that disables the protocol's liquidation mechanism. This is caused by using the wrong interface when interacting with Curve's Twocrypto-NG pools. This can potentially lead to bad debt accumulation and the stability pool becoming insolvent. To fix this, the correct interface should be used when interacting with the Twocrypto-NG pool.

title: [H-05] Bypassing withdrawal timelock via pre-requests and transfers
description:
_Resolved_

## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

A design flaw in the `requestWithdraw` function allows users to completely bypass the protocol's withdrawal timelock and same-block flash-loan protection mechanisms. The vulnerability stems from the lack of balance validation when queuing withdrawal requests, which can be exploited through a simple token transfer strategy to enable instant withdrawals of newly deposited funds.

The issue lies in the requestWithdraw function's failure to validate that the requesting user actually possesses the RTokens they wish to withdraw:

```solidity
    function requestWithdraw(uint256 amount) external whenNotPaused() notBlacklisted(msg.sender) {
        ...
        timelock.amount = amount; // @audit no balance check
        timelock.readyAt = uint64(block.timestamp + parameters.withdrawTimelockDuration);
        timelock.expireAt = uint64(block.timestamp + parameters.withdrawTimelockDuration + parameters.withdrawTimelockDelay);

        emit WithdrawQueued(msg.sender, amount, timelock.readyAt);
    }
```

This allows users to queue withdrawal requests for arbitrary amounts without ownership validation, effectively pre-authorizing future withdrawals before acquiring the necessary tokens.

Consider a scenario:

- An attacker can use two addresses (or a collaborator) to execute this exploit. Let's call them Bob (Attacker) and Alice (Depositor).
- Bob Queues Withdrawal: Bob, who has an RToken balance of zero, calls `requestWithdraw(1000)`. Since there is no balance validation, the transaction succeeds, and a withdrawal request is queued for his address.
- Bob waits for the withdrawal timelock period (e.g., 30 minutes) to expire. His withdrawal request is now "ready" to be executed.
- In a new block, Alice deposits 1000 crvUSD into the LendingPool and receives 1000 RToken.
- Alice immediately transfers her 1000 RToken to Bob. This is a standard ERC20 transfer and is not tracked by the LendingPool's internal state.
- Bob immediately calls `withdraw(1000)`. The LendingPool performs the following checks against Bob's address (msg.sender):
    - The `CannotWithdrawInSameBlock` check (`depositBlock[Bob] == block.timestamp`) passes because `depositBlock[Bob]` is 0. The flash-loan protection is bypassed.
    - The timelock check (`_executeWithdrawTimelock`) passes because Bob's withdrawal request is valid and the timelock has expired. The withdrawal timelock is bypassed.
- Alice's funds, which should have been subject to a withdrawal delay, have been withdrawn instantly.

## Recommendations

Add a balance check in `requestWithdraw()` to ensure users can only request withdrawals for funds they actually possess:

```solidity
function requestWithdraw(uint256 amount) external whenNotPaused() notBlacklisted(msg.sender) {
    ...
    
    // Add balance validation
    require(RToken(reserve.reserveRTokenAddress).balanceOf(msg.sender) >= amount, 
            "Insufficient balance for withdrawal request");
    }
    
    ...
}
```
summary: The bug report discusses a vulnerability in the `requestWithdraw` function of a protocol. This flaw allows users to bypass the withdrawal timelock and flash-loan protection mechanisms by exploiting a lack of balance validation. This means that users can withdraw funds that they do not actually possess. The report provides a scenario to explain how this exploit can be carried out. The recommendation is to add a balance check in the `requestWithdraw` function to prevent this vulnerability from being exploited.

title: [H-04] LiquidationSwap at risk of sandwich attacks due to spot price reliance
summary: This bug report discusses a vulnerability in the LiquidationSwap contract that can be exploited by attackers, potentially causing financial loss for the Stability Pool. The contract relies on a spot price calculation for slippage protection, which can be manipulated by attackers before a liquidation transaction. This renders the slippage protection mechanism ineffective, making the liquidation a target for high-value attacks. The report recommends applying the slippage protection percentage to a weighted average price instead of the spot price, or finding another approach to avoid blocking liquidations. This bug has been resolved with medium severity and high likelihood.

title: [H-03] Incorrect utilization rate in deposit and withdraw operations
summary: The `updateInterestRatesAndLiquidity` function in the protocol is not properly updating the `reserve.totalUsage` value during deposit and withdrawal operations. This leads to incorrect interest rate calculations, which can affect the protocol's revenue and user returns. The function relies on two components: `reserve.totalLiquidity` and `reserve.totalUsage`, but only the latter is updated during debt operations. This means that the `totalUsage` value can become stale and result in a lower calculated utilization rate. This can lead to suppressed borrowing and supply rates, less protocol fee collection, and incorrect borrowing fees. It is recommended to update the `totalUsage` value before calculating the utilization rate.

title: [H-02] `_harvestYield` incorrectly uses total deposits when calculating `totalYield`
summary: The bug report describes an issue in a code that calculates the yield for a vault. When the function `_harvestYield` is called, it uses the total assets deposited into the vault and the difference between the latest vault price per share and the recorded price per share in the pool to calculate the total yield. However, this calculation is incorrect as it does not take into account the number of shares received. This results in an overcalculation of the total yield, leading to incorrect `unclaimedRewards` and lower reserve assets stored in the lending pool. The recommendation is to use shares when updating `vaultRewards.totalDeposits` to avoid this issue.

title: [H-01] StabilityPool functions skip the latest LendingPool index update
summary: This bug report is about a problem with the `deposit` and `withdraw` operations in the code. When these operations are called, they use an outdated value for `poolIndex`, which leads to incorrect amounts of tokens and interest being minted. To fix this, the report recommends triggering an update to the `poolIndex` value within the `deposit` and `withdraw` operations. This will ensure that the correct values are used and the operations work as intended. The severity of this bug is considered medium and the likelihood of it occurring is high.

title: [C-04] Incorrect `DEToken` interest causes pool drainage and loss
description:
_Resolved_

## Severity

**Impact:** High  

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `DEToken` contract has multiple flaws in how it calculates interest during token transfers. These issues allow attackers to artificially mint more interest than intended, drain the Stability Pool, and cause users to lose their accumulated interest.

### Interest incorrectly calculated on transferred tokens enables Stability Pool drainage

The `_update` function incorrectly calculates interest on the entire `_userDeposits[to]` amount, including newly transferred tokens that should not earn historical interest. This means that when tokens are transferred to an address with `_userIndexes[to] > 0`, the interest calculation is performed on the total deposit after the transfer, rather than only on the previously held balance.

Example scenario:

- Attacker creates multiple fresh addresses (Addr1, Addr2, ..., AddrN).
- Transfers 0 DETokens to each, setting `_userIndexes[addr] = currentPoolIndex`.
- Waits for the pool index to increase.
- Transfers DETokens to Addr1.
- Interest is calculated on the full transferred amount with historical index difference, artificially inflating balance.
- Chains this through Addr1 -> Addr2 -> Addr3, compounding the interest calculation error.
- Withdraws from the Stability Pool, draining real RToken assets.

### Recipient receives interest on transferred tokens using an outdated index

The contract uses the recipient’s old `_userIndexes` to calculate interest on the new, larger `_userDeposits[to]`, which includes the transferred tokens. This means the recipient effectively earns interest as if they held the new tokens since their earlier index.

For example:

- Pool Index: 1.5.
- Bob has 100 tokens with index 1.1.
- Alice has 1000 tokens with index 1.5.

When Alice transfers 1000 tokens to Bob:

1. Bob’s `_userDeposits` becomes 1100.
2. Interest is calculated using Bob’s previous index (1.1) and new total deposit (1100).
3. Bob receives interest as if all 1100 tokens had been deposited since index 1.1, earning 1100 × (1.5 - 1.1) = 440, even though Alice’s 1000 tokens were just moved.
4. Alice’s unclaimed interest on her 1000 tokens is lost entirely.

### Sender loses accumulated interest when transferring DEToken

When users transfer DETokens, the interest accumulated from their last `_userIndexes` to the current pool index is not calculated. The `_update` function simply decreases the sender’s `_userDeposits`:

```solidity
if(from != address(0) && from != to) {
    _userDeposits[from] -= amount;
}
```

## Recommendations

- Update the `_update` function to calculate and mint interest for both the sender (`from`) and the recipient (`to`) **before modifying their `_userDeposits` or `_userIndexes`**.
- Ensure that:
  - For the sender, compute and mint any accrued interest based on their current `_userDeposits` and `_userIndexes`, then update their index to the current pool index.
  - For the recipient, if `_userIndexes[to] == 0`, initialize it to the current pool index; otherwise, calculate and mint interest on their previous balance before adding the new deposit, then update their index.
- Do not include the newly transferred amount when calculating the recipient’s interest. Interest should only accrue on balances held prior to the transfer.
- After processing interest and updating indexes for both parties, adjust `_userDeposits` to reflect the transferred amount.
- Ensure `balanceOf` reflects accrued interest to prevent underflows if a user transfers their full visible balance.
- Consider adding explicit tests to simulate transfers between accounts with different indexes to verify that no over-minting or loss of accrued interest occurs.
summary: The `DEToken` contract has several issues with how it calculates interest during token transfers. These problems allow attackers to create more interest than they should, drain the Stability Pool, and cause users to lose their earned interest. One issue is that interest is calculated on the entire transferred amount, even for new tokens that should not earn interest. This allows attackers to artificially inflate their balance and drain the Stability Pool. Another issue is that the recipient of transferred tokens receives interest based on an outdated index, causing them to earn more interest than they should and causing the sender to lose their earned interest. The recommendation is to update the `_update` function to properly calculate and mint interest for both the sender and recipient before modifying their balances and indexes. Additionally, the transferred amount should not be included in the recipient's interest calculation and the `balanceOf` function should reflect accrued interest to prevent underflows. It is also recommended to add tests to ensure that transfers between accounts with different indexes do not cause over-minting or loss of accrued interest.

title: [C-03] Incorrect `DebtToken` scaling inflates totals miscalculating rates
description:
_Resolved_

## Severity

**Impact:** High  

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `DebtToken` contract incorrectly handles the aggregation of total borrows and applies the interest index multiple times. When users borrow funds through `mint`, the function adds the borrow `amount` directly to `_rawTotalBorrows`. However, this `amount` is already tied to the current `usageIndex`. Later, `totalSupply()` multiplies `_rawTotalBorrows` by the latest `usageIndex`, effectively applying the index twice. This leads to overstating the protocol’s total debt.

Similarly, in the `burn` function, repayments reduce `_rawTotalBorrows` by the full repayment `amount`, which also includes accrued interest. As a result, `_rawTotalBorrows` decreases faster than it should, undercutting the actual principal owed.

This causes:

- Inflated or deflated total debt values.
- Incorrect utilization rates, directly impacting calculated borrow and supply interest rates.
- Possible misalignment with borrow caps or protocol risk models.

### Example scenario

1. User A borrows `100` when `usageIndex = 1.0`.
   ```
   _rawTotalBorrows = 100
   totalSupply = 100 * 1.0 = 100
   ```

2. The index grows to `2.0` over time.
   ```
   totalSupply = 100 * 2.0 = 200
   ```

3. User B borrows another `100` when `usageIndex = 2.0`.
   ```
   _rawTotalBorrows += 100 = 200
   totalSupply = 200 * 2.0 = 400
   ```
   However, this means User B’s new borrow of `100` is effectively doubled immediately by the current index, overstating the total debt.

Similarly, when repayments occur, the protocol reduces `_rawTotalBorrows` by the full `amount`, including interest, causing it to decrease too aggressively.

## Recommendations

Instead of updating `_rawTotalBorrows` with the interest-adjusted `amount`, track scaled principal amounts by dividing by the current `usageIndex`. Then apply the index only in `totalSupply()`.

```
uint256 scaledAmount = amount.rayDiv(usageIndex);
_scaledTotalBorrows += scaledAmount;

function totalSupply() public view returns (uint256) {
    return _scaledTotalBorrows.rayMul(ILendingPool(_lendingPool).getNormalizedDebt());
}
```

When burning (repaying), apply the same scaled reduction:

```
_scaledTotalBorrows -= amount.rayDiv(usageIndex);
```

This ensures the interest index is applied exactly once, maintaining accurate total debt accounting and consistent utilization and interest rates.
summary: The DebtToken contract has a bug that causes the total amount of borrowed funds to be calculated incorrectly. This is because the contract applies the interest index multiple times when users borrow or repay funds. This leads to inflated or deflated values for total debt, incorrect utilization rates, and possible misalignment with protocol risk models. To fix this, the contract should track scaled principal amounts and only apply the interest index once in the totalSupply function.

title: [C-02] Wrong index-based balance calculations
description:
_Resolved_

## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The protocol's index-based accounting system, designed to track interest accrual over time, contains a mathematical error. Instead of calculating compound interest through proportional scaling, the implementation uses a linear approximation that becomes increasingly inaccurate as indexes grow beyond their initial value.

Correct Compound Interest Formula: `Scaled_Balance = Raw_Balance × (Current_Index / User_Last_Index)`
Implemented formula: `Scaled_Balance = Raw_Balance + Raw_Balance × (Current_Index - User_Last_Index) / RAY`

This linear approximation is only accurate when User_Last_Index = RAY (1e27).

Consider the scenario:

- User deposits 1,000 tokens when index = 2.0 RAY (protocol has doubled in value).
- Index grows to 2.2 RAY (10% growth period).
- Expected Balance: 1,000 × (2.2 / 2.0) = 1,100 tokens.
- Contract Calculation: 1,000 + 1,000 × (2.2 - 2.0) = 1,200 tokens.

As indexes continue to grow, this error compounds. It leads to wrong RToken, DEToken, and DebtToken interest calculation and balances.

## Recommendations

The calculation must be changed from an additive difference based model to a multiplicative ratio based model across all indexed tokens. This ensures that user balances and debts scale correctly in proportion to the index growth.
summary: The bug report states that there is a mathematical error in the protocol's index-based accounting system, which is used to track interest accrual over time. The error occurs because the implementation uses a linear approximation instead of the correct compound interest formula. This results in inaccurate calculations when the indexes grow beyond their initial value. This error can lead to incorrect interest calculations and balances for RToken, DEToken, and DebtToken. The report recommends changing the calculation method to a multiplicative ratio based model to ensure accurate scaling of user balances and debts.

title: [C-01] `_update` inside `DEToken` causes incorrect accounting
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `_update` function in the code. The function is triggered by `burn`, `mint`, and transfer operations and updates both `_userDeposits` and `_scaledTotalSupply`. However, when `mint` or `burn` is called, it incorrectly updates the `_scaledTotalSupply` and double-mints interest for the user. This happens because the function adds the `amount` to the user deposit and when `setUserDeposit` is called, it does not update the `_scaledTotalSupply` correctly. The report suggests skipping the `mint` and `burn` scenario in the `_update` function to fix this issue.

title: [H-31] Rewards boosts distribute more rewards than available
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

`BaseGauge` applies a boost over the rewards of the users, but these extra rewards received by the users are not backed by new deposits of reward tokens.

As a result, more rewards than the available tokens are distributed over the period. This will cause some users might not be able to claim their rewards.

## Recommendations

The boost system should be either removed or redesign to ensure that the gauge rewards are always backed by the available tokens.
summary: The report discusses an issue with the `BaseGauge` function, which is responsible for distributing rewards to users. It has been found that the function is giving out more rewards than there are tokens available, which can cause some users to be unable to claim their rewards. It is recommended that the boost system be either removed or redesigned to ensure that rewards are always backed by available tokens. The severity of this issue is medium, but the likelihood of it occurring is high.

title: [H-30] `getNextCycleStart()` returns incorrect value at the end of a cycle
summary: The bug report discusses an issue with the function `GaugeRewardsDistributor.getNextCycleStart()` in the code. This function is used to set the start of a new distribution cycle. However, when the function is called at the exact end of a cycle, it returns a value that is one cycle ahead instead of the current timestamp. This results in the cycle being extended by one more period, causing problems with the rewards accumulation logic. The report recommends a fix to the code to prevent this issue from occurring.

title: [H-29] `GaugeRewardsDistributor` distributes rewards to gauges not registered
summary: The report describes a bug in the GaugeRewardsDistributor contract where it distributes tokens to all active gauges, instead of only the ones that have been registered to receive rewards for that specific token. This results in incorrect distribution of tokens and some gauges not being able to receive them. The recommended solution is to add a condition to only distribute tokens to gauges that have been registered for that token.

title: [H-28] Deposits during liquidation enable collateral lockup
summary:
This bug report describes a high severity issue in the function `StabilityPool.liquidateBorrower()` which can be exploited by borrowers to prevent their collateral from being liquidated. The bug occurs because the borrower is able to increase their balance even while under liquidation. This can be done by invoking the `depositAsset()` function at any time, which updates the borrower's balance. This causes the `validateLiquidationData()` function to fail, aborting the liquidation process and locking the collateral indefinitely. 

The report recommends blocking deposits during liquidation in the `LendingPool.depositAsset()` function by adding a check to prevent any balance changes once liquidation has begun. This will prevent borrowers from exploiting the bug and ensure that liquidation can proceed smoothly.

title: [H-27] Unrestricted `FeeCollector.collectFee` enables unauthorized fee extraction
summary:
This bug report discusses an issue with the `LendingPool.borrowWithInsurance` function in the LendingPool contract. This function requires users to pre-approve the insurance fee to the `feeCollector` before calling the function. However, there is no access control on the `FeeCollector.collectFee` function, which means that an attacker can drain the victim's approved tokens via a frontrun attack, even if the victim never calls `borrowWithInsurance`. 

The report recommends performing a pull from the user's balance within the `borrowWithInsurance` function instead of requiring pre-approval. This would prevent the attacker from draining the victim's approved tokens.

title: [H-26] Stale interest accrual allows over-borrowing
summary: This bug report discusses a problem in the LendingPool._borrow() function where the validation of a borrower's debt occurs before the accrual of interest and update of scaled debt indices. This results in an under-reported debt balance and allows borrowers to slip in extra debt until the next reserve update, bypassing intended collateral limits. The report recommends changing the order of operations to first update the reserve state and then validate the debt.

title: [H-25] Lock overwrite in `createLock` causes undercredited withdrawals
summary: The bug report describes a problem with the `createLock` function in the `LockManager` contract. This function is used to create a lock for a specific user, which prevents them from withdrawing funds for a certain period of time. The bug occurs when the `veRAACToken.lock()` function is called twice, with a time difference between the calls. This causes the first lock to be overwritten by the second, resulting in the user being charged twice but only one amount being recorded in the locked positions. This means that during a withdrawal, only one amount can be retrieved instead of both. The bug has a high impact and a medium likelihood of occurring. The recommendation is to disallow multiple locks per user to prevent this issue.

title: [H-24] Unclosed liquidation blocks collateral recovery
summary: This bug report discusses an issue where a user's position remains stuck under liquidation even after their debt has been fully repaid. This prevents the user from withdrawing collateral or finalizing their stability pool, causing a high impact and medium likelihood issue. The report includes code snippets and a test case to demonstrate the problem and recommends updating the `closeLiquidation()` function to bypass the grace period check if the user's debt is zero. This would allow the position to be closed even after the deadline has passed.

title: [H-23] FeeCollector will be dos
summary: This report discusses a bug in the FeeCollector contract where the `claimNFTUnderlying` function is vulnerable to malicious attacks. The function allows users to withdraw tokens from a designated address and update the collected fees. However, there is no security check for the input `target` which can be manipulated by malicious users to increase the collected fees. This can result in an overflow and cause issues with normal operations and fee distribution. The recommendation is to add a sanity check for the input `target` to prevent these attacks.

title: [H-22] Users can steal rewards from SP
summary: This bug report discusses an issue in a system where users deposit a token (RToken) to receive a different token (DEToken). When users withdraw the DEToken, they can also receive rewards. However, the problem is that the system does not keep track of the claimed rewards. This allows malicious users to repeatedly withdraw small amounts of DEToken and steal rewards from the system. The severity of this bug is medium, as it can impact the rewards of legitimate users. The likelihood of this bug occurring is high. To fix this issue, it is recommended to calculate the reward per DEToken and record the claimed rewards.

title: [H-21] Users may be forced to pay more interest
summary: This bug report is about a problem in a lending pool where users can repay each other's debt using a function called `repayOnBehalf`. The issue is that if a malicious user repays a very small amount of debt for another user, the total debt for that user's position does not change. However, the raw balance, which is used to calculate interest, is increased. This means that the user may end up paying more interest than they should. The report suggests adding a minimum amount that must be repaid or preventing users from repaying debt without the owner's approval.

title: [H-20] Users can avoid insurance fee when reborrowing debt
summary: The report states that there is a bug in a lending pool where users can repay their debt through a function called `repay`. After repaying all debt, a certain variable called `position.rawInsuredBalance` is reset to make sure that if the user takes a loan again, the insurance will be reset and the user will have to insure again. However, the bug is that another variable called `position.isInsured` is not reset, which means that if the user takes another loan after repaying all debt, the new loan will still have insurance even though it shouldn't. The recommendation is to also reset `position.isInsured` when all debt is repaid.

title: [H-19] Users may fail to withdraw from lending pool
summary: This bug report discusses an issue in a lending pool where lenders are unable to withdraw their crvUSD funds. The severity of the issue is medium and the likelihood of it occurring is high. The problem occurs when the current buffer is not enough to cover the withdrawal, causing the system to withdraw from the curve vault. However, this withdrawal results in a charge of yield, which can cause the RToken contract to not have enough crvUSD to pay the withdrawal. The report recommends considering the possible yield deduction when calculating the required amount for withdrawal.

title: [H-18] Inflation attack in RWA Vault
summary: The bug report discusses a problem with a process called "liquidation" in a system that allows users to borrow and lend digital assets. The process involves swapping one type of token for another, but the calculation used to determine the amount of the swap may not be accurate if the price of the first token is manipulated. This can happen if a user donates assets to a specific part of the system, causing the price of the token to increase. This can lead to later users paying more for the token when they deposit, causing them to receive fewer shares. The report recommends changing the calculation to take into account the potential for price manipulation and suggests allowing the system owner to set a minimum amount for the swap.

title: [H-17] Incorrect totalSupply calculation
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description
In a lending pool, we use RToken as the lender's share and use DebtToken as the borrower's debt share. Lenders' raw balance means lenders' principle. Each lender has their own liquidity index. When users want to withdraw, we will calculate the loan interest based on the difference between the current liquidity index and this lender's index. Debt token is one similar case. It means that users' raw balances no matter RToken or DebtToken are not normalized.

If the raw balance is not normalized, when we multiply the normalization index, the result is incorrect. The result might be larger than the expected result. All functions which depend on `totalSupply` will be impacted.

```solidity
    function totalSupply() public view override(ERC20, IERC20) returns (uint256) {
        return super.totalSupply().rayMul(ILendingPool(_lendingPool).getNormalizedIncome());
    }
```

## Recommendations
In order to calculate the total supply conveniently, we should normalize our share.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue in a lending pool where the raw balances of lenders and borrowers are not normalized. This means that when users want to withdraw, the loan interest is calculated incorrectly, potentially resulting in a larger than expected result. This can also impact all functions that depend on the `totalSupply` calculation. The recommendation is to normalize the shares in order to accurately calculate the total supply.

title: [H-16] Reward rate can be manipulated in first cycle
summary: This bug report is about a problem in the GaugeRewardsDistributor contract, where users can add rewards before a certain time and have them distributed between the current timestamp and a specific time. However, the issue is that users can notify rewards multiple times during this period, which can lead to malicious users manipulating the reward rate and causing other users to miss out on their rewards. The recommendation is to accrue the rewards during this period to prevent this from happening.

title: [H-15] Malicious users can distribute more rewards to the same gauge
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the GaugeRewardsDistributor contract, where malicious users can re-distribute rewards to the same gauge multiple times. This can happen if the `pendingAllocations` variable is reset to zero after distributing rewards to a gauge. The function `_checkAndAddGaugeToCycle` is responsible for adding new active gauges to the reward allocation, but it can mistakenly add the same gauge if the `pendingAllocations` variable is zero. To prevent this, it is recommended to prevent re-distribution for the same gauge.

title: [H-14] Incorrect reward calculation in `_calculatePendingRewards`
summary: This bug report is about a problem in the BaseGauge system where stakers are not receiving the correct amount of rewards. This is because the reward calculation is based on the reward rate, which is obtained from the reward distributor. However, the rewards in the distributor may be distributed to different gauges, causing the reward rate to be lower in the base gauge. This leads to incorrect reward calculations. The report recommends fixing this issue by calculating the reward rate based on the actual amount of rewards.

title: [H-13] Permanent loss of rewards when distribution fails
summary: This bug report describes an issue in the `RAACMinter` contract, which is used to distribute rewards to different pools. The problem occurs when the contract tries to distribute rewards to the pools. If the distribution fails, the contract is unable to recover the tokens that were meant for that distribution. This is because the contract clears the excess tokens before attempting to distribute them, and the failed distribution amount is only stored in a temporary memory variable. This means that the tokens are permanently lost and cannot be recovered. To fix this issue, the report recommends modifying the functions to store the necessary information in a more permanent storage location.

title: [H-12] Underflow forces full interest payment in debt token
summary: The `DebtToken` contract has a bug that affects the `burn()` function. This function allows users to repay their debt and accrued interest by burning tokens. However, if a user tries to make a partial repayment that is less than their accrued interest, the transaction will fail. This is because the contract does not check if the repayment amount is greater than the accrued interest before calculating the remaining amount to be burned. To fix this issue, the `burn()` function should be modified to first pay off the accrued interest and then calculate the remaining amount to be burned.

title: [H-11] Randomness can be manipulated in `RWAVault` redemptions
summary: The RWAVault contract has a vulnerability that allows users to manipulate the randomness of selecting NFTs for redemption. This means that users can repeatedly redeem NFTs until they get the one they want, which is unfair. To fix this issue, a cooldown period should be implemented for NFT re-deposits after redemption.

title: [H-10] `Treasury` deposit functions can be DoSed due to unsafe accounting
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

The `Treasury` contract stores in the `_totalValue` state variable the total amount of all tokens deposited in the contract. As deposits can be made in any token through the `deposit()` and `distributeRewards()` functions, anyone can deposit a dummy token for an amount equal to `type(uint256).max - _totalValue`, causing every new call to `deposit()` or `distributeRewards()` to revert with an overflow error.

The `distributeRewards()` function is called by the fee collector for fee distribution, and the `deposit()` function is called by the stability pool for the liquidation process. The DoS of the liquidation process is of particular concern, as it is a time-sensitive process that should not be blocked in order to maintain the system collateralization.

Once the DoS is detected by the protocol team, the following actions would be required:
- To resume fee distributions, the treasury address should be changed in `FeeCollector` to a new address that does not have the overflow issue.
- To resume the liquidation process, given that the treasury address cannot be updated, treasury fees should be permanently disabled by setting `liquidationSplit.mintPercentage` to 0.

## Recommendations

It is recommended to remove the `_totalValue` state variable, as it does not provide any useful information, given that is mixing the balances of different tokens.
summary: The Treasury contract has a bug where anyone can deposit a dummy token for a large amount, causing an overflow error and blocking important functions such as fee distribution and liquidation. To fix this, the `_totalValue` state variable should be removed as it does not serve any useful purpose. In the meantime, the fee collector should change the treasury address and the liquidation process should disable treasury fees permanently.

title: [H-09] Removing distribution pool in `RAACMinter` does not update `totalWeight`
summary: This bug report is about a function called `RAACMinter.removeDistributionPool()` which allows a certain role to remove a distribution pool. However, the function has a mistake where it deletes a certain mapping before updating another one, causing the weight of the pool to not be subtracted from the total weight. This results in lower rewards being distributed to the remaining pools and some rewards not being distributed at all. The report suggests a simple fix of deleting the mapping after updating the total weight.

title: [H-08] First deposit front-running attack
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

The `RWAVault` contract is subject to a common issue of ERC-4626 vaults, where the first deposit is front-run by an attacker.

1. A user will deposit assets into the contract to mint shares.
2. The attacker front-runs the user's transaction by minting one share and donating to the adapter 50% of the assets deposited by the user.
3. The user transaction is executed, and the shares minted are calculated as `depositedAssetValue * supplyBefore / assetsBefore`. As `assetsBefore` (assets in all the adapters) is inflated by the attacker's donation, the division is truncated, and the user mints only 1 share: `x * 1 / (0.5x + 1) = 1`.
4. Both the attacker and the user have 1 share each (50% of the total supply), but the amount deposited by the user represents 2/3 of the total assets.

## Recommendations

There are different ways to mitigate this issue, including:

- Use of dead shares: Forces to deposit assets on the contract's deployment.
- Use of virtual deposit: OpenZeppelin's ERC4626 implements this solution and is [well documented](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/erc4626).
summary: The RWAVault contract has a high impact and medium likelihood bug where the first deposit can be front-run by an attacker. This means that the attacker can manipulate the transaction and cause the user to only receive 1 share instead of the intended amount. To fix this issue, there are suggestions to use dead shares or virtual deposit, which can be found in OpenZeppelin's ERC4626 documentation.

title: [H-07] Timelock withdrawal mechanism in `LendingPool` can be bypassed
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The lending pool has a configurable timelock duration for withdrawals that is initialized to 30 minutes. This is a common practice to prevent flash loan attacks and other types of atomic operations where a user can deposit and withdraw funds in a single transaction.

However, the timelock mechanism for withdrawals is flawed, as `requestWithdraw()` does not check if the user has enough balance to withdraw.

Users can preemptively request withdrawals for different amounts using different accounts and, after the timelock period, they can deposit and withdraw any of the requested amounts in the same transaction.

## Recommendations

Check if the user has enough balance to withdraw in `requestWithdraw()`.
summary: This bug report discusses a flaw in the lending pool's timelock mechanism for withdrawals. The timelock duration is set to 30 minutes to prevent flash loan attacks and other types of atomic operations. However, the `requestWithdraw()` function does not check if the user has enough balance to withdraw. This allows users to request withdrawals for different amounts using multiple accounts and then deposit and withdraw any of the requested amounts in a single transaction after the timelock period. The recommendation is to fix this by checking the user's balance in the `requestWithdraw()` function.

title: [H-06] Borrowed amounts can be insured for free
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

`LendingPool` allows users to pay for insurance on borrowed assets. This insurance allows users to repay their debt in case of liquidation during a grace period.

However, on repayment, it is not checked if the amount insured can cover the amount being repaid, but only if the position is insured.

Consider the following scenario:
- Alice borrows 34 wei of crvUSD, paying a 3% insurance fee, which is 1 wei.
- Alice borrows 1,000 crvUSD using the `borrow()` function (no insurance).
- Alice's position is set for liquidation.
- Alice repays her debt of 1,000 tokens + 34 wei of crvUSD. She only insured 34 wei, so the insurance for the 1,000 crvUSD has been free.

## Recommendations

Set `position.isInsured` to `false` in the `borrow()` function.
summary: The report is about a bug in the `LendingPool` feature that allows users to pay for insurance on borrowed assets. The bug occurs when a user repays their debt during a grace period and the system does not check if the amount insured is enough to cover the amount being repaid. This can result in the user not having enough insurance coverage for their debt, leading to potential losses. The severity of this bug is medium and the likelihood of it occurring is high. The recommended solution is to set `position.isInsured` to `false` in the `borrow()` function.

title: [H-05] Overwrite in `RToken.burn()` can cause undesired behavior
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

In `RToken.burn()`, when the amount to be burned for a user is greater than his balance, the amount is overwritten to the user's balance.

```solidity
	if(amount > userBalance){
		amount = userBalance;
	}
```

This will have the following consequences when `LendingPool.withdraw()` is called:

- The user might receive fewer tokens than expected, if the available balance was overestimated. Given that no value is returned by the `withdraw()` function, the user will assume that the amount withdrawn is the same as the amount requested. This can be especially problematic in the case of contract interactions.

- Anyone with a minimum deposit (e.g. 1 wei) can spam the protocol to withdraw all the deposits from the vault in order to cover his withdrawal.

Consider the following scenario:
1. Alice deposits 1 wei into the `LendingPool`.
2. The total deposits are 10,000 crvUSD, 2,000 of which are in the `RToken` contract and 8,000 in the Curve pool.
3. Alice withdraws 10,000 crvUSD, causing 8,000 crvUSD to be withdrawn from the Curve pool. When `RToken.burn()` is executed, the amount is overwritten to 1 wei and the withdrawal is successful.


## Recommendations

Revert when the amount to be burned is greater than the user's balance.
summary: This bug report describes a medium severity issue in the `RToken.burn()` function. When the amount to be burned for a user is greater than their balance, the amount is being overwritten to their balance. This can cause problems when the `LendingPool.withdraw()` function is called, as the user may receive fewer tokens than expected and anyone with a minimum deposit can spam the protocol to withdraw all deposits from the vault. The report recommends that the code be updated to revert when the amount to be burned is greater than the user's balance.

title: [H-04] `LendingPool.withdrawAsset()` does not take into account debt interests
summary: The bug being reported is in the `LendingPool._validateBorrow()` function. This function is used to calculate the current debt of a user's position. However, it does not take into account the debt accumulated by the increase of the usage index, which leads to an underestimation of the debt. This means that users are able to borrow more assets than they should be able to, leaving their position undercollateralized. To fix this issue, the code needs to be updated to use the `getPositionScaledDebt()` function instead of `getPositionDebt()`. This will ensure that the correct debt is calculated and prevent users from borrowing more than they should.

title: [H-03] `DebtToken` total supply is inflated
summary: The bug report discusses a medium severity bug in the `DebtToken` contract. The total supply of the token is calculated incorrectly, leading to an inflation of the supply. This is due to the fact that the `mint()` and `burn()` functions normalize the current balance of the user by the usage index, but this is not taken into account when calculating the total supply. This affects various calculations that rely on the total supply, such as the validation of the borrow supply cap and the `reserve.totalUsage` value. To fix this bug, it is recommended to track separately the amount of tokens minted by borrowed amounts and normalize it by the usage index when calculating the total supply.

title: [H-02] Rewards from vault in `LendingPool` improperly collected
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

When there is a withdrawal from the vault in the `LendingPool`, the proportion of the withdrawn amount that corresponds to the appreciation in the share price is considered to yield and kept as a reward for the protocol to be collected.

The problem is that `vaultRewards.lastSharePrice` is updated even if it has decreased, which means that the protocol might be accruing rewards when it should not, provoking a loss of funds for the depositors.

Consider the following scenario:

- 1,000 tokens are deposited in the vault, being a share price of 1.
- Share price decreases to 0.9 due to unrealized losses.
- 100 tokens are withdrawn and `lastSharePrice` is updated to 0.9.
- Share price increases to 0.95.
- 500 tokens are withdrawn and it is considered that a 0.05 appreciation in the share price has occurred, so 25 tokens are kept as rewards for the protocol to be collected.
- The protocol has collected 25 tokens as rewards, while the position in the vault is still at a loss.

## Recommendations

Update `lastSharePrice` only when the share price increases.
summary: The report discusses a bug in the `LendingPool` where a proportion of the withdrawn amount is considered as yield and kept as a reward for the protocol. The issue is that the `lastSharePrice` is being updated even when it decreases, causing the protocol to accrue rewards when it should not. This can lead to a loss of funds for depositors. The report recommends updating `lastSharePrice` only when the share price increases.

title: [H-01] Malicious users can extend the reward period
summary: This bug report is about a medium severity issue in the GaugeRewardDistributor contract. The problem is that anyone can deposit a small amount of rewards, which can dilute the reward rate and make it harder for normal users to receive their expected rewards. The code snippet provided shows that when the function `_handleRewardNotification` is executed, it updates the `rd.rate` and `rd.periodFinish` variables, which can cause issues if the function is called multiple times. The report recommends revisiting the distribution logic and provides a suggested change to the code.

title: [C-08] Incorrect lock duration causes extended voting power retention
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `getVotingPowerAtBlock()` function in the `PowerCheckpoint` library incorrectly uses `maxLockDuration` as the `totalTime` parameter instead of the actual lock duration (`lock.end - lock.start`) when calculating the decayed balance using `LockManager.calculateExpectedBalanceAfterDecay()`.

```solidity
return LockManager.calculateExpectedBalanceAfterDecay(
    lock.amount,
    state.lockState.maxLockDuration, // @audit incorrect
    timeElapsed,
    state.lockState.maxLockDuration
);
```

This causes the following issues:

1. User locks tokens for a minimum duration (7 days).
2. After the duration ends, `getVotingPowerAtBlock()` calculates decay using maximum lock duration (1 year).
3. The user will have 10x voting power.

Note: `PowerCheckpoint.getPastTotalSupply()` contain the same issue.

## Recommendations

Use `lock.end - lock.start` as the `totalTime`:

```solidity
return LockManager.calculateExpectedBalanceAfterDecay(
    lock.amount,
    lock.end - lock.start,  // Use actual lock duration
    timeElapsed,
    state.lockState.maxLockDuration
);
```
summary: The reported bug is a high severity issue that is likely to occur. The `getVotingPowerAtBlock()` function in the `PowerCheckpoint` library is not working correctly. It is using the wrong parameter when calculating the decayed balance, resulting in incorrect voting power calculations. This happens when a user locks tokens for a minimum duration of 7 days and then the function calculates decay using the maximum lock duration of 1 year. This results in 10 times more voting power for the user. The recommended solution is to use the actual lock duration instead of the maximum lock duration when calculating the decayed balance.

title: [C-07] Users can accumulate rewards after lock expiry due to stale user block
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `veRAACToken` contract incorrectly allows users to continue accumulating rewards even after their token lock period has expired. This occurs because the reward calculation relies on `uData.lastUserBlock` which remains unchanged unless explicitly updated through user actions like locking or unlocking tokens:

```solidity
    function getNewUserRewards(
        address user,
        address token
    ) internal view returns (uint256) {
        UserRewardData memory uData = userRewardData[user][token];
        uint256 userPower = balanceOfAt(user, uData.lastUserBlock);
        uint256 rewardPerTokenStored = rewardPerToken(token);
        return
            (userPower *
                (rewardPerTokenStored - uData.userRewardPerTokenPaid)) /
            PRECISION;
    }
```

For example:

1. User locks RAAC tokens, setting `uData.lastUserBlock` to the current block.
2. Lock period expires, reducing user's voting power to 0.
3. User continues to earn rewards based on their historical balance at `lastUserBlock`.
4. Rewards accumulate indefinitely until the user performs an action that triggers `updateReward()`.

This creates a vulnerability where users can earn rewards without maintaining the required locked position, effectively stealing rewards from other users.

## Recommendations

Use an epoch-based reward calculation, where a new epoch begins each time `notifyRewardAmount()` is called. Calculate each user's updated rewards based on the `lastDistributionBlock` for that specified epoch.
summary: The bug report describes a high severity issue where users are able to continue earning rewards even after their token lock period has expired. This is because the reward calculation relies on a value that does not change unless the user performs certain actions. This creates a vulnerability where users can earn rewards without maintaining the required locked position, potentially stealing rewards from other users. To fix this, the recommendation is to use an epoch-based reward calculation where rewards are calculated based on the last distribution block for that specific epoch.

title: [C-06] Stale total voting power snapshot leads to incorrect reward distribution
summary: The bug report discusses an issue with the `veRAACToken` contract, which is used to distribute rewards to users based on their voting power. The `rewardPerToken()` function, which calculates rewards, is using an outdated snapshot of the total voting power, leading to incorrect distribution of rewards. This can result in users receiving more rewards than they should, causing the system to run out of reward tokens. The report recommends updating the function to use the current total voting power instead of the snapshot.

title: [C-05] Double-counting stored rewards causes reward inflation
summary:
Summary:

A bug has been found in the `BaseGauge.sol` file where the `_calculatePendingRewards()` function is returning the entire stored rewards plus the newly calculated share instead of just the delta. This is causing the rewards to be double-counted and leading to an exponential inflation of rewards for users. The bug has been identified in the code and a recommendation has been made to only return the delta or overwrite the existing balance instead of adding to it.

title: [C-04] Failure to update user integral enables double reward accrual
summary:
The bug report is about an issue in the code of a smart contract called `BaseGauge.sol`. This contract has a function called `updateUserRewards()` which is supposed to update the rewards for users. However, there is a problem where the function does not update a key variable called `integral`, which causes a discrepancy when another function called `claimRewards()` is called later. This results in users receiving double the amount of rewards they should be getting. 

The cause of the issue is that the `updateUserRewards()` function updates some variables, but not the `integral` variable. This causes the `claimRewards()` function to think that no rewards have been claimed, resulting in it issuing a second round of rewards. This can be exploited by attackers to drain the reward pool.

The recommendation to fix this issue is to add a line of code after line 368 in the `updateUserRewards()` function to update the `integral` variable. This will prevent the discrepancy and ensure that users receive the correct amount of rewards.

title: [C-03] Incorrect boost application leads to inflated rewards in gauges
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `BaseGauge` contract implements a reward distribution system where users can stake tokens and earn rewards based on their stake amount and boost multiplier. The boost mechanism is designed to incentivize long-term staking by providing increased rewards to users who lock their tokens. However, there is an issue in how the boost is applied when calculating pending rewards, leading to users receiving significantly fewer rewards than intended.

The issue lies in the `_calculatePendingRewards()` function of `BaseGauge`, which is responsible for determining how many rewards a user has earned since their last update. While the function correctly calculates the base reward share proportional to the user's stake, it fails to properly apply the boost multiplier to this share.

The core of the problem is in how the boost value returned from `_applyBoost()` is used. The boost value is expressed in basis points (e.g., 10000 = 1.0x boost, 20000 = 2.0x boost), but the function directly assigns this basis point value as the user's share without converting it to the actual boosted amount:

```solidity
uint256 boost = _applyBoost(user, userShare);
userShare = boost > 0 ? boost : userShare;
```

This is incorrect because it replaces the user's actual share (which is a large number of tokens) with just the boost multiplier (which is in basis points). For example, if a user should receive 100e18 tokens with a 2.0x boost (20000 basis points), they would instead receive just 20000 tokens.

This contrasts with the correct implementation in `_updateUserReward()` which properly applies the boost:

```solidity
uint256 workingBalance = (workingBalance * boost) / WEIGHT_PRECISION;
```

### Proof of Concept

1. Alice stakes 1000e18 tokens in the gauge.
2. The gauge accumulates rewards over time.
3. When Alice checks her pending rewards:
   - Base reward calculation: 100e18 tokens earned.
   - Boost calculation returns 20000 (2.0x boost).
   - Instead of receiving 200e18 tokens (1000 * 2.0).
   - Alice only receives 20000 tokens (the boost basis points value).

## Recommendations

Modify the boost application in `_calculatePendingRewards()` to match the calculation in `_updateUserReward()`:

```diff
- userShare = boost > 0 ? boost : userShare;
+ userShare = boost > 0 ? (userShare * boost) / WEIGHT_PRECISION : userShare;
```
summary: The `BaseGauge` contract has a bug that affects how rewards are calculated and distributed to users who stake tokens. This bug can result in users receiving significantly fewer rewards than intended. The problem lies in how the boost multiplier is applied when calculating pending rewards. Instead of properly converting the boost value to the actual boosted amount, the function directly assigns the basis point value as the user's share. This means that instead of receiving the correct amount of tokens, users may only receive the basis point value of the boost. To fix this, the boost application in the function needs to be modified to match the calculation in another function.

title: [C-02] `getAssetValue()` does not check if `user` is the owner of the asset
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `getAssetValue()` function in `ERC721AssetAdapter` receives a `user` parameter, but this value is not used to validate that token is deposited in the contract by the user.

As this function is used in `LendingPool._validateBorrow()`, users can borrow against assets that they do not own.

## Recommendations

Validate that the `user` is the depositor of the asset in the `getAssetValue()` and `getWithdrawValue()` functions.
summary: The bug report addresses a problem with the `getAssetValue()` function in the `ERC721AssetAdapter` code. This function has a parameter called `user`, but it is not being used to check if the token being deposited in the contract belongs to that user. This can lead to a high impact and likelihood of users being able to borrow assets that they do not actually own. The report recommends adding validation to the `user` parameter in both the `getAssetValue()` and `getWithdrawValue()` functions to prevent this issue.

title: [C-01] Users can steal lending interest
summary: This report describes a bug in the RAAC system that allows malicious users to earn more interest than expected by transferring RToken from one account to another. This is because when RToken is transferred, the pending interest is not processed and the liquidity index is not updated. To fix this, the report recommends accruing the pending interest and updating the user's index when RToken is transferred.

title: `BebopRouter::settle` lets relayers steal `exactIn` user input by substituting unbound PMM calldata that under-delivers or redirects output
summary: The report describes a bug in the gasless `BebopRouter::settle` function. This function allows the user to authorize the router to pull a certain amount of input tokens, but the relayer can manipulate the output by supplying raw PMM calldata. The router checks the signature of the user and the router, but the hash only includes certain fields and not the `bebopPmmCalldata` bytes. This allows a malicious relayer to exploit the mismatch between the authorized input and the manipulated output in three ways: under-filling the order, redirecting the output, or delivering native tokens instead of ERC-20 tokens. This can result in the user losing their authorized input without receiving the expected output. The bug has been fixed in the `Bebop` code, and the fix has been verified by `Cyfrin`.

title: [H-31] Rewards boosts distribute more rewards than available
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** Medium

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

`BaseGauge` applies a boost over the rewards of the users, but these extra rewards received by the users are not backed by new deposits of reward tokens.

As a result, more rewards than the available tokens are distributed over the period. This will cause some users might not be able to claim their rewards.

## Recommendations

The boost system should be either removed or redesign to ensure that the gauge rewards are always backed by the available tokens.
summary: The BaseGauge feature is causing a problem where users are receiving extra rewards without any new deposits of reward tokens. This could result in some users not being able to claim their rewards. It is recommended that the boost system is either removed or redesigned to make sure that the rewards are always backed by the available tokens. This will prevent any issues with claiming rewards in the future.

title: [H-30] `getNextCycleStart()` returns incorrect value at the end of a cycle
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `GaugeRewardsDistributor.getNextCycleStart()` function.
