However, there is some discussion about the presence of a fallback function that could potentially create new pools, leading to a debate about the severity of the bug.

title: A user’s balance can be bonded against their will
summary:
This bug report describes a medium difficulty issue related to cryptography. The problem occurs when a user approves the response module to handle their tokens, which can result in all of their tokens being bonded without their consent. This happens when a user proposes a response to a request and approves the response module to handle their deposited token balance. However, the function that allows this also allows the dispute module to provide an arbitrary proposer address, which can be controlled by anyone. This means that anyone can create a malicious request and use it to bond another user's tokens. 

To fix this issue, the report recommends enforcing that only specific and approved modules can be used for each request. In the long term, it suggests creating a specification for access control and data validation to guide future development and reduce the attack surface of the system. It also suggests redesigning the system so that each oracle only has one set of modules, which would simplify access control and further reduce the risk of this type of attack.

title: Use of low-level calls can compromise access control
summary: The report discusses a low-level data validation bug found in the CallbackModule, MultipleCallbacksModule, and CircuitResolverModule contracts. These contracts are used in the overall protocol and have substantial permissions. Malicious users can exploit this bug to steal user funds by calling functions in the AccountingExtension and BondEscalationAccounting contracts, as well as the Oracle contract. The bug can be exploited by setting a specific callback target and data, allowing the malicious user to transfer funds to themselves. The report recommends replacing the arbitrary low-level callbacks with a specific callback interface in the short term and not allowing calls from privileged contracts to user-chosen endpoints in the long term.

title: Dispute pledges for a NoResolution dispute can be stolen by anyone
summary: This bug report is about a medium difficulty issue related to data validation in the BondEscalationAccounting contract. The contract allows users to withdraw their pledged tokens after a dispute has been resolved. However, there is a flaw in the code that allows anyone to steal all of the pledged tokens if the dispute status is marked as "NoResolution". This can be exploited by creating multiple accounts and calling the claimEscalationReward function for each one. The report recommends a short-term fix and a long-term improvement for this issue.

title: Ine�ective access control can lead to user funds being stolen
description:
## Vulnerability Report

## Difficulty
Low

## Type
Data Validation

## Affected Files
`prophet-modules/solidity/contracts/extensions/{BondEscalationAccounting.sol, AccountingExtension.sol}`

## Description
The `onlyAllowedModule` modifier used as access control in the `BondEscalationAccounting` contract can be easily bypassed by creating an arbitrary request in the Oracle contract. This allows a malicious user to steal the token balance of any user for any token used inside the system.

The `BondEscalationAccounting` module allows users to deposit and pledge funds to be used for bond escalation. Several of the contract’s functions use the `onlyAllowedModule` modifier to prevent arbitrary users from calling the contract functions and updating important state variables. The `AccountingExtension` uses the same modifier to provide access control to its functions:

```solidity
modifier onlyAllowedModule(bytes32 _requestId) {
    if (!ORACLE.allowedModule(_requestId, msg.sender)) revert AccountingExtension_UnauthorizedModule();
    _;
}
```

**Figure 5.1:** The `onlyAllowedModule` modifier in `AccountingExtension.sol`

The `allowedModule` function of the Oracle contract will look up if the address is included in the request modules and returns a Boolean. However, since anyone can create any arbitrary request in the Oracle contract, this means that the modifier can be easily bypassed.

A malicious user could exploit this issue to:
- Pledge to a dispute on behalf of someone else using any arbitrary token and amount.
- Settle a bond escalation to freeze or steal assets.
- Bond a user’s tokens against their will in the `AccountingExtension`.
- Trigger an underflow in the `claimEscalationReward` function.
- Release a pledge for any dispute to steal assets.

## Exploit Scenario
A dispute is escalated and has gathered 100,000 USDC in value, pledged by various users. Eve notices the incorrect access control and creates a request that has her own address as an allowed module. She calls the `releasePledge` function and steals all of the tokens from this contract by bypassing the `onlyAllowedModule` access control. She repeats this action for any dispute that has a non-zero value of pledges in order to drain the system.

## Recommendations
- **Short term:** Set the address of the modules that are expected to call functions from the `BondEscalationAccounting` and `AccountingExtension` contracts when deploying the contracts. Replace the `onlyAllowedModule` modifier with an access control that ensures that only one specific contract can call each function.
  
- **Long term:** Retroactively create an access control and data validation specification for the system. Use this specification to guide the further development of your testing suite and evaluate how access control can be modified to reduce the attack surface of the system. Consider redesigning the system so that each oracle has only one set of modules to reduce the attack surface and simplify access controls.
summary: This bug report is about a low difficulty issue in the data validation process of the BondEscalationAccounting contract. The report states that the onlyAllowedModule modifier used for access control can be easily bypassed by creating an arbitrary request in the Oracle contract. This allows a malicious user to steal the token balance of any user for any token used in the system. The report also explains that this issue can be exploited in various ways, such as freezing or stealing assets, bonding a user's tokens without their consent, and triggering an underflow. The report recommends short-term solutions, such as setting specific addresses for modules and replacing the onlyAllowedModule modifier with a more secure access control. It also suggests long-term solutions, such as creating a data validation specification for the system and redesigning it to reduce the attack surface.

title: Arbitrary request data can be provided to module functions in order to bypass validation
summary: This bug report discusses a low difficulty bug related to access controls in the Wonderland Prophet system. Specifically, it is possible for users to bypass module validation by not validating the requestId against the provided dispute data. This can lead to various issues such as bypassing voting deadlines, revealing windows, and manipulating dispute resolution. The report also mentions that this issue is present in multiple components of the system. The suggested exploit scenario involves a user creating a request for pricing data and another user manipulating the result of the dispute by deploying their own ERC20 token and using it in the pledgeAgainstDispute function. The report recommends short-term and long-term solutions to address this issue.

title: Lack of contract existence check on low-level calls
summary: This report discusses a bug related to data validation in the Wonderland Prophet software. The bug occurs when the software uses a low-level call to a contract that does not exist or has been destroyed. This call will still return a successful result, even though no code is actually executed. This can lead to unexpected behavior and potential exploits. The report recommends implementing a contract existence check before each low-level call and reviewing the Solidity documentation for potential pitfalls.

title: No LSTs transfer on node operator withdrawals resulting in stuck funds and loss for node operators
summary: This bug report highlights an issue in the `OperatorStakingPool` code, where node operators are unable to withdraw their staked LST tokens. This results in the funds being stuck and can lead to a loss for the operators. The code responsible for withdrawing the tokens does not transfer the LST tokens back to the operator, leaving them stuck in the `OperatorStakingPool`. This issue can be reproduced by running a test script and can potentially happen every time the `withdraw` function is called. The impact of this bug is considered medium, as it locks the funds temporarily and can be resolved by the owner redistributing the funds back to the operators. The report recommends adding a transfer function in the `_withdraw` method to send the LST tokens back to the operator after updating the total shares.

title: Unaccounted Amount Trimming
summary: The report describes a bug in the Spoke.instantActions code that causes assets to become stuck in the WormholeTunnel and renders the spoke in a pending state. This is due to the code not accounting for the trimming behavior of the Wormhole token bridge, which normalizes token amounts to 8 decimals. As a result, any extra decimal places are removed, but the code fails to account for this and the dust remains in the WormholeTunnel. This accumulation of dust is undesirable and can cause cross-chain transaction failures. The bug has been fixed in the latest patch.

title: Incorrect Logical Operator In Tranche Validation
description:
##### Description

The `getTrancheAmountFractionInWad` and `getTrancheFeeFractionInWad` functions from ProtectionLibV1 aims to extract a fraction value associated with a specific tranche from a packed uint256 encoding. They both uses the same condition to validate the tranche.

```
        if ((tranche < 1) && (tranche > numberOfTranches)) revert Errors.InvalidTrancheNumber(tranche);
```

  

The condition uses the logical AND operator (`&&`), which means the revert statement will only be executed if both conditions are true simultaneously. A tranche number cannot be both less than 1 and greater than `numberOfTranches` at the same time. These two conditions are mutually exclusive.

As a result, invalid tranche numbers that are either less than 1 or greater than `numberOfTranches` will not trigger the revert, potentially leading to incorrect calculations or out-of-bounds errors later in the function.

##### BVSS

[AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:N/A:M/D:L/Y:N/R:N/S:C (7.0)](/bvss?q=AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:N/A:M/D:L/Y:N/R:N/S:C)

##### Recommendation

The correct logical operator to use in this context is the OR operator (`||`):

```
if ((tranche < 1) || (tranche > numberOfTranches)) revert Errors.InvalidTrancheNumber(tranche);
```

##### Remediation

**SOLVED:** The **Concrete team** fixed the issue as recommended.

##### Remediation Hash

<https://github.com/Blueprint-Finance/sc_hub-and-spokes-libraries/commit/b006fbf82e3e4f5c230dbe3f28220d93a9ee1b44>

##### References

[Blueprint-Finance/sc\_hub-and-spokes-libraries/src/libraries/ProtectionLibV1.sol#L385](https://github.com/Blueprint-Finance/sc_hub-and-spokes-libraries/blob/db3349a45ff583af41cc2f8879eb8dd9f63dfba2/src/libraries/ProtectionLibV1.sol#L385)

[Blueprint-Finance/sc\_hub-and-spokes-libraries/src/libraries/ProtectionLibV1.sol#L392](https://github.com/Blueprint-Finance/sc_hub-and-spokes-libraries/blob/db3349a45ff583af41cc2f8879eb8dd9f63dfba2/src/libraries/ProtectionLibV1.sol#L392)
summary: This bug report is about two functions in the ProtectionLibV1 library, `getTrancheAmountFractionInWad` and `getTrancheFeeFractionInWad`, that are not working as intended. The functions are supposed to extract a fraction value associated with a specific tranche from a packed uint256 encoding, but the condition used to validate the tranche is incorrect. This means that invalid tranche numbers may not trigger an error, potentially leading to incorrect calculations or errors later in the function. The recommended solution is to use the OR operator instead of the AND operator in the condition. The issue has been fixed by the Concrete team and the fix can be found on GitHub.

title: Incorrect Encoding Due To Operation Precedence
summary: The function `encodeFeesAreBorrowedAndCreditInterestsAccrueOnUser` is supposed to combine two numbers into one, but there is a mistake in how it is coded. This causes the second number to be encoded incorrectly and the function `decodeCreditInterestsAccrueOnUser` to always return false. A suggestion is made to fix the code by adding parentheses and type casting. The issue has been solved by the Concrete team by removing the function from the contract. The code that was changed can be found in the references section.

title: Inconsistent Bit Shifting Leading To Incorrect Permission Handling
summary: The Uint8CodecLib contract has a bug in the permission management system. The `_updateNthByte` function treats the position as a bit index, while the `_decodeNthByte` function treats it as a byte index. This causes the encoding and decoding processes to operate on different bit positions, resulting in incorrect permission values being stored and retrieved. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate the issue. The BVSS score for this bug is 9.4, indicating a high severity. The recommendation is to standardize the bit-shifting operations in both functions to use consistent units. The issue has been fixed by the Concrete team and the remediation hash can be found on GitHub.

title: Protection Claim After Lender-Side Liquidation Causes Funds To Be Locked
summary: The protocol allows users to protect their positions against risks that could lead to liquidation. However, there is a bug where if a user's position is liquidated on the lender side, they can still claim protection funds. This results in the funds becoming trapped within the contract and the position becoming unrecoverable. The recommended solution is to update the foreclosure logic to handle this scenario and prevent users from claiming protection on already liquidated positions. The Concrete team has solved the issue by adding a function to handle expired policies and locked funds due to lender side liquidation.

title: Incorrect Borrowing Modality Leads to Broken Functionality
summary: The `supplyBorrowAndProtect` function allows users to supply liquidity, borrow, and open a protection policy in a single transaction. However, there is a bug where if the `ONLY_SECOND_STEP` modality is used, the transaction will fail unexpectedly. This is because the funds were not sent to the Blueprint beforehand. To fix this, the `ONLY_SECOND_STEP` modality should be replaced with the `ONLY_FIRST_STEP` modality. This bug has been solved by the Concrete team by removing the `supplyAndProtect` and `supplyBorrowAndProtect` functions from the User Blueprint Base contract.

title: Incorrect Protection Period Checks May Deny Valid Claims
summary: The `canClaimProtection` function in the `UserBase` contract is used to determine if a user can claim protection under a specific Blueprint. However, there is a bug in the function that makes it return false when it should be returning true. This is because the condition used to check if the protection period has expired is inverted. This means that legitimate claims can be incorrectly denied, which undermines the protection mechanism. To fix this, the logic in the function needs to be corrected by changing the direction of the inequality. The issue has been solved by the Concrete team and the fix can be found in the referenced commit.

title: Lack Of Protection Policy Validation
summary: The CCCM (Concrete Credit Control Module) has a bug that allows users to make unauthorized protection claims, which can lead to financial losses and decrease the integrity of the protocol. This is because the protection system does not validate the claim against the encoded protection data, and does not enforce checks for claims within a specified buffer. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate the issue. The BVSS score for this vulnerability is 7.5. The recommendation is to implement comprehensive validation checks for protection policy data to ensure all claims adhere to the encoded parameters. The Concrete team has solved the issue by adding additional checks to the protocol to verify protection data consistency and ensure claim amounts and fees are within bounds. The remediation hash can be found at <https://github.com/Blueprint-Finance/sc_spokes-v1/commit/164bc71f59d5c712d616531823f7055267e2faeb>.

title: Incorrect Function Call Leads to Loss Of Claim Router Assets
summary: The FundsRequesterConnector contract is used to manage interactions with the funds requester and handle foreclosure and debt repayment processes. However, there is a bug in the contract that mistakenly calls the wrong function, leading to a situation where users can exploit the protocol and receive more tokens than they initially deposited. This can result in significant financial losses for the system. The bug has been fixed by the Concrete team and users are advised to ensure that the correct function is invoked in the mentioned functions.

title: Incorrect Namespace Used On Boolean Commit
description:
##### Description

In the `RegistryManager` contract, the implementation of the `_commitNewBoolForAddressOnRemoteRegistry` function incorrectly uses the `replaceKeyNamespace(BYTES32, key)` function when updating the namespace. Since the function deals with boolean values, it should use the `replaceKeyNamespace(BOOL, key)` function instead.

Using the wrong namespace can lead to inconsistencies in how the storage is accessed and managed, potentially causing incorrect data retrieval or unintended behavior in the protocol. This misalignment between the data type and the namespace could affect how boolean values are stored and accessed, causing logical errors in the contract.

##### BVSS

[AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:H/A:N/D:N/Y:N/R:N/S:U (7.5)](/bvss?q=AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:H/A:N/D:N/Y:N/R:N/S:U)

##### Recommendation

Update the implementation of `_commitNewBoolForAddressOnRemoteRegistry` to use the correct namespace replacement function.

##### Remediation

**SOLVED**: The **Concrete team** solved the issue by removing the function.

##### Remediation Hash

26faabb856f98d774ddbe689f6ee2327d0c538f5
summary: The `RegistryManager` contract has a bug where the `_commitNewBoolForAddressOnRemoteRegistry` function uses the wrong namespace when dealing with boolean values. This can cause inconsistencies and incorrect data retrieval, potentially leading to logical errors in the contract. The recommendation is to update the function to use the correct namespace replacement. The issue has been solved by the Concrete team by removing the function. The remediation hash for this bug is 26faabb856f98d774ddbe689f6ee2327d0c538f5.

title: Missing Access Control in Policy termination blueprint
description:
##### Description

The functions `forecloseLite`, `forecloseBeforeExpiration`, and `reclaimOrForecloseAfterExpiration` in the `PolicyTerminationBlueprint` contract lack any form of access control protection. Without proper access control, any entity can call these functions to trigger foreclosure or reclamation operations on the remote chain for any loan, irrespective of whether they have the authority to do so.

This vulnerability can lead to several critical issues: - Unauthorized users can trigger foreclosure actions on loans they do not own. - Malicious actors could modify loan fee values, triggering unintended consequences across the system. - The protocol could suffer financial losses or inconsistencies by allowing foreclosure operations without proper checks.

Currently, there are no restrictions that limit who can call these functions, which opens up the system to exploitation. These functions should either be protected by access control or restricted to loan owners.

##### BVSS

[AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:C/A:C/D:C/Y:C/R:N/S:C (10.0)](/bvss?q=AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:C/A:C/D:C/Y:C/R:N/S:C)

##### Recommendation

1. **Implement Access Control:** Use role-based access control to limit who can call these sensitive functions. For instance, restricting these functions to be called only by the `BLUEPRINT_CALLER` role.
2. **Restrict to Loan Owner:** Alternatively, the functions should only be callable by the owner of the loan to prevent unauthorized access. This could be achieved by checking the loan ownership before proceeding.
3. **Combining Both Approaches:** The protocol can implement both access control and ownership checks for added security, ensuring only specific roles (like bots) or the loan owner can trigger these actions.

By applying these restrictions, the protocol ensures that only authorized entities can perform sensitive operations, reducing the risk of malicious exploitation and preserving the integrity of the loan management system.

##### Remediation

**SOLVED**: The **Concrete team** solved the issue by adding the access control.

##### Remediation Hash

26faabb856f98d774ddbe689f6ee2327d0c538f5
summary: This report highlights a vulnerability in the `PolicyTerminationBlueprint` contract that allows anyone to trigger foreclosure or reclamation operations on loans without proper authorization. This can lead to unauthorized access, financial losses, and system inconsistencies. The suggested solutions are to implement access control, restrict the functions to only be callable by the loan owner, or combine both approaches for added security. The issue has been solved by the Concrete team by adding access control.

title: Lack of Access Control in Pong handlers
description:
##### Description

The `BasePongHandler` and `PongHandlerImplementation` contracts lack proper access control mechanisms on critical functions like `pongHandler`, `registryPongHandler`, and `configPongHandler`. These functions can be called by any external address, allowing arbitrary users to commit data into important namespaces (`REGISTRY` and `COMMON`) using any known `packetId`.

This means an attacker could: - Commit data with a success status when it should not be committed. - Prevent valid commits by passing an invalid `success` value. - Clear the `ACTIVE_PACKETS_HASHES` entry, causing the `packetId` to be processed incorrectly, leading to protocol state inconsistencies.

This vulnerability could result in unauthorized modifications of protocol-critical data, impacting the reliability and security of cross-chain communication or other inter-contract processes.

##### Proof of Concept

```
function test_pong_handler() external {
    vm.prank(ADMIN);
    accessControlManager.grantRole(bytes4(keccak256("COMMON_STAGE")), address(pongHandlerImplementation));

    bytes32 packetId = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("test"));
    pongHandlerImplementation.pongHandler(packetId, 0);
}

```

##### BVSS

[AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:C/A:C/D:C/Y:C/R:N/S:C (10.0)](/bvss?q=AO:A/AC:L/AX:L/C:N/I:C/A:C/D:C/Y:C/R:N/S:C)

##### Recommendation

Introduce strict access control, ensuring that only authorized addresses (e.g., app chain relayers) are allowed to call these functions. Implement an `onlyRole` modifier for these functions, or restrict access to an account that has validated the remote transaction event status.

##### Remediation

**SOLVED**: The **Concrete team** solved the issue by adding access control. A new role, `PONG_HANDLER_CALLER`, has been created and is required to call any pong handler function.

##### Remediation Hash

26faabb856f98d774ddbe689f6ee2327d0c538f5
summary: The `BasePongHandler` and `PongHandlerImplementation` contracts have a bug that allows anyone to access important functions, such as `pongHandler`, `registryPongHandler`, and `configPongHandler`. This means that an attacker could modify critical data or prevent valid commits. The team has fixed the issue by adding access control measures and creating a new role, `PONG_HANDLER_CALLER`, to limit access to these functions.

title: Incorrect Balance Updates in ERC721Logic and Internals
summary: The `update` function in the `ERC721LogicContract` and `ERC721_Internals` contracts has a critical issue where token balances are not properly updated in storage. This can cause discrepancies in ownership and token balances, leading to potential issues in the protocol's token transfer system. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate this issue. To fix the problem, the `update` logic should be modified to update balances in storage, and the correct balance keys should be used for both the `from` and `to` addresses. The Concrete team has solved this issue by removing the `ERC721Logic` contract.

title: Incorrect Fragment Count Leading to External Call Error
summary: The report shows that the `extractSubset` function is using the wrong value for `temp.lastFrgmtCnt`. This is causing the function to select the wrong packet for an external call, resulting in incorrect data being used. A test was done to prove this issue and a recommendation is made to increment the `temp.lastFrgmtCnt` value by one to fix the problem. The Concrete team has solved the issue by making this change and the remediation hash is provided.

title: Packets Error Handling: EVM revert in ABI Decoding
summary:
**Bug Report Summary: EVM Error Encountered due to Incorrect Structure of ModifiedPacket in Solidity Code**

The bug report describes an issue where an EVM error is encountered in the Solidity code due to the incorrect structure of the `modifiedPacket` variable. This variable is used in the `abi.decode` function to extract an address and bytes data, but the current structure does not match the expected format. This results in an EVM error during the decoding operation. The root cause of the issue is identified as the insufficient length of `modifiedPacket` and the incorrect target address. The recommended solution is to fix the structure of `modifiedPacket` to ensure it contains valid target addresses and data. The Concrete team has already solved this issue by properly extracting the `calldata` from a packet and calling the target address with it.

title: H-4: Liquidity is incorrectly calculated during `addLiquidity()` for V3AMO, causing DoS.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the calculation of liquidity in a cryptocurrency protocol called SolidlyV3. The problem is that when adding liquidity, the calculation is incorrect and can lead to a denial of service attack. This is caused by a mistake in the way the amount of liquidity is calculated, which can be exploited by attackers who can easily add positions to the pool. This can cause the function to fail and also affect the stability of the currency. The report includes a detailed explanation of the root cause and a proof of concept for the bug. To fix this issue, the report suggests using a different library for calculating liquidity.

title: H-3: V3AMO integration with V3 does not collect LP fees when burning liquidity.
summary: The bug report is about an issue with the V3AMO integration in V3 that prevents the collection of LP fees when burning liquidity. This issue was found by user pkqs90. The root cause of the issue is that the fees are not updated correctly in SolidlyV3, which is a fork of UniswapV3. In UniswapV3, the fees are calculated and collected within the Pool, but in SolidlyV3, they are not updated at all. The fees are now distributed through a separate contract called RewardsDistributor, and a new function needs to be added to retrieve the fees for SolidlyV3AMO. This bug prevents the retrieval of LP fees for SolidlyV3AMO.

title: H-2: V2AMO is not compatible with Velodrome/Aerodrome.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the compatibility of the SolidlyV2AMO technology with the Velodrome/Aerodrome pools. According to the documentation, the SolidlyV2AMO should work with these pools, but it is currently not compatible. The root cause of the issue is identified as two parts of the integration with Velodrome/Aerodrome being buggy: the gauge and router. The main differences between the Aerodrome interface and the SolidlyV2AMO interface are highlighted. The impact of this bug is that the SolidlyV2AMO does not function as expected with Aerodrome/Velodrome. There is currently no mitigation or proof of concept provided for this bug.

title: H-1: Boost buyback burns incorrect amount of liquidity
description:
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-10-axion-judging/issues/114 

## Found by 
0x37, carrotsmuggler, pkqs90, s1ce, spark1, vinica\_boy
### Summary

The function `_unfarmBuyBurn` in the V3AMO contract is a public function open to everyone and calculates the amount of liquidity to burn from the pool. This function basically burns LP positions to take out liquidity and uses the usd to buy up boost tokens and burns them to raise the price of boost tokens.

The issue is in the `_unfarmBuyBurn` function when it tries to estimate how much liquidity needs to be taken out.

https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-10-axion/blob/main/liquidity-amo/contracts/SolidlyV3AMO.sol#L320-L326

As seen above, first the token reserves of the pool are checked. Then, the `liquidity` to be burnt is calculated from the difference of the reserves.

```solidity
liquidity = (totalLiquidity * (boostBalance - usdBalance)) / (boostBalance + usdBalance);
liquidity = (liquidity * LIQUIDITY_COEFF) / FACTOR;
```

However, this calculation is not valid for V3/CL pools. This is because in V3 pools, single sided liquidity is allowed which adds to the `totalLiquidity` count, but increases the reserves of only 1 token. If a user adds liquidity at a tick lower than the current price, they will be adding only usd to the pool.

For example, lets say the price currently is below peg, at 0.9. Say there are 1000 boost and 900 usd tokens in the pool, similar to a V2 composition. Now, since its a V3 pool, a user can come in and add 100 usd to the pool at a price of 0.5. Since this price is lower than the spot price, only usd will be needed to open this position. Now, the total reserves of both boost and usd are 1000 each, so the calculated `liquidity` amount to be removed will be 0.

Thus the `liquidity` calculated in the contract has absolutely no meaning since it uses the reserves to calculate it, which is not valid for V3 pools. In the best case scenario, this will cause the function to revert and not work. In the worst case scenario, the liquidity calculated will be overestimated and the price will be pushed up even above the peg price. This is possible if users add single sided `boost` to the pool, increasing the `liquidity` amount calculated without changing the price. In this case, the contract assets will be used to force the boost token above peg, and malicious actors can buy the boost token before and sell it after for a handy profit.

### Root Cause

The main cause is that `liquidity` is calculated from the reserves. This is not valid for V3, since it can have single sided liquidity, and thus the reserves does not serve as an indicator of price or in this case the deviation from the peg.

### Internal pre-conditions

None

### External pre-conditions

Any user can add boost-only liquidity to make the contract overestimate the amount of liquidity it needs to burn

### Attack Path

Users can add boost-only liquidity to make the contract overestimate the amount of liquidity it needs to burn. When extra liquidity is burnt and extra boost is bought back and burnt, the price will be pushed up even above the peg price. Users can buy before trigerring this and sell after for profit.

### Impact

Price can be pushed above the peg price

### PoC

None

### Mitigation

Use the `quoteSwap` function to calculate how much needs to be swapped until the target price is hit.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue found in the V3AMO contract. The function `_unfarmBuyBurn` is used to burn liquidity and buy boost tokens to raise their price. However, the calculation used to estimate the amount of liquidity to be taken out is not valid for V3 pools. This is because V3 pools allow for single-sided liquidity, which increases the reserves of only one token. This means that the calculated `liquidity` amount has no meaning and can cause the function to revert or overestimate the amount of liquidity to be removed. This can be exploited by malicious actors to push the boost token price above the peg price and make a profit. The root cause of this issue is the use of reserves to calculate `liquidity`, which is not valid for V3 pools. The report suggests using the `quoteSwap` function to calculate the amount of liquidity to be swapped.

title: Sender can brick stream by forcing overﬂow in debt calculation
summary: The report discusses a bug found in the SablierFlow smart contract, specifically in the _ongoingDebtOf() internal function. The bug occurs when the function calculates the scaledOngoingDebt by multiplying the seconds that have passed since the last snapshot by the rate per second. If the result of this multiplication is greater than uint128, it will overflow and cause the contract to revert. This can happen even with a small balance of tokens, as long as the ratePerSecond is set to a high value. This bug can lead to the permanent loss of funds and can be exploited by a sender to lock the recipient's funds or accidentally set a high ratePerSecond. The report recommends using uint256 for scaledOngoingDebt and carrying this type through all functions until it is compared to the balance. The bug has been fixed in PR 296 and confirmed by Cantina Managed. The risk level of this bug is considered to be medium.

title: [H-03] `order.amount` not accounted when filling
summary: The bug report is about two functions, `fillAskOrder()` and `fillBidOrder()`, which are not working properly when trying to trade more than one token. The function `fillAskOrder()` is supposed to take `order.amount` as its value, but it does not account for this value when executing the trade. This means that the function is only able to trade one token at a time. There is another function, `fulfillMultipleOrders()`, which does account for `order.amount` and allows for trading with multiple tokens. The recommendation is to fix the issue in the necessary functions to allow for trading with more than one token.

title: [H-02] Use of `msg.value` inside a loop
summary: The report states that there is a bug in the `batchCommitToMint` function, which is used to call the `commitToMint` function multiple times in a loop. The problem occurs when the same `msg.value` (transaction value) is used in each iteration, causing the transaction to fail due to insufficient funds. The severity of this bug is medium and the likelihood of it occurring is high. To fix this issue, it is recommended to make changes to both functions to prevent the `msg.value` from being used multiple times.

title: [H-01] Signatures can be replayed using different addresses
summary: This report describes a bug in the `commitToMint` function of a smart contract. This bug allows anyone to replay signatures using different addresses, potentially leading to a loss of funds. The severity of this bug is medium and the likelihood of it occurring is high. To fix this issue, it is recommended to include the address of the executor in the hash that is signed, preventing the signature from being valid for other addresses.

title: [H-01] Potential issues that can arise from BGT being reward token
summary:
This bug report describes an issue with the expected reward token for staking on berachain. The token, Bera Governance Token (BGT), is non-transferrable except by specified senders. However, during certain actions such as deposits, withdrawals, and rebalancing, the token is attempted to be transferred to a farming contract, which is not an approved sender. This causes the functions to fail and potentially leaves the claimed rewards stuck in the farming contract. 

The report recommends introducing checks for whitelisted status before transferring tokens and setting the farming contract. This would ensure that only approved contracts can receive the tokens and prevent them from getting stuck. The fix will depend on the protocol's plans for the tokens, but the token's properties should be taken into consideration.

title: [C-01] DoS attack on Aegis Vault when staking is enabled
summary: A bug has been found in the Aegis Vault's staking capability, which is used to earn rewards on the Berachain network. This bug can be exploited by attackers to cause a denial of service (DoS) and freeze the Aegis Vault. The bug occurs when the `preAction` and `postAction` functions interact with the Berachain reward vault. The bug is caused by a vulnerability and a dangerous assumption in the code, which causes the `exit` function to always fail when the caller has a balance delegated by other users. This can be exploited by attackers who delegate their stake to the Aegis Vault, increasing its `delegateTotalStaked` value and causing the `exit` function to revert. This bug can be fixed by using the `withdraw` function instead of `exit` when disabling staking.

title: [H-02] `CDPVault.sol#liquidatePositionBadDebt()` doesn't correctly handle profit and loss
description:
<https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/main/src/CDPVault.sol#L702> 

<https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/main/src/PoolV3.sol#L593>

### Impact

When liquidating bad debt, the profit and loss is not correctly handled. This will cause incorrect accounting to lpETH stakers.

### Bug Description

*Note: This is based on the 2024-07 Loopfi audit [H-12](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi-findings/issues/57) issue. This protocol team applied a fix, but the fix is incomplete.*

There are two issues that needs to be fixed in the new codebase:

1. The `profit` that is passed in `pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, profit, loss);` should actually use `debtData.accruedInterest`. This is because we should first "assume" full debt and interest is paid off, and calculate the loss part independently.

2. The `loss` is correctly calculated in `PoolV3#repayCreditAccount`, but the if-else branch is incorrectly implemented. Currently, it can't handle the case where both profit and loss is non-zero. This would cause a issue that the loss will not be accounted, and will ultimately cause loss to lpETH holders (loss will be implicitly added to the users who hold lpETH) instead of lpETH stakers.

The second fix was also suggested in the original issue, but it isn't applied.

CDPVault.sol:

```solidity
        takeCollateral = position.collateral;
        repayAmount = wmul(takeCollateral, discountedPrice);
        uint256 loss = calcTotalDebt(debtData) - repayAmount;
        uint256 profit;
        if (repayAmount > debtData.debt) {
@>          profit = repayAmount - debtData.debt;
        }
        ...
@>      pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, profit, loss); // U:[CM-11]
        // transfer the collateral amount from the vault to the liquidator
        token.safeTransfer(msg.sender, takeCollateral);
```

PoolV3.sol:

```solidity
    function repayCreditAccount(
        uint256 repaidAmount,
        uint256 profit,
        uint256 loss
    )
        external
        override
        creditManagerOnly // U:[LP-2C]
        whenNotPaused // U:[LP-2A]
        nonReentrant // U:[LP-2B]
    {
        ...
        if (profit > 0) {
            _mint(treasury, _convertToShares(profit)); // U:[LP-14B]
@>      } else if (loss > 0) {
            address treasury_ = treasury;
            uint256 sharesInTreasury = balanceOf(treasury_);
            uint256 sharesToBurn = _convertToShares(loss);
            if (sharesToBurn > sharesInTreasury) {
                unchecked {
                    emit IncurUncoveredLoss({
                        creditManager: msg.sender,
                        loss: _convertToAssets(sharesToBurn - sharesInTreasury)
                    }); // U:[LP-14D]
                }
                sharesToBurn = sharesInTreasury;
            }
            _burn(treasury_, sharesToBurn); // U:[LP-14C,14D]
        }
        ...
    }
```

### Recommended Mitigation Steps

In CDPVault, change to `pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, debtData.accruedInterest, loss)`.

In PoolV3:


summary:
Impact:
The bug affects the accounting of lpETH stakers when liquidating bad debt, causing incorrect calculations and ultimately resulting in loss for lpETH holders. 

Bug Description:
The bug has two issues that need to be fixed. Firstly, the `profit` value being passed in `pool.repayCreditAccount` should use `debtData.accruedInterest` instead of `debtData.debt`. Secondly, the if-else branch in `PoolV3#repayCreditAccount` is not correctly implemented and cannot handle cases where both profit and loss are non-zero. This results in the loss not being accounted for and being implicitly added to lpETH holders instead of lpETH stakers.

Recommended Mitigation Steps:
To fix the bug, the code in CDPVault should be changed to use `pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, debtData.accruedInterest, loss)`. In PoolV3, the code should be modified to handle both profit and loss separately.

title: [H-01] Rewards might be lost due to the error that `_updateRewardIndex()` might advance `lastBalance` without advancing index for a token
description:
The function `_updateRewardIndex()` is used to update the `lastBalance` and `index` of each reward token. This function will be called when a user deposits, withdraws collateral or claims rewards.

However, the function might not advance `index` when `accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0`. This might happen when `totalShares` is too big and `accrued` is too small. One case is that the number of decimals for the reward token is too small.

<https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L74>

For example, the USDC token only has 6 decimals.

Suppose `accrued` = `$100 = 100*10**6`, and `totalShares` `= 200M = 200 * 10** 6 * 10**18`; then we have  `accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0`.

Furthermore, if function `_updateRewardIndex()` is called more frequently, either because a malicious user keeps calling `getRewards()` (the gas fee is low on Arbitrum) or simply because the community is large so there is a high chance that for each block (per 12 seconds on Ethereum), there is someone who calls a `withdraw`/`deposit`/`getRewards` function. As a result, `accrued` could be small, leading to `accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0`. Meanwhile, `_updateRewardIndex()` always advances `lastBalance` when `accrued !=0`:

<https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L78>

This means the accrued rewards are lost! Nobody will receive the rewards since index has not changed.

More importantly, due to the rounding down error for `accrued.divDown(totalShares)`, there is always a slight loss for the rewards, which is accumulative over time.

### Recommended Mitigation Steps

The fix is simple. Calculate `deltaIndex = accrued.divDown(totalShares)` and advance `lastBalance` by `deltaIndex.mulDown(totalShares)`. In this way, `index` and `lastBalance` will always advance in the same pace; in particular if index does not advance, then `lastBalance` will not advance either. The rounding down error is eliminated too since the `lastBalance` will not be `accrued` but by `deltaIndex.mulDown(totalShares)`.

### Assessed type

Math

**[0xtj24 (LoopFi) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi-findings/issues/25#event-14924296502)**

**[0xAlix2 (warden) commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi-findings/issues/25#issuecomment-2471431354):**
 > @Koolex - I agree that this is an issue; however, the audit [docs](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi?tab=readme-ov-file#general-questions) states that the ERC20s that are used by the protocol are WETH and PendleLPs which are both 18 decimals.
> 
>> `ERC20 used by the protocol | WETH, PendleLPs`
> 
> But I'm not sure if that should be considered valid in this context.

**[Koolex (judge) commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi-findings/issues/25#issuecomment-2483641241):**
 > There is another issue here. 
> 
> > malicious user keeps calling `getRewards()`

***
summary: The `_updateRewardIndex()` function is used to update the `lastBalance` and `index` of each reward token when a user deposits, withdraws collateral, or claims rewards. However, there is a bug where the function may not advance the `index` value when `accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0`. This can happen when the total number of shares is too large and the accrued rewards are too small, which can occur if the reward token has a small number of decimals. This bug can result in lost rewards and a slight loss of rewards over time. The recommended fix is to calculate `deltaIndex` and advance `lastBalance` by that amount to ensure that `index` and `lastBalance` always advance at the same pace. There is also an issue with a malicious user repeatedly calling `getRewards()`, which could further exacerbate this bug.

title: [H-12] Adversary can block the counterpart deployment of cross-chain DAOs
summary: The report discusses a bug in the `deploySAFE()` function of the `Deployer` contract which creates a Safe for a DAO. The bug can cause a transaction to fail if another Safe with the same `nonce` has been created on the same chain. This can be exploited by an attacker to prevent the creation of a DAO on another chain. The report suggests a solution to remove the `try/catch` block and precompute the expected address of the Safe to prevent this issue.

title: [H-11] No refund nor retry mechanism for failing cross-chain transactions
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

When performing cross-chain transactions, the transaction may always revert to the destination chain under certain circumstances or for certain values.

Users will deposit tokens or pay fees in the source chain that will be lost when those reverts occur on the destination chain and can't be recovered by them.

For the cross-chain buy operation: The user will deposit tokens on the source chain via `crossChainBuy()`. If `crossChainMint()` reverts, no DAO token will be minted. This may happen for different reasons:

- If the amount is not valid (depends on DAO balance, token price, and distribution amount in the DAO chain)
- If `maxTokensPerUser` would be surpassed
- If `distributionAmount` would be surpassed
- If the total deposit for the user is below or above a limit
- If the user is not whitelisted
- If token gating is applied
- User errors

It is important to note that most of these conditions depend on moving values, and any off-chain validation might be true when sending the source chain transaction, but may not hold when the cross-chain transaction is executed. Validations on the source chain would not be sufficient, as the source of truth is ultimately on the chain to which the DAO contract was deployed.

In addition, this could theoretically happen for cross-chain DAO deployments too, but not likely. A possible revert might be on an invalid `_depositTokenAddress` that can't be queried for its `decimals()` (although the deployment wouldn't make sense with an invalid address). Other checks are performed in `_createERC20DAO()` or `_createERC721DAO()`, but with the same values as for the source chain, so they would have reverted on the original transaction. Other statements in the destination chain should not revert but bear in mind that they would lead to the scenario described in this report.

## Recommendations

Provide a refund mechanism for users who made deposits but didn't receive their DAO tokens. Also, consider allowing to retry messages that may temporarily revert.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with cross-chain transactions, where the transaction may always fail and result in lost tokens or fees for the user. This can happen for various reasons, such as invalid amounts, surpassing limits, or user errors. It is important to note that off-chain validations may not be sufficient, as the source of truth is on the chain where the DAO contract was deployed. The report recommends implementing a refund mechanism for affected users and allowing for retrying of temporarily reverted messages.

title: [H-10] User address may not be accessible on other chains
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

A smart wallet is deployed in one chain and has a specific address. But it is possible that trying to deploy a smart wallet with the same address won't be possible on other chains. For example, if the deployer is not available on the destination chain, or if it is not possible to set the same salt/noce. Also on chains like zkSync that `create` operations will always lead to different addresses with the same deployment parameters. In any of these cases, the user won't be able to control the same address on both chains.

Some cross-chain functions assume that the same address in the source chain will also be controlled on the destination chain.

`crossChainBuy()` sets the receiver of the DAO tokens to `msg.sender`. The tokens might be sent to an address they don't control.

`createERC20DAO()` and `createERC721DAO()` set the same `admins` as the source chain for their cross-chain Safe. So admins might not be able to control the Safe, and not be able to transfer locked funds in the DAO (among other admin functions).

## Recommendations

- For `crossChainBuy()`: A simple mitigation would be allowing cross-chain buy operations just for EOAs. A more robust but complex mitigation would let users set a specific receiver on the destination chain. However, it would have to consider any side effects of such refactoring, as it would open the possibility of minting tokens on behalf of other users, which isn't possible now.
- For `createERC20DAO()`: Allow DAO creators to provide specific `admins` for each deployed cross-chain DAO
summary:
The report highlights a bug in a smart wallet that is deployed on one chain, but may not be able to be deployed on other chains with the same address. This can be due to various reasons, such as the deployer not being available on the destination chain or different deployment parameters. This can result in the user not being able to control the same address on both chains. 

Additionally, certain cross-chain functions assume that the same address on the source chain will also be controlled on the destination chain. However, this may not always be the case, leading to potential issues such as tokens being sent to an address the user does not control, or admins not being able to control the Safe and transfer locked funds in the DAO.

To address these issues, the report recommends implementing a mitigation that only allows cross-chain buy operations for EOAs (externally owned accounts), or allowing users to set a specific receiver on the destination chain. For the `createERC20DAO()` function, it is suggested to allow DAO creators to provide specific admins for each deployed cross-chain DAO.

title: [H-09] DAO creators can avoid paying creation fees
summary: This bug report talks about a problem with two functions called `createERC20DAO()` and `createERC721DAO()`. These functions check if enough tokens were sent as fees using another function called `checkCreateFeesSent()`. The issue is that when no tokens are sent, the transaction still goes through without any error. This is because there is no check to prevent this from happening. Additionally, there is a condition in the code that prevents any errors from happening, even if the transaction is not successful. The recommendation is to add a check to make sure that fees are paid when the DAO is only deployed to the source chain.

title: [H-08] Cross-chain deposits will fail when the deposit token is the native token
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

The `crossChainMint()` function calculates the `_daoBalance` as:

```solidity
uint256 _daoBalance = IERC20(_daoDetails.depositTokenAddress).balanceOf(_daoAddress);
```

The problem is that the cross-chain DAO can be deployed with the native token (defined in the contract as address: `0xEeeeeEeeeEeEeeEeEeEeeEEEeeeeEeeeeeeeEEeE`).

So, anytime a user tries to buy cross-chain DAO tokens, they will deposit tokens but the transaction on the destination chain will always revert as it will try to perform a `balanceOf()` call on a non-existing contract.

## Recommendations

Check the native token balance in case the cross-chain DAO was deployed with it.
summary: This bug report discusses a problem with the `crossChainMint()` function in a cross-chain DAO contract. The function calculates the `_daoBalance` using a `balanceOf()` call on a contract address, but the issue is that the DAO can be deployed with a native token that does not have a contract address. This means that any user trying to buy DAO tokens will have their transaction fail because the function is trying to call `balanceOf()` on a non-existing contract. The recommendation is to check the balance of the native token in case the DAO was deployed with it.

title: [H-07] Imprecise validation of deposit amounts
summary: The report discusses a bug in a blockchain contract that affects the minting operations, which are used to create new tokens. The bug is considered to have a medium impact and a high likelihood of occurring. The report explains that the problem is caused by the way the contract checks the total amount of tokens that have been deposited. The contract checks the balance of the DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) at a specific moment, but this balance can change over time. This means that the total amount raised may not be accurately calculated, which can lead to errors. The report recommends keeping track of the total amount of tokens deposited instead of relying on the balance of the DAO contract. This will ensure more accurate calculations and prevent potential errors.

title: [H-06] Token-gated airdrops don't work with ERC20 DAOs
summary: The `claim()` function in the `Claim` contract is not working properly when used with `ERC20DAO` tokens. This is because the function first checks if the token supports an interface, but `ERC20DAO` does not have this interface. This means that the function will always fail when used with `ERC20DAO` tokens. To fix this, it is suggested to make `ERC20DAO` inherit from `ERC165Upgradeable` or to use `ERC165Checker` to check for interface support.

title: [H-05] Incorrect value will get sent to the commLayer
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

The `factory.createERC20DAO()` function creates cross-chain DAOs using LayerZero. Users can specify msg.value, which is distributed across multiple chains. For example, if there are 5 chains and msg.value is 1000, each chain receives 200. This value is forwarded to the commLayer.

The \_depositChainIds array is intended to manage the distribution across chains. For instance, if a user wants to create a DAO on the primary chain and 2 secondary chains:

- Bob wants to create a DAO on the primary chain (Ethereum) and 2 secondary chains (Binance and Arbitrum One).
- Bob wants to forward 250 value to each secondary chain, so he must pass 500.
- The depositChainIds array would be:

```solidity
uint256[] memory depositChainIds = new uint256[](3);
        depositChainIds[0] = 1; // Ethereum
        depositChainIds[1] = 56; // Binance
        depositChainIds[2] = 42161; // Arbitrum One
```

However, there are two issues:

1. **Incorrect Division:** The value calculation divides by 3 instead of 2, incorrectly including the primary chain.
2. **Decreasing Value:** The value shrinks with each iteration, while \_depositChainIds.length remains constant. For example:

- First Iteration:

```
i = 0 (i < _depositChainIds.length - 1)
value = msg.value / _depositChainIds.length = 500 / 3 = 166
```

- Second Iteration:

```
i = 1 (i < _depositChainIds.length - 1)
value = msg.value / _depositChainIds.length = 334 / 3 = 111
```

Only 277 (166 + 111) is forwarded instead of the intended 500. The remaining 223 is left in the factory, withdrawable only by the owner.

## Recommendations

Update the value calculation in createERC20DAO() and createERC721DAO() functions:

```solidity
                ICommLayer(commLayer).sendMsg{value: (msg.value - fees) / (_depositChainIds.length - (i + 1))}(
                    commLayer, _payload, abi.encode(_depositChainIds[i + 1], msg.sender)
                );
```

- First Iteration:

```
i = 0 (i < _depositChainIds.length - 1)
value = msg.value / (_depositChainIds.length - (i + 1)) = 500 / 2 = 250
```

- Second Iteration:

```
i = 1 (i < _depositChainIds.length - 1)
value = msg.value / (_depositChainIds.length - (i + 1)) = 250 / 1 = 250
```
summary:
This bug report discusses an issue with the `factory.createERC20DAO()` function, which is used to create cross-chain DAOs using LayerZero. The function allows users to specify a value, which is then distributed across multiple chains. However, there are two issues with this process. 

Firstly, there is an incorrect division in the value calculation, which includes the primary chain in the distribution instead of just the secondary chains. This leads to an incorrect distribution of funds. 

Secondly, there is a problem with the value shrinking with each iteration, while the length of the depositChainIds array remains constant. This means that not all of the intended value is forwarded to the secondary chains, and the remaining value is left in the factory. 

To fix these issues, the value calculation in the createERC20DAO() and createERC721DAO() functions should be updated to exclude the primary chain and ensure that the correct value is forwarded to each secondary chain.

title: [H-04] Malicious dao owner can break lz communication
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the LayerZeroImpl contract, which uses the NonBlockingLzApp from the LZ SDK to store failed messages. The function responsible for this uses up a lot of gas and if the NonBlockingLzApp also uses up all of its allocated gas, there is not enough left to store the failed message. This can lead to a revert in the Endpoint try/catch handling, which blocks the pathway. A malicious DAO owner can exploit this by setting up a large number of tokens for token gating, causing an "Out Of Gas" error and resulting in a blocked pathway. The recommendation is to limit the number of tokens that can be added by the owner to prevent this issue.

title: [H-03] Users can break the lz communication
summary: This bug report discusses an issue in the LayerZeroImpl contract. This contract uses a function called `_blockingLzReceive` to store failed messages for future retries, but there is a problem with how this function uses gas. The function reads up to 150 bytes of returndata and uses up to `gasleft()` gas, which means that if the `nonblockingLzReceive` function uses all of its allocated gas, there is only a small amount of gas left to store the failed message. This is not enough, as storing a failed message requires more gas than is left. This can result in a revert and block the pathway. A malicious user can exploit this by wasting all of the allocated gas using the `onERC721Received` function. This can happen when a smart contract with malicious code calls the `crossChainBuy` function, triggering a call stack that eventually leads to the `onERC721Received` function. To fix this issue, the recommendation is to use `mint` instead of `safeMint` and to clearly document this in the code.

title: [H-02] It is possible to override DAO details
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

Code uses `create` to deploy DAO token in Deployer contract, so the DAO address only depends on Deployer contract addresses and its deployment nonce. If two chains have the same Deployer contract address then DAO created in those chains would have the same addresses. This would cause congestion when some DAOs deploy on both of those chains. An attacker can use this to override the DAO's details in the other chain. So when a DAO uses multi-chain deployments it would be possible to deploy the same DAO in the cross-chain and the result would be that the real DAO's information in the factory can be overwritten.

This is the POC:

1. User1 wants to deploy his DAO in chain1 and chain2. He creates a tx deploys his DAO in chain1 and uses chain2 as the second chain. The DAO address will be determined only by the result of `create` opcode which is based on Deployer contract address and its deployment `nonce`.
2. If Chain1 and Chain2 had the same Deployer contract address then the attacker can create a DAO in chain2 whose addresses would be the same and the attacker would set chain1 as a side chain for his DAO.
3. As a result the Factory contract in chian2 would send a message to Chain1 to deploy the attacker-specified DAO in the chain1 in the same DAO address of the User1 and it would cause a rewrite of the User1's DAO.

## Recommendations

Make sure DAOs have different addresses in different chains.
summary: The bug report discusses a potential issue with the deployment of DAO tokens using the `create` function in the Deployer contract. This could result in the same DAO address being used on multiple chains, causing congestion and allowing an attacker to override the details of the DAO. The report suggests ensuring that DAOs have unique addresses on different chains to prevent this issue.

title: [H-01] Bypassing `maxTokensPerUser` limits for ERC721 DAO
summary: The bug report is about a medium severity bug that has a high likelihood of happening. The issue occurs when users call a specific code, which performs checks and then calls another function. The problem is that there is no protection against reentrancy, which allows users to bypass the checks and buy more tokens than they are supposed to. This is especially problematic for DAOs that have whitelists, as one user can buy more tokens than allowed. The report suggests using a reentrancy guard or a different coding pattern to prevent this issue from happening.

title: [C-03] Native tokens can be drained from the Factory contract
summary:
This bug report discusses a vulnerability in the Factory contract that allows an attacker to steal all native tokens. This is a high severity issue as it can result in the loss of valuable assets. The likelihood of this attack is also high as it can be carried out by any user.

The vulnerability lies in the `crossChainBuy()` function, specifically in the calculation of `value: msg.value - fees`. The error allows an attacker to send a LayerZero message with a higher value than intended and receive a refund for the excess amount. This means that the protocol fees, which should remain in the Factory contract until claimed by the protocol owner, can be stolen by the attacker.

The report also mentions that the native tokens deposited are sent to the Safe/DAO, while a fee is sent to the DAO owner. This is done by the Factory contract and can also be exploited by an attacker to create a fake DAO and receive these funds.

To fix this issue, the report recommends correctly calculating the remaining `value` to send to LayerZero, taking into account factors such as the deposit token, deposit amount, owner share, deposit fees, and KYC fees. This will ensure that the correct amount of native tokens is sent to LayerZero and prevent the theft of assets.

title: [C-02] Native tokens in the DAOs are stuck
summary: This bug report is about a problem where native tokens deposited into a DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) cannot be moved from there. This issue is considered to have a high impact and likelihood, meaning that it can cause significant problems and is likely to happen for all DAOs with native token deposits. The report suggests adding a parameter to the `updateProposalAndExecution()` function in both `ERC20DAO` and `ERC721DAO` to transfer the native tokens. It also recommends making the function `payable` to allow the DAO to make external calls with value without using its deposits.

title: [C-01] The LayerZero implementation contract is the receiver of DAOs fees on cross-chain buy operations
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

## Description

Whenever a cross-chain DAO is created via `createCrossChainERC20DAO()` or `createCrossChainERC721DAO()`, it assigns the `ownerAddress` as the `msg.sender`. The problem is that the `msg.sender` will always be the LayerZero Deployer contract:

```solidity
    function createCrossChainERC20DAO(...) {
@>      require(msg.sender == commLayer, "Caller not LZ Deployer");
        bytes memory _payload = abi.encode(_daoAddress, msg.sender, _numOfTokensToBuy, _tokenURI, _merkleProof);
        ccDetails[_daoAddress] =
            CrossChainDetails(
                _commLayerId,
                _depositChainIds,
                false,
@>              msg.sender,          // @audit ownerAddress
                _onlyAllowWhitelist
            );
    }
```

So, each time a cross-chain buy operation is performed, the fee will be attempted to be sent to the LayerZero Deployer, instead of the DAO owner address:

```solidity
    payable(
        ccDetails[_daoAddress].ownerAddress != address(0)
@>          ? ccDetails[_daoAddress].ownerAddress
            : IERC20DAO(_daoAddress).getERC20DAOdetails().ownerAddress
    ).call{value: ownerShare}("");
```

The fee won't be sent anywhere as the LayerZero Deployer doesn't have a `receive() payable {}` function, and the result from the `call` is not checked. In any case, the DAO owner's address will not receive the corresponding fees.

## Recommendations

Allow the DAO creator to specify an `ownerAddress` for each cross-chain DAO deployment (as they may not have control over the same address on all chains).
summary: This bug report addresses a problem with creating a cross-chain DAO using `createCrossChainERC20DAO()` or `createCrossChainERC721DAO()`. The issue is that the `msg.sender` is always assigned as the `ownerAddress`, which is actually the LayerZero Deployer contract. This means that the fees for cross-chain buy operations will be sent to the LayerZero Deployer instead of the actual DAO owner. The report recommends allowing the DAO creator to specify an `ownerAddress` for each cross-chain deployment.

title: [H-02] ETH gets locked in the `GroupcoinFactory` contract
summary: This bug report discusses an issue where some ETH may not be added to a newly created Uniswap v3 pool when launching a Groupcoin. This can result in the ETH being permanently locked in the GroupcoinFactory contract. The report recommends adding an "onlyOwner" function to withdraw any excess ETH from the contract.

title: [H-01] The same Groupcoin can be launched more than once
description:
## Severity

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

## Description

In `launchGroupCoinToUniswapV3`, there is no validation that the Groupcoin hasn't already been launched. Under normal circumstances, this is not a problem because it's not possible to create multiple pools with the same token pair and fee. However, it's possible for the owner to change the fee at any time via `setUniswapConfig`. As a result, if the owner changes the fee, any Groupcoin that was previously launched with the old fee can now be launched again.

Re-launching a Groupcoin causes additional tokens to be minted, causing its `totalSupply` to exceed the intended 10m token maximum. Additionally, since ETH is also provided to the liquidity position and the ETH received from initially selling the Groupcoin has already been used in the previous launch, this will take ETH received from other Groupcoin sales, preventing other Groupcoins from being launched.

## Recommendations

Trigger a revert at the top of `launchGroupCoinToUniswapV3` if `launched[tokenId] = true`.
summary: This bug report discusses a problem in the code for `launchGroupCoinToUniswapV3`. This function does not check if a Groupcoin has already been launched, which can cause issues if the fee is changed by the owner. This can lead to the Groupcoin being launched again, causing more tokens to be minted and exceeding the intended maximum. Additionally, this can also prevent other Groupcoins from being launched. The report recommends adding a check at the beginning of the function to prevent this issue from occurring.

title: [C-02] Tokens can be launched to Uniswap v3 anytime, allowing to drain ETH
summary: This bug report describes a high severity bug in the code for GroupcoinFactory. The bug allows attackers to launch tokens to Uniswap v3 without meeting the intended criteria, which can result in them taking ETH from the contract and selling their tokens for a higher price. The report recommends fixing the code by ensuring that a specific value is not unset.

title: [C-01] Uniswap v3 launch can be enabled without raising enough ETH
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `enableUniswapV3Launch` function in a smart contract. This function can only be used if a certain amount of ETH has been paid to purchase the token, but it has been found that users can purchase a lower amount of tokens than needed to meet this requirement. This can lead to the contract becoming insolvent and unable to launch Uniswap v3. The recommended solution is to limit the use of `enableUniswapV3Launch` based on the total number of tokens purchased to ensure enough ETH has been paid.

title: Users May Lose The Ability to Transfer Their Tokens
description:
Whenever a change is made to the voting power of any user, the [`_moveVotingPower`](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L142) function is called. It handles several different scenarios, such as a [voting power change during token transfer](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L162-L166) or [during delegations](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L168-L178). Another scenario involves [claiming the tokens](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L157-L161) from the [`Claim`](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Claim.sol#L19-L237) contract. Before doing that, users have to [prove their balance](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L64) inside the `Claim` contract. Although the tokens are vested over time, whenever a user proves their balance, their delegatee [immediately receives](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L68) the voting power from the tokens to be claimed. Because of that, when they finally receive the vested tokens, the voting power of their delegatee [does not change](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L161) as it has already been accounted for in the past.


However, it is possible to execute the [code](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L156-L161) responsible for handling claims during normal token transfer. It can happen when a user transfers tokens to any account while having a non\-zero claimable balance and the `Claim` contract as their current delegatee. In such a case, during the tokens transfer, the `_moveVotingPower` function will be [executed](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L102) with `claimContractAddress` as the second argument, and since the user has a non\-zero amount of claimable tokens, [this check](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L157) will pass. In order to illustrate the possible consequences of this behavior, consider the following attack scenario where there are two users: Alice and Bob.


Alice has two accounts: one having a non\-zero balance and some proven unclaimed tokens to claim from the `Claim` contract, and a second account with a zero token balance that has Bob as its delegatee. Bob has a non\-zero balance in his account. Now, Alice can:


1. Call [`proveAndDelegate`](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L63) from her first account and specify the `Claim` contract as the delegatee.
2. Transfer her balance to her second account. Since Alice's first account delegates to the `Claim` contract and its claimable balance is non\-zero, [no change will be made](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L157) to the voting power of her second account's delegatee.
3. Change the delegatee of her first account to itself and transfer the tokens back from her second account to her first account. As a result, the second account's delegatee, Bob, will [lose](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L183-L187) a corresponding amount of his voting power.


Consequently, Bob will not be able to transfer his tokens in the future as an integer underflow will occur during [the attempt to decrease his voting power](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/governance/Anvil.sol#L183-L187).


Consider not allowing users to delegate to the `Claim` contract and handling the accounting of the `accountProvenUnclaimedAmount` outside the `_moveVotingPower` function.


***Update:** Resolved in [pull request \#279](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/pull/279) at commit [a6cac6a](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/commit/a6cac6ac065e7176c31296e3846fde3174da2d72).*
summary: The bug report discusses an issue with the `_moveVotingPower` function in the `Anvil.sol` contract. This function handles changes to a user's voting power, including during token transfers and delegations. However, there is a scenario where the function can be executed during a normal token transfer, causing unexpected consequences. This can lead to an attack where a user can manipulate the voting power of another user by transferring tokens and changing delegatees. The suggested solution is to not allow users to delegate to the `Claim` contract and handle the accounting of unclaimed tokens separately from the `_moveVotingPower` function. The bug has been resolved in a recent pull request.

title: Funds May Be Locked Inside TimeBasedCollateralPool
description:
Users' deposits are represented by units instead of tokens in the [`TimeBasedCollateralPool`](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L22-L1210) contract. This is because any amount of staked tokens may be [claimed](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L561) at any time by an account with the [claimant role](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L31) and the total amount of tokens inside the pool will decrease in such a case. As such, the users will not be able to receive their full deposit when they unstake their tokens. Instead, they will receive the amount of tokens [proportional](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L164-L179) to their unit's balance. All the unit\-related calculations are performed by the [`calculateProportionOfTotal`](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/Pricing.sol#L98-L111) function of the [`Pricing`](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/Pricing.sol#L4-L124) library.


Every time users [stake](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L1075) their tokens, they receive the amount of units [proportional](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L1093-L1097) to their contribution to the entire token pool balance. This, combined with the claims that may happen over time, may drastically increase the amount of units needed to represent a single token. For this reason, the [reset](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L623) functionality has been introduced in order to manually [release](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L1039) all tokens staked in the pool. This is so that the balance between tokens and units is [brought](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L1082-L1086) back to a 1:1 ratio when users stake their tokens again. However, there are possible scenarios where users are allowed to deposit their tokens but cannot unstake these tokens later on due to the Integer Overflow exception. One such scenario is described below.


Assume that there is some amount of tokens deposited into the pool, but the units are diluted. For example, let's say that for a token with `18` decimals, the pool holds a total of `1e26` units, but only a dust amount of tokens due to claims. It can either naturally happen over time, or by way of an attack where there is a transaction issued by an account with the claimant role in order to claim the entire collateral, but an attacker front\-runs it and deposits `1 wei` of the token into the pool. This will avoid [resetting](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L591-L594) the pool and will quickly dilute the units.


Afterward, another user deposits some `1e8` tokens to the pool and receives a very large amount of units `~1e52`. After some time, they want to withdraw their assets so they schedule a withdrawal. When the withdrawal is finally processed after two epochs, the user will not be able to claim it as [this line](https://github.com/AmperaFoundation/sol-contracts/blob/c6e940c12044c8994f778c978e34582449229df8/contracts/TimeBasedCollateralPool.sol#L1128-L1132) will revert.
