```rust
            let token_balance = if is_deposit {
                balance
                    .checked_add(amount)
                    .map_err(|_| Error::MissingConfig)?
            } else {
                balance
                    .checked_sub(amount)
                    .map_err(|_| Error::MissingConfig)?
            }
            .then(TokenBalance::Tracked);

            TOKEN_BALANCES.save(storage, key.clone(), &token_balance)?;
        }
@>      Some(_) | None => (),
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

If the interchain token is not deployed on the destination chain, even if the message is approved, tokens cannot be bridged because the token is not deployed. However, we can consider scenarios where the remote interchain token deployment request is frontrunned. For canonical tokens, anyone can deploy remote interchain tokens, so it's easy to create a scenario where token transfer is requested first, followed by a request to deploy the remote interchain token.

Consider the following example:

1. The token deployer requests remote interchain token deployment to chain B. This will be frontrunned.
2. Front-running (1), a request is made to transfer 100 ether of tokens.
3. ITSHub first executes `ItsMessage::InterchainTransfer`. As the interchain token is not yet deployed on chain B, the balance for chain B remains `None`.
4. ITSHub then processes `ItsMessage::DeployInterchainToken`, initializing the balance of chain B to 0.
5. After the remote interchain token deployment is completed on chain B, the attacker executes `execute` to receive the bridged tokens.

The balance in ITSHub is 0, but there are 100 ether of bridged tokens on chain B. This balance mismatch can cause problems such as DoS. For example, if another user bridges tokens from chain A to B, increasing the ITSHub balance, the attacker can bridge back from B to A, reducing the ITSHub balance. If a user then tries to bridge from B to A again, they won't be able to due to insufficient balance in ITSHub.

### Recommended Mitigation Steps

The problem is allowing bridging to chains where the remote interchain token is not deployed. The implementation of `update_token_balance` should be changed to allow bridging only to chains where the balance has been initialized.

If you don't want to track the balance of the source chain, instead of judging by balance initialization, you should accurately identify the source chain and handle it.

### Assessed type

DoS

**[milapsheth (Axelar) confirmed and commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network-findings/issues/43#issuecomment-2334749343):**
 > The report is valid. We agree with the Medium severity since assets can't be stolen, and ITS hub can be upgraded easily to fix the balance invariant. We do plan to restrict transfers if the token isn't initialized yet to handle this scenario. As mentioned, it requires more careful tracking of the source chain of the token.

**[0xsomeone (judge) increased severity to High and commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network-findings/issues/43#issuecomment-2362278336):**
 > The Warden outlines a discrepancy in the token accounting system of the ITS service that would permit a chain that does not yet have an interchain token deployment in it to process messages for it incorrectly.
> 
> The vulnerability stems from the same root cause as submission [#77](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-08-axelar-network-findings/issues/77), and I believe both descriptions merit a high severity rating. This particular submission directly outlines how funds could be stolen by front-running the deployment of an interchain token and bridging back, thereby causing funds bridged by other users to become "locked" in the attacked chain.

***
summary: This bug report outlines a vulnerability in the ITSHub system used for bridging tokens between different chains. The issue occurs when tokens are transferred to a chain where the interchain token has not yet been deployed. This can lead to a discrepancy in the token balance, causing a DoS attack on the bridge. The recommended mitigation steps suggest changing the implementation to only allow bridging to chains where the balance has been initialized. The severity of the bug was originally marked as Medium, but was later increased to High due to the potential for funds to be stolen. The bug has been confirmed by the team and they plan to address it by restricting transfers to unitialized chains.

title: [H-01] Cool-off period for deposits in swap pools can be bypassed
summary: This bug report discusses a problem with the deposit cool-off period in the swap pool. This period is meant to prevent immediate withdrawals, but it can be bypassed by transferring LP tokens to another address. The report provides a code snippet to demonstrate the issue and suggests a solution to update the cool-off period for each address. However, this solution may also be vulnerable to DoS attacks, so a better solution would be to track the number of tokens in cool-off for each address.

title: [H-01] Users can bypass `shareUnlockTime`
summary: The report discusses a bug where users are able to transfer their shares before the designated time period on a cross-chain platform. This is due to a function called `depositAndBridge` which immediately transfers the token to the vault and mints shares on the destination chain. The report suggests passing additional data or flags in the operation and calling a function called `_afterPublicDeposit` to prevent this issue. It is recommended to make these changes to avoid potential abuse of the system.

title: [H-02] `getPrice()` will always revert due to absence of `fallback()` and `receive()` functions
description:
**Description:**

The `getPrice()` function is designed to calculate the price of `saleToken` by dividing the contract's ETH balance by the balance of `saleToken` held by the contract. However, the function will always revert due to the absence `fallback()` or `receive()` function, and the constructor is also not marked as payable. As a result, the ETH balance of the contract will always be zero, causing the function to revert whenever it is called.

**Code Snippet**

```solidity
    function getPrice() public view returns (uint256) {
        ...

        if (saleTokenBalance == 0) revert saleTokenBalanceZeroError();
@>      if (ethBalance == 0) revert EthBalanceZeroError();

        ...
    }
```

**Impact:**

Due to absence of Eth balance in the contract, `getPrice()` will always revert and no user will be able to buy or sell tokens

**Recommendation:**

To remediate this issue, it is recommended to implement either a `receive` function or a `fallback` function. Additionally, ensure the constructor is marked as payable if ETH is intended to be sent during contract deployment.
summary: The getPrice() function in the contract is not working properly because it always reverts due to the absence of a receive or fallback function. This means that the ETH balance of the contract is always zero, causing the function to fail whenever it is called. This bug prevents users from being able to buy or sell tokens. To fix this, a receive or fallback function should be implemented and the constructor should be marked as payable if ETH is intended to be sent during contract deployment.

title: [H-01] Missing access control in `updateFairLaunchProperties()` function
description:
**Description:**

The `updateFairLaunchProperties()` function allows external callers to update the `fairLaunchProperties` variable, which is used to determine whether the token is available for buying or selling. This function lacks proper access control, enabling any unauthorized user to modify the `fairLaunchProperties` variable

**Impact:**

Unauthorized users could enable or disable token trading, leading to potential market manipulation or disruption.

**Recommendation:**

To remediate this issue, it is recommended to implement access control mechanism in `updateFairLaunchProperties()` function. This can be achieved using Solidity's `onlyOwner` modifier from the OpenZeppelin library or a custom access control mechanism.

```diff
- function updateFairLaunchProperties(FairLaunchProperties memory _fairLaunchProperties) external returns (bool) {....}
+ function updateFairLaunchProperties(FairLaunchProperties memory _fairLaunchProperties) external onlyOwner returns (bool) {....}
```
summary: The `updateFairLaunchProperties()` function in the code allows anyone to change the `fairLaunchProperties` variable, which controls whether the token can be bought or sold. This can lead to unauthorized users manipulating the market. To fix this, it is recommended to add a security measure, such as the `onlyOwner` modifier, to restrict access to this function. This can be done using a library like OpenZeppelin or by creating a custom security mechanism.

title: Incorrect Token Refunded
description:
**Update**
The client fixed the issue in commit `7dc6cc7d1f09d688a6af848a655ed4345c86bd02` by removing the `transfer()` call.

**File(s) affected:**`FinanceToken.sol`

**Description:** The function `FinanceToken.purchaseNMTWithToken()` intends to return any excess `_paymentToken` to the caller, but `nmtToken` is always returned instead. There is no need to refund any payment as only the `useAmount` is transferred from the caller, not the full `_paymentAmount`.

**Recommendation:** Remove the `transfer()` call on #L158.
summary: The report states that there was a bug in the `FinanceToken.sol` file where the function `purchaseNMTWithToken()` was not returning the correct amount of `_paymentToken` to the caller. Instead, it was always returning the `nmtToken`. The client fixed the issue by removing a `transfer()` call in commit `7dc6cc7d1f09d688a6af848a655ed4345c86bd02`. The recommendation is to remove the `transfer()` call on line 158.

title: `AccountManage` Can Be Initialized With No Required Signers
description:
**Update**
The client fixed the issue in commit `56fe445287d8dbde412d6d47fbfddfe070dabe6d` by initializing `signNum`to `2`. Since the `AccountManage` contract is already deployed, the client called `updateSignNum()` to set `signNum` to `2`.

**File(s) affected:**`AccountManage.sol`

**Description:** Currently, `AccountManage.init()` does not assign a `signNum` for the contract, meaning that after initialization, the `signNum` has a zero value. This means that `withdrawComputingFee()` can be invoked without any signatures necessary, allowing any address to withdraw the accumulated `providerFeeSum` amount of NMT tokens from this contract. During the audit, we notified the team of their live contract with a `signNum` of zero with ~18 NMT at stake for withdrawal by any party. As of 12 pm ET on July 12th, the `signNum` has not been updated and remains at a zero value.

**Recommendation:** During initialization of `AccountManage`, assign `signNum` a non-zero value. Note that if `AccountManage` is already deployed, `signNum` must be updated via `AccountManage.updateSignNum()`.
summary: A bug has been found in the `AccountManage` contract where the `signNum` is not being assigned a value during initialization. This means that anyone can withdraw NMT tokens without needing any signatures, which could result in a loss of tokens. The issue has been fixed in a recent update, but if the contract has already been deployed, the `signNum` must be manually updated using the `updateSignNum()` function. It is recommended to assign a non-zero value to `signNum` during initialization to prevent this issue from occurring.

title: Centralization Risks
description:
**Update**
The client acknowledged the issue and provided the following explanation:

> FixedLock.sol: This contract is used for locking early cooperative users' assets. The logic of this contract includes reward-related logic, but it will never distribute any rewards.
> 
> 
> RewardContract: In this system, the calculation and distribution of rewards are carried out by the collaboration of on-chain and off-chain services. This is because the evaluation of contributions from the off-chain Netmind-GPU network (such as GPU operation status detection, network speed, and other performance checks) is involved. Since this data cannot be directly migrated to the blockchain, we introduced a consensus network maintained by multiple cooperating parties to ensure fairness based on this situation.

**File(s) affected:**`Purchase.sol`, `FixedLock.sol`, `Pledge.sol`, `LongTermPledge.sol`, `RewardContract.sol`

**Description:** This protocol contains significant centralization, as some roles in the system have excessive privileges and key protocol actions take place in undocumented off-chain processes. We include a non-exhaustive list of the most striking examples of this centralization below:

*   Depositors into `FixedLock` will only earn rewards if the team deposits enough Rewards to fund reward claims. If both Alice and Bob were to stake for the same amount of time, but the team deposited rewards that were only sufficient for Alice to claim, and Alice claimed first, Bob would have no way of claiming his rewards until the team deposits again.

*   On-chain, there is no synchronization between the stakes made in either `Pledge` or `LongTermPledge` and the rewards that can be claimed in `RewardContract`. The smart contracts enforce no guarantee of rewards for stakers, and when rewards are claimed, there is no consideration of the existing stake that was made on-chain. As a result, staked users looking to claim rewards at `RewardContract.withdrawToken()` are totally reliant on the nodes defined in `Pledge` (more specifically, `conf.Staking()`) acting honestly to grant the expected rewards to the staker. It is worth emphasizing here that the reward calculation is done in an undocumented process, off-chain.

*   Documentation from the NMT team suggests that `Purchase.swapToken()` is a method allowing users to purchase training services through USDC. During discussions during the audit, the NMT team described that a user purchasing Training Tasks with fiat will have their account managed off-chain instead of in the `AccountManage` contract. Native NMT depositors have access to increase or decrease their balance, providing significantly more account control to users who purchase using fiat. If a user were to `Purchase.swapToken()` to provide an increase to a balance for Training Tasks, this user must completely trust the NMT Team to honor their purchased amount and adequately manage the account off-chain.

*   `Conf.wards` authorized accounts have excessive privileges, and a malicious ward address can compromise the system (see [NETM-3](https://certificate.quantstamp.com/full/net-mind/e7dfdc3c-7589-4fc8-b3d8-4872c783a735/index.html#findings-qs3)).

**Recommendation:** Make clear this centralization to users. Looking forward, the team should consider putting more of these processes on chain, or providing clear documentation to users on the specifics of off-chain components.
summary: This bug report discusses issues with centralization in a protocol that involves locking assets and distributing rewards. The report highlights specific examples of centralization and suggests that the team should make this centralization clear to users and consider putting more processes on the blockchain or providing clear documentation. The report also mentions that some roles in the system have excessive privileges and that a malicious address could compromise the system.

title: Excessive Privileges for Wards
description:
**Update**
The client acknowledged the issue and provided the following explanation:

> This permission is exclusively held by the management contract, which requires voting to execute any operation.

**File(s) affected:**`Conf.sol`

**Description:**`Conf.wards` is a mapping containing privileged addresses that can invoke `Conf.file()` to assign values to crucial protocol state such as contract addresses, privileged executors, and fees. Additionally, any privileged `ward` has the ability to `rely()` or `deny()` another address to be either included or removed from this privileged mapping. This is an excessive privilege that can be abused by a single malicious `ward`.

Consider if a `ward` address was compromised and needs to have their privileges removed, which means the `deny()` function has to be invoked. This malicious ward could, in theory, never be denied privilege by continuously front-running the `deny()` transaction with a `rely()` transaction to delegate that privilege to another address they own. Further, this compromised ward could deny every other ward in the system, becoming the sole entity that can configure the protocol and reconfigure all protocol values to something malicious.

**Recommendation:** Instead of allowing for `wards` to deny or rely other wards, consider only allowing that functionality to happen from a separate privileged role, such as an owner.
summary: The client has reported a bug in the `Conf.sol` file where the `Conf.wards` mapping contains privileged addresses that can make changes to important protocol settings. This can be abused by a malicious address that has been granted this privilege. If this address is compromised, they can continuously front-run the removal of their privileges and delegate them to another address they own, giving them complete control over the protocol. The recommendation is to only allow this privilege to be managed by a separate, more secure role such as an owner.

title: Signature Replay
description:
**Update**
The client fixed the issue in commit `ca190112e3f1651680f8330f808100b95b11b239`. The functions `distribute()`, `agentDistribute()`, and `refund()` now all mark a digest as used. As these actions are processed, it is enforced that the hash of the parameters (e.g., `paymentId`, `amt`, etc.) has not been seen before, preventing the possibility of signatures being used more than once.

**File(s) affected:**`Payment.sol`

**Description:** The functions `distribute()` and `agentDistribute()` are susceptible to signature replay since a nonce is not included in the digest. After either function is called, anyone can reuse the calldata, which consists of the authorized account signatures, to replay the distribute transaction. The transaction can be replayed continuously until the payment has no remaining funds or the `expir` time is reached.

**Exploit Scenario:**

1.   Bob calls `payment()` and deposits 10 NMT into the `Payment` contract.
2.   Bob is charged two NMT for GPU fees and one NMT for platform fees.
3.   The distribution digest is created using the payment ID, GPU provider's address, GPU fee amount, platform fee amount, and the digest expiration time.
4.   Authorized accounts sign the distribution digest.
5.   The signatures are collected and `distribute()` is called. Two NMT are transferred to the GPU provider, and one NMT is transferred to the `feeTo` address. Bob's payment `distributed` amount is now three NMT.
6.   Before the `expir` time is reached, a malicious actor finds the distribution transaction and replays the transaction with the same calldata. Again, three NMT of Bob's payment is transferred between the GPU provider and the `feeTo` address. Bob's payment `distributed` amount is now six NMT.
7.   The malicious actor replays the transaction again. Bob's payment `distributed` amount is now nine NMT. 
8.   The transaction cannot be replayed again as Bob's payment only has one NMT remaining.

**Recommendation:** Implement a nonce per `paymentId`, include it in the distribution digest, and increment the nonce when executing the distribution.
summary: The report discusses an issue in the `Payment.sol` file where the functions `distribute()` and `agentDistribute()` can be replayed multiple times without authorization. This means that someone can use the same transaction data to transfer funds repeatedly until the payment has no more funds or expires. The report recommends adding a unique number to each payment and including it in the transaction data to prevent this from happening.

title: Liquidated users can mix and manipulate stable and variable borrowings through exploitative liquidation process
summary: The report is about a vulnerability in the Folks Finance smart contract on the testnet platform. This vulnerability allows users to mix their stable and variable borrowings, which can lead to protocol insolvency. The exploit involves manipulating a check in the liquidation process, which allows users to bypass the system and combine different types of borrowings. This can be done intentionally or by someone else liquidating them. If exploited on a large scale, this vulnerability can undermine the financial stability of the platform and violate the intended logic of the system. A detailed proof of concept is provided in the report to demonstrate how this vulnerability can be exploited.

title: Incorrect Updates to pooldepositDatatotalAmount and loancollateralUsed During Repayment with Collateral
summary: This report is about a bug found in a smart contract on the testnet platform called "Snowtrace". The bug affects the contract's ability to operate and could result in the theft of unclaimed yield. The bug is related to a mathematical flaw in the protocol's repayment with collateral mechanism, specifically in the way it updates the total amount of deposited funds. This flaw causes the total amount to become inflated, leading to several issues such as incorrect utilization ratios, interest rates, and deposit indexes. The bug can be fixed by making a small change to the code in the affected function. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate the impact of the bug.

The recommendation is to set an allowance for the poolManager in the TransferProxy. The bug has been fixed in the Centrifuge and Spearbit commits.

title: Centrifuge router can perform untrusted actions on behalf of open vaults
summary: The Centrifuge router has a critical bug that allows anyone to request deposits and redemptions on behalf of an owner, even if they are not authorized to do so. This is because the router is added as an endorsed operator, but there is no validation on the vault side. To fix this, the code needs to be updated to only allow the asset owner to access these actions. This bug has been fixed in the latest version of Centrifuge and Spearbit.

title: Wrong borrow balance calculation in the getLoanLiquidity function
summary: This report is about a bug found in a smart contract on the testnet platform Snowtrace. The bug affects the protocol's solvency, which means that it can cause financial problems. The bug is related to the calculation of the borrow balance in the getLoanLiquidity function. When the executeLiquidation function is called, the prepareLiquidation function checks whether the violator is liquidatable by using the getLoanLiquidity function. However, the function calculates the borrow balance incorrectly for stable borrow loans. This can result in a lower borrow balance for the violator, causing the liquidate function to revert even if the violator is in a liquidatable state. The bug can be fixed by correctly calling the calcBorrowBalance function in the getLoanLiquidity function. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate the bug.

title: \_pendingWithdrawalAmount CAN BE ARBITRARILY RESET
summary: The Tagus protocol has a function called `getTotalDeposited()` which collects all tokenized assets under it. This function has a variable called `_pendingWithdrawalAmount` that keeps track of assets requested for redemption from EigenLayer. This variable increases when assets are undelegated and decreases when withdrawals are claimed. However, the `claimCompletedWithdrawals()` function has no restrictions and can be called by anyone, which can reset the variable to 0. This can disrupt the ratio of the vault. To fix this issue, the Tagus Labs team has implemented a check on `claimCompletedWithdrawals` to ensure that the restaker is known by the contract.

title: VAULTS ARE VULNERABLE TO A DONATION ATTACK
summary: The bug report describes a vulnerability in the ratio computation mechanism of the vault, which can be manipulated through a "donation attack". This attack occurs when a large amount of tokens is donated to the vault before any other transaction, causing the share price to become permanently fixed at 1. This distorts the share-to-asset conversion process and can result in a total loss of deposited assets for users. The report includes a proof of concept test and a recommendation to mitigate the vulnerability by pre-minting shares and implementing safeguards against zero share minting. The bug has been solved by the Tagus Labs team by implementing a check to ensure depositors receive shares when depositing tokens.

title: Hub missing check for available liquidity could lead to locked fund and utilization ratio exceeding
summary: This is a report about a bug found in a smart contract on the testnet platform. The bug can lead to temporary or permanent freezing of funds, as well as griefing and the smart contract being unable to operate due to lack of token funds. The bug occurs when the Hub doesn't check for available liquidity, allowing for a borrow/withdraw operation to succeed even when there is not enough liquidity in the spokeToken. This can result in high interest rates and locked funds for users. The bug can also be triggered by race conditions and is more likely to occur in cross-chain operations. The report includes a recommendation to add a check for available liquidity to prevent this bug from happening. A proof of concept test was conducted to demonstrate the bug and its impact.

title: Vulnerability in getLoanLiquidity leads to undervaluing stable debt
summary: This report is about a bug found in a smart contract on the testnet platform called Snowtrace. The bug affects the way the contract calculates the liquidity for loans, causing the effective borrow value to be undervalued for stable loans. This means that an attacker could potentially steal funds from the protocol by taking advantage of this bug. The severity of this bug is considered high, as it could lead to protocol insolvency or direct theft of user funds. The bug can be fixed by simply correcting the order of parameters in the affected function. A proof of concept test was conducted to demonstrate the impact of the bug.

title: Attacker can Inflate `effectiveCollateralValue`
summary: In summary, there is a bug in the smart contract on the testnet platform snowtrace.io that allows users to exploit the `LoanManager::deposit()` function by depositing 0 tokens multiple times, resulting in duplicate pool IDs being added to the `colPools` array. This can lead to an inflated `effectiveCollateralValue` and potential financial losses within the protocol. The bug can be exploited in various scenarios, allowing users to borrow more than they should, withdraw collateral they aren't entitled to, or avoid liquidation. A proof of concept has been provided for further understanding.

title: [H-02] Bonding token transfers DOS after the pair was created
summary: This bug report describes a problem where users are unable to transfer bonding tokens before the initial sale is completed and the Token/WETH pair is created. This is meant to protect against attacks, but it can be exploited to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) after the pair is created. The report includes a code example of how this can be done. The recommendations suggest adding a condition to prevent this exploit.

title: [H-01] The bonding curve implementation can not be fully changed
summary: This bug report is about a function in the `BondingERC20TokenFactory` that is not working as intended. The function is supposed to update the bonding curve implementation, but it does not update the `getOutputPrice` function, which calculates the token price. This can lead to incorrect token prices at the end of the curve. The recommendation is to implement the `getOutputPrice` function in a different contract to fix this issue.

title: [C-03] Blocking the initial liquidity seed with a 1 wei donation
summary: This bug report describes a scenario where an attacker can create an empty token pair on Uniswap and manipulate the reserve values, causing a failure in the protocol when trying to create a pair after the initial sale phase. The report suggests a solution to directly interact with the Uniswap pair instead of relying on a router to prevent this issue.

title: [C-02] Creating a token with a poisoned router
description:
**Severity**

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

**Description**

The `BondingERC20TokenFactory.deployBondingERC20Token` function does not validate the user's input. So it is possible to create a bonding token with a fake router to steal all ETH from the token sales.

```solidity
    function deployBondingERC20Token(
>>      address _router,
        string memory _name,
        string memory _symbol,
        LP_POOL _poolType
    )
        public
        returns (address)
    {
        ContinuosBondingERC20Token _bondingERC20Token = new ContinuosBondingERC20Token(
>>          _router,
            _name,
            _symbol,
            treasury,
            buyFee,
            sellFee,
            bondingCurve,
            initialTokenBalance,
            availableTokenBalance,
            _poolType
        );
        emit TokenDeployed(address(_bondingERC20Token), msg.sender);

        return address(_bondingERC20Token);
    }
```

ContinuosBondingERC20Token.sol

```solidity
    constructor(
>>      address _router,
        string memory _name,
        string memory _symbol,
        address _treasury,
        uint256 _buyFee,
        uint256 _sellFee,
        IBondingCurve _bondingCurve,
        uint256 _initialTokenBalance,
        uint256 _availableTokenBalance,
        LP_POOL _poolType
    )
        ERC20(_name, _symbol)
    {
>>      router = _router;
```

**Recommendations**

Consider checking the router address with the values from the DEXes official documentation:
https://support.traderjoexyz.com/en/articles/6807983-contracts-api
https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v2/reference/smart-contracts/v2-deployments
summary: This bug report is about a function in the `BondingERC20TokenFactory` contract that does not properly validate user input. This can lead to the creation of a fake bonding token with a fake router, which can then be used to steal all ETH from token sales. To fix this issue, it is recommended that the router address is checked against the values from the official documentation of DEXes, such as Trader Joe and Uniswap.

title: [C-01] Creating a pair while the token is in the initial sale phase
summary: This bug report discusses a high severity issue in a smart contract where a user can buy more tokens than are available for sale, resulting in the excess ETH being refunded to them. This can be exploited by a malicious contract to create a Token/WETH pair and disable a condition that prevents the attack from reverting. This can lead to the sale being stuck and trapping the collected ETH and minted tokens. The report recommends making a small change to the contract to prevent this exploit from occurring.

title: Proofs Based On beaconStateRoot Break After Electra Upgrade
summary: The Electra upgrade has caused a bug that affects the BeaconChainProofs library. This is because the upgrade has increased the height of the BeaconState tree, which breaks proofs that rely on the `beaconStateRoot` constant. This means that the `verifyValidatorFields()` and `verifyBalanceContainer()` functions do not support proofs after Electra. Additionally, the increase in tree height allows for a second pre-image attack on the balance container proof, but this is only possible for very high `validatorIndex` values. The recommendation is to use a different beacon state root tree height after the Electra fork timestamp, similar to how withdrawal proofs were handled in a previous upgrade. The EigenLayer team has acknowledged the issue and plans to make the necessary changes closer to the release of Electra.

title: Incorrect Integration of Permit2 in StarBaseDCA, StarBaseLimitOrder ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `claimTokens` function in the `StarBaseDCA` and `StarBaseLimitOrder` contracts. The problem is caused by calling the same `permit` function twice, which invalidates the second call due to a change in the nonce value. This results in the `InvalidNonce` error and makes the function unusable. The report suggests reviewing the logic of using separate `claimTokens` calls or using the `permit` function with the `PermitBatch` input struct. It also recommends adding an `if` statement to check if the allowance has already been granted and adding test cases to ensure the code works correctly.

title: Improper Use of ArgumentsDecoder Leads to Incorrect curTakerFillAmount Decoding ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with incorrect padding in the `decodeUint256` function of the `ArgumentsDecoder` contract, which is causing problems in the `fillDCA` function of the `StarBaseDCA` contract. This is leading to incorrect decoding of the `curTakerFillAmount` variable, resulting in a larger value than expected. This can potentially lead to tokens being stolen from the `StarBaseDCABot` contract. The report recommends reviewing and correcting the padding logic or creating a separate function for decoding without padding, and adding tests to the code before deployment.

title: Incorrect inAmount Passed to the Order in StarBaseDCA ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



 In the `2b508ff772206751317e8b0c6f5f70d4987a2b5e` commit provided for the fix review the issue has been fixed with the comment:
“The precondition is not aligned, `inAmount` Variable is not total principal.(Code comments are wrong). Missunderstand that there are problems with the business and realign the audit”.
Additionally the comment has been changed to `// One of the total (numberOfTrade)` instead of `// total principal`.
 

#### Description


In the `StarBaseDCA` contract, there is an `Order` struct designed to be executed `numberOfTrade` times, with the total amount of principal in the order represented by the `inAmount` variable. The StarBase team has confirmed that `inAmount` represents the full amount of tokens.


However, in the `fillDCA` function, starting with the very first order execution in the `claimTokens` call, all of the `inAmount` tokens are transferred from the maker to the taker. The problem with this design is that any subsequent call to `fillDCA` for the order cannot be executed after the first call, as all of the allowance is used. This means the dollar cost averaging mechanism will not function as intended. Additionally, other variables in the struct are meant to be correct for one cycle, such as the `minOutAmountPerCycle` or `maxOutAmountPerCycle` variables. Executing the order for the full amount of principal while using the `minOutAmountPerCycle` variable for one cycle will allow frontrunning of the order, leading to the loss of tokens, or using the `maxOutAmountPerCycle` variable for one cycle will allow keeping all of the leftover tokens at the maker’s address.


#### Examples


**starbase\-limitorder/src/StarBaseDCA.sol:L26\-L37**



```
struct Order {
    uint16 cycleSecondsApart; // executed per minute
    uint16 numberOfTrade; // executed 5 times
    address inputToken; // sell
    address outputToken; // buy
    address maker;
    uint160 inAmount; // total principal
    uint256 minOutAmountPerCycle; //min out amount
    uint256 maxOutAmountPerCycle; //max out amount
    uint256 expiration;
    uint256 salt;
}

```
**starbase\-limitorder/src/StarBaseDCA.sol:L108\-L114**



```
IStarBaseApproveProxy(_StarBase_APPROVE_PROXY_).claimTokens(
    order.maker,
    msg.sender,
    order.inAmount,
    permitSingle,
    permitSignature
);

```
#### Recommendation


We recommend executing the `claimTokens` function not for the full `inAmount` value, but only for the amount of tokens suitable for one cycle. Additionally, we recommend writing tests for the code.
summary: The `StarBaseDCA` contract has a bug where the `inAmount` variable, which represents the total amount of tokens in an `Order` struct, is not being used correctly in the `fillDCA` function. This means that the dollar cost averaging mechanism will not work as intended, and there is a risk of losing tokens or having leftover tokens at the maker's address. The recommended solution is to only transfer the amount of tokens suitable for one cycle in the `claimTokens` function and to write tests for the code.

title: Missing Validation of _FEE_RATE_ Variable ✓ Fixed
summary:
The bug report is about a problem with the code in the `2b508ff772206751317e8b0c6f5f70d4987a2b5e` commit. The issue was only partially fixed and the fix was only applied to one function in the `StarBaseDCA` contract. This means that the problem still exists in other functions and the `constructor` of the contract. Additionally, there is a mistake in the comment for a new variable, which could cause confusion. The report recommends adding validation checks and fixing the comment to avoid any further issues. 

In an update, the maximum fee limit was changed to 10%. However, this could still be a problem because the protocol owner can change the fees without giving users enough time to cancel their orders. It is suggested to add a timelock mechanism to prevent this issue. 

The bug is caused by the `_FEE_RATE_` variable being able to be set to any `uint160` value, which could result in fees as high as 100%. This could be exploited by the owner to steal tokens and cause excessive fees during transactions. The report recommends adding checks to limit the fee rate to a more reasonable amount, such as below 100%.

title: Anyone Can Steal All Funds From a DCA Order ✓ Fixed
summary: The report discusses a bug in the `StarBaseDCA` contract where an invalid `takerInteraction` parameter can cause the taker to receive more tokens than intended. This is due to a lack of validation on the `takerInteraction` parameter, which can result in the `curTakerFillAmount` being zero. This means that the taker will transfer zero tokens to the maker, but will still receive the `order.inAmount` tokens, essentially stealing tokens from the order. To fix this issue, it is recommended to add validation for the `order.minOutAmountPerCycle` in all circumstances.

title: Malicious Taker Can Use Permit From Different Trades for Gains ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report discusses a vulnerability in the `2b508ff772206751317e8b0c6f5f70d4987a2b5e` commit of the `StarBaseLimitOrder` and `StarBaseDCA` contracts. The lack of validation between the `inputToken` or `makerToken` in an order and the token in the `permitSingle` variable puts users with multiple active orders at risk. A malicious user can exploit this vulnerability by using the `permitSingle` data from one order to fill a different order, resulting in a gain of tokens. To fix this issue, the `PERMIT2` library needs to be fully removed and validation should be added to ensure that the token and amount in the `permit` data match the specific order.

title: Front-Running in NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report discusses a vulnerability in the NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer, which is used to pay a delegator for executing a delegation. The issue is that another redeemer can front-run the original redeemer by using the same payment delegation. This vulnerability can be prevented by using the ArgsEqualityCheckEnforcer, which checks that the delegation can only be executed by the original redeemer. However, this enforcer is currently optional and does not protect against front-running when the delegation is open. The recommendation is to add a require statement in the afterHook function to ensure that the immediate delegator is equal to the redeemer. This issue has been fixed in the PR16.

title: Open Delegations Combined With NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer Are Not Protected Against Front-Running ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



Fixed in [PR16](https://github.com/MetaMask/delegation-framework/pull/16).


`ArgsEqualityCheckEnforcer` enforcer terms contain the delegation hash and the redeemer. This prevents an external actor from front\-running the payment when executing a delegation.




#### Description


The `NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer` is an enforcer that, combined with a delegation `D1`, ensures a `delegate` pays to redeem `D1`. The `delegate` that redeems the delegation `D1` must include in the arguments of this enforcer a delegation `D2` to the `NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer` itself. It will give the right to the enforcer to pull the amount specified in the first place in the terms of the `NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer` to exercise the delegation `D1`.


To prevent front\-running and the use of the second delegation `D2` by a malicious actor who inspects the mempool, the usage of the `ArgsEqualityCheckEnforcer`  enforcer is recommended with `terms` being the `delegationHash` of the first delegation `D1`. This will ensure that the delegation that is being paid for with the delegation `D2` is the delegation `D1`.
While this works well when the delegation `D1` is restricted to a specific delegate, it is not sufficient in the case of open delegations.


The Delegator framework offers the possibility to create an open delegation. The purpose of an open delegation is that it can be redeemed by anyone.


The problem is that the computed `delegationHash`, is based on the fields of the delegation structure and the enforcers terms. However, in case of an open delegation, the `delegate` field will contain the same value (`ANY_DELEGATE`) regardless of who is currently redeeming the delegation.


The `DelegationManager` contract will accept the redeem from anyone when the delegation `delegate` field is `ANY_DELEGATE`.


**src/DelegationManager.sol:L154**



```
if (delegations_[0].delegate != msg.sender && delegations_[0].delegate != ANY_DELEGATE) {

```
In such a scenario, anyone using `D1` would share the same `delegationHash` in the arguments. Consequently, someone could watch the mempool and front\-run a legitimate redeem by leveraging the delegation `D2`. The attacker would be able to execute his own action with the delegation `D1` but use the delegation `D2` (which was generated by someone else) to pay the right to exercise it.


#### Recommendation


Ensure that the consumer of the delegation `D2` (also known as immediate delegator) is the current redeemer of the delegation `D1`.
This could be done using the `redeemer` parameter of the `afterHook` function of the `NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer`  enforcer.
summary:
The bug report discusses an issue with the Delegator framework, specifically with the `NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer` enforcer. This enforcer is used to ensure that a delegate pays to redeem a delegation. However, there is a vulnerability that allows a malicious actor to front-run the payment and use the delegation for their own actions.

The bug is caused by the `ArgsEqualityCheckEnforcer` enforcer, which checks the delegation hash and the redeemer. This prevents an external actor from front-running the payment when executing a delegation. However, this only works when the delegation is restricted to a specific delegate. In the case of open delegations, where anyone can redeem the delegation, the `delegate` field will always be the same value, making it easy for a malicious actor to front-run the payment.

To fix this issue, the recommendation is to ensure that the consumer of the delegation is the current redeemer. This can be done by using the `redeemer` parameter of the `afterHook` function of the `NativeTokenPaymentEnforcer` enforcer. This will prevent anyone else from using the delegation for their own actions.

The bug has been fixed in [PR16](https://github.com/MetaMask/delegation-framework/pull/16).

title: Oracle.periodCumulativesInside Can Return a Wrong Result ✓ Fixed
summary: The report discusses a bug in the Ramses V3 code which tracks several amounts outside of a tick. The bug occurs when the tick is crossed and the initialization value is not properly set, resulting in a wrong result for the seconds per liquidity within a period between two ticks. The bug can occur if the block's timestamp is a multiple of 1 week. The report recommends a solution to fix the bug by adjusting the code in the Oracle function to return the SPL at time `period * 1 weeks - 1` instead of `period * 1 weeks`. It also suggests adjusting the sanity check to prevent the bug from occurring on Ethereum mainnet.

title: If secondsPerLiquidityInsideX128 - secondsPerLiquidityPeriodStartX128 Returns a Negative Value While Minting, Accounting for the Position Will Be Incorrect  Partially Addressed
summary: The bug report discusses an issue in the Ramses-V3 code that can lead to incorrect position accounting. This issue has been partially fixed, but further testing is required to confirm that the fix holds in all cases. The issue occurs when a position is burned and then minted again, resulting in a negative value for the `secondsPerLiquidityInsideX128` variable. This can lead to incorrect calculations of the position's provided liquidity during a given period. The report suggests increasing test coverage and using fuzzing to ensure the fix is effective. The report also mentions two mechanisms in the code that work together to keep track of the correct amount of SPL accrued by each position. However, there is a concern that the code may not work correctly when ticks are cleared, and further investigation is needed to confirm the solution.

title: Debt Is Added Instead of Subtracted in positionPeriodSecondsInRange ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



 Fixed in commit [1f0b7a520f7a9378affab0578d872779ad2562d2](https://github.com/RamsesExchange/Ramses-V3/commit/1f0b7a520f7a9378affab0578d872779ad2562d2)


#### Description


When liquidity is added to or removed from a position, the `secondsDebtX96` member of the reward information gets updated. The intention here is to have a *corrective* value that allows to calculate the period\-seconds the position has been in range from its liquidity and period\-SPL *at the end of the period*.


More specifically, when liquidity is *added* to a position, we’ll later *overestimate* the period\-seconds in range, and we’re *increasing* the `secondsDebt96`. If, on the other hand, liquidity is *removed* from a position, we’ll later *underestimate* the period seconds in range, and `secondsDebt96` is *decreased*:


**contracts/CL/core/libraries/Position.sol:L124\-L134**



```
int256 secondsDebtDeltaX96 = SafeCast.toInt256(
    FullMath.mulDivRoundingUp(
        liquidityDelta > 0 ? uint256(uint128(liquidityDelta)) : uint256(uint128(-liquidityDelta)),
        uint256(uint160(secondsPerLiquidityPeriodIntX128)),
        FixedPoint32.Q32
    )
);

self.periodRewardInfo[period].secondsDebtX96 = liquidityDelta > 0
    ? self.periodRewardInfo[period].secondsDebtX96 + secondsDebtDeltaX96
    : self.periodRewardInfo[period].secondsDebtX96 - secondsDebtDeltaX96; // can't overflow since each period is way less than uint31

```
Based on this logic – positive liquidity delta increases debt, negative liquidity delta decreases debt – the correct thing to do in `positionPeriodSecondsInRange` is *subtracting* `secondsDebtX96` from the product of the positions’s liquidity and its period\-SPL, both taken at the end of the period. However, what actually happens is that the value is *added*:


**contracts/CL/core/libraries/Position.sol:L246\-L255**



```
periodSecondsInsideX96 = FullMath.mulDiv(liquidity, secondsPerLiquidityInsideX128, FixedPoint32.Q32);

// Need to check if secondsDebtX96>periodSecondsInsideX96, since rounding can cause underflows
if (secondsDebtX96 < 0 || periodSecondsInsideX96 > uint256(secondsDebtX96)) {
    periodSecondsInsideX96 = secondsDebtX96 < 0
        ? periodSecondsInsideX96 - uint256(-secondsDebtX96)
        : periodSecondsInsideX96 + uint256(secondsDebtX96);
} else {
    periodSecondsInsideX96 = 0;
}

```
Note also that the conditon in the `if` statement is the correct one for subtracting, and, finally, that the name “debt” also suggests that the value should be subtracted instead of added. So this is clearly a careless mistake, and not a subtle error, but the consequences are severe: The result returned by `positionPeriodSecondsInRange` is wrong, unless `secondsDebtX96` happens to be 0\. As this value is used for the calculation of rewards, this also means that the rewards are generally wrong. Moreover, it is directly exploitable: By starting with a low\-liquidity position and adding a lot of liquidity a bit later, thereby creating a huge debt, the period\-seconds in range for the position – and therefore the rewards – can be excessively inflated.


#### Recommendation


The addition has to be changed to a subtraction. Concretely, the two lines



```
                ? periodSecondsInsideX96 - uint256(-secondsDebtX96)
                : periodSecondsInsideX96 + uint256(secondsDebtX96);

```
have to be replaced with



```
                ? periodSecondsInsideX96 + uint256(-secondsDebtX96)
                : periodSecondsInsideX96 - uint256(secondsDebtX96);

```
Since this mistake does not only surface for exotic edge cases but almost always leads to a wrong reward when positions are modified, the presence of this bug also exhibits deficiencies with the test methodology. We strongly recommend implementing a rigorous and comprehensive test methodology before considering a production deployment.
summary: This report discusses a bug in the Ramses-V3 code, specifically in the `secondsDebtX96` member of the reward information. The bug causes incorrect calculations for the period-seconds a position has been in range, leading to incorrect rewards. The bug is caused by a careless mistake in the code, where the value is added instead of subtracted. This bug can be exploited by adding large amounts of liquidity to a low-liquidity position, resulting in inflated rewards. The recommendation is to fix the code by changing the addition to a subtraction and to implement a more rigorous testing methodology before deploying the code.

title: Two nonReentrancy Modiﬁers Prevent liquidate() Execution
description:
## Description

Two `nonReentrant` modifiers are executed in a single call, causing `ReentrancyGuard` to revert during `liquidate()`.

When the function `AbstractLender.liquidate()` is called, the following call sequence occurs:

1. `AbstractLender.liquidate()` is called on the lender contract. The function has a `nonReentrant` modifier. At this point, `_reentrancyStatus` is set to `_REENTRANCY_ENTERED`.
2. `IPeerToPeerOpenTermLoan(loanAddr).liquidate()` is called on the respective loan contract. This code may execute `InitializableOpenTermLoan.liquidate()`.
3. `IHookableLender(lender).notifyLoanMatured()` is called on the lender contract. The function has a `nonReentrant` modifier as described in `HookableLender.sol`.

Since the `_reentrancyStatus` of the lender contract was already set to `_REENTRANCY_ENTERED` in step (1), the call in step (3) would cause a revert on `BaseReentrancyGuard._nonReentrantBefore()`. The result is that `AbstractLender.liquidate()` will revert.

The impact is rated as medium severity as being unable to call `liquidate()` prevents losses from being accounted for at the pool level.

## Recommendations

Consider removing one of the `nonReentrant` modifiers, either on `AbstractLender` or `HookableLender` contract.

## Resolution

The issue was resolved on commit `2196d53`. The `nonReentrant` modifier on `AbstractLender.liquidate()` was removed.
summary: This bug report describes an issue where two nonReentrant modifiers are being executed in a single call, causing the ReentrancyGuard to revert during the liquidate() function. This occurs because the _reentrancyStatus is set to _REENTRANCY_ENTERED in step (1) and then a call is made to the lender contract in step (3), causing a revert on the _nonReentrantBefore() function. This prevents the liquidate() function from being called and can result in losses at the pool level. The recommendation is to remove one of the nonReentrant modifiers on either the AbstractLender or HookableLender contract, which was eventually resolved in a commit.

title: Use EIP-712-style Signed Hashing to Prevent Cross-Chain Signature Replaying ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



Addressed in stages:


* [PR 822](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/822) by adding the chainId to the hashed data.
* [PR 916](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/916), [PR 1041](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/1041), and [PR 1054](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/1054) by modifying the signed struct to be fully [EIP\-712](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/master/EIPS/eip-712.md) compliant.




#### Description


The current implementation uses a raw `ecrecover` function to verify whether a user signed a data structure by hashing the data directly. This approach is susceptible to cross\-network replay attacks. To enhance security and prevent such issues, the implementation should use a domain separator as specified in EIP\-712\.


**contracts/src/core/BatcherPaymentService.sol:L230\-L244**



```
function verifySignatureAndDecreaseBalance(
    bytes32 hash,
    SignatureData calldata signatureData,
    uint256 feePerProof
) private {
    bytes32 noncedHash = keccak256(
        abi.encodePacked(hash, signatureData.nonce)
    );

    address signer = ecrecover(
        noncedHash,
        signatureData.v,
        signatureData.r,
        signatureData.s
    );

```
#### Recommendation


Utilize the OpenZeppelin [EIP712](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/cryptography/EIP712.sol) and [ECDSA](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/cryptography/ECDSA.sol) libraries to implement domain\-bound signatures. These libraries provide robust and battle\-tested solutions for signature validation, mitigating common issues associated with ECDSA and preventing cross\-network replay attacks.
summary: This bug report discusses a potential security vulnerability in the implementation of a payment service contract. The current method of verifying user signatures is susceptible to cross-network replay attacks, which can compromise the security of the system. To address this issue, the report recommends implementing domain-bound signatures using the OpenZeppelin EIP712 and ECDSA libraries. This will provide a more robust and secure solution for signature validation. The bug has been resolved in stages through a series of pull requests, including adding the chainId to the hashed data and modifying the signed struct to be fully EIP-712 compliant.

title: Batcher Balance May Be Insufficient ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



 Addressed in [yetanotherco/aligned\_layer\#876](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/876) by introducing a new function `depositToBatcher(address account)` that allows to increase the balance of a given `account` by `msg.value` sent along with the transaction. This allows to top off the batcher’s balance so the task can be responded to.
Additionally, PR [yetanotherco/aligned\_layer\#804](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/804) also helps alleviate the problem of insufficient batcher balance, as now previously submitted Merkle roots can be re\-submitted with another sender with sufficient balance as the associated batcher to create the task.
 

#### Description


The `AlignedLayerServiceManager` contract maintains a balance tracker, `batchersBalances[]`, which is updated either through the `receive()` function from a user or during `createTask()`. The latter requires a non\-zero value to be sent with the message:


**contracts/src/core/AlignedLayerServiceManager.sol:L65\-L69**



```
if (msg.value > 0) {
    batchersBalances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
}

require(batchersBalances[msg.sender] > 0, "Batcher balance is empty");

```
Once a task is created for a batcher address, it remains associated with that address and cannot be removed. When responding to the task, the system verifies that the batcher has sufficient funds to cover the transaction:


**contracts/src/core/AlignedLayerServiceManager.sol:L104\-L107**



```
require(
    batchersBalances[batchesState[batchMerkleRoot].batcherAddress] > 0,
    "Batcher has no balance"
);

```
**contracts/src/core/AlignedLayerServiceManager.sol:L139\-L143**



```
require(
    batchersBalances[batchesState[batchMerkleRoot].batcherAddress] >=
        txCost,
    "Batcher has not sufficient funds for paying this transaction"
);

```
The initial check ensures a non\-zero balance, while the second check requires a specific amount and will revert if the balance is insufficient. This can lead to a situation where a batcher’s task becomes unrespondable if their balance is depleted, whether due to malicious intent or an error. Furthermore, the balance tracker is only updated through `receive()` or `createTask()`, and there is no mechanism to top off a batcher’s balance without their direct involvement.


#### Recommendation


Consider


* asking for specific funds during createTask so the rest of the flow goes through
* allowing for admins to remove tasks
* scratching the refund mechanism
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `AlignedLayerServiceManager` contract, specifically with the `batchersBalances` balance tracker. The problem arises when a batcher's balance becomes depleted, making it impossible for them to respond to tasks. This can happen due to malicious intent or an error, and there is currently no way to top off a batcher's balance without their direct involvement. The report recommends implementing a new function, `depositToBatcher(address account)`, to increase the balance of a given account by the amount sent along with the transaction. It also suggests allowing for admins to remove tasks and considering removing the refund mechanism. These changes have been addressed in two pull requests, [yetanotherco/aligned\_layer\#876](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/876) and [yetanotherco/aligned\_layer\#804](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/804).

title: tx.gasprice Allows a Malicious User to Steal All Funds From the Batcher Balance ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



Addressed in:


* [PR 869](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/869) by allowing users to specify a maximum fee to be taken for processing their signatures
* [PR 910](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/910) by limiting the fee that the aggregator can take for processing the batch


Additionally, [PR 883](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/883) was introduced that further protects the system by placing an authentication check on `respondToTaskV2()` so that only the aggregator may call it to safeguard against frontrunners that would otherwise be able to steal the fee meant for the aggregator.




#### Description


To calculate the refund for a user, the contracts use `tx.gasprice`. However, this is an effective gas price that the user pays, not a system\-set price. In particular, it consists of two gas prices:


* base fee, as set by the system
* priority fee, which is tipped to the miner and defined by the user.


This gas price is used to calculate the transaction cost to refund the user:


**contracts/src/core/AlignedLayerServiceManager.sol:L137**



```
uint256 txCost = (initialGasLeft - finalGasLeft + 70000) * tx.gasprice;

```
In the event that a user\=\=miner, they can:


1. set an absurdly high transaction price
2. call `respondToTask()`
3. perform the transaction
4. get the inflated transaction refund which would siphon all the funds out from the `batchersBalances[batchesState[batchMerkleRoot].batcherAddress]`


#### Recommendation


Consider redesigning the refund mechanism to not be susceptible to user\-given parameters, such as a flat refund or a base fee\-focused refund.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the calculation of refunds for users in a contract system. Currently, the system uses the gas price set by the user, which includes a base fee and a priority fee. However, this can be manipulated by users who are also miners, allowing them to siphon funds meant for the system. The report recommends redesigning the refund mechanism to avoid relying on user-defined parameters. The issue has been addressed in several pull requests, including one that adds an authentication check to protect against potential attacks by frontrunners.

title: Frontrunning DoS on createNewTask Allows Anyone to Block Legitimate batchMerkleRoot Submissions ✓ Fixed
summary: The report describes a bug in the `AlignedLayerServiceManager.createNewTask()` function, which can be exploited by malicious actors to cause Denial of Service (DoS) attacks. This is due to a lack of authentication and insufficient balance management. The function only requires a small amount of funds to be set as the batcher for a merkle root, which can lead to extortion or DoS conditions. The function also emits a user-provided `batchDataPointer` in events, which can be manipulated by front-running legitimate task creations. The report recommends implementing a minimum balance requirement, removing transaction cost reimbursement, and authenticating the function. It also suggests using a more efficient data type for the `batchDataPointer` input.

title: BatcherPaymentService - onlyBatcher Restriction, batchMerkleRoot Verification, pausable, and feePerProof Can Be Bypassed Completely by Calling AlignedLayerServiceManager Directly  Partially Addressed
summary: This bug report highlights several vulnerabilities in the Batcher and Aligned Layer contracts. These vulnerabilities allow unauthorized actions and bypass essential validations, potentially compromising the security and integrity of the system. The report recommends implementing access control and authentication checks in the contracts to prevent unauthorized access and ensure proper validation of data. It also suggests reviewing fee structures to prevent fee evasion.

title: Public Visibility on checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures Allows for DOS Attacks and User Fund Loss ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



Addressed with [yetanotherco/aligned\_layer\#801](https://github.com/yetanotherco/aligned_layer/pull/801) by changing the function name from `checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures` to `_checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures` and visibility from `public` to `private`. The function `verifySignatureAndDecreaseBalance` also had its name changed to `_verifySignatureAndDecreaseBalance` to follow style. The client provided the following statement:



> Visibility was changed to private, and private functions were refactored to start with \_ .
> Contracts were also redeployed in anvil.




#### Description


When a new task is created through `BatcherPaymentService`, the `createNewTask()` function is called with appropriate signature arguments to validate user submissions, subtract funds from their accounts, and ultimately create the task via a call to `AlignedLayerServiceManager.createNewTask()`.


However, the signature validation and balance adjustment happens in an intermediate function called `checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures()` which takes almost the same parameters:


**contracts/src/core/BatcherPaymentService.sol:L173\-L178**



```
function checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures(
    bytes32[] calldata leaves,
    bytes32 batchMerkleRoot,
    SignatureData[] calldata signatures,
    uint256 feePerProof
) public {

```
The issue is that this function is `public` with no modifiers, unlike `createNewTask()` which is both `onlyBatcher` and `whenNotPaused`. There are no further checks for `msg.sender`. As a result, any user can call `checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures()` directly with correct signature parameters by frontrunning the `createNewTask()` transaction, and the contract would validate the signatures and subtract user balances.


Two additional outcomes here are that:


* The user nonces are now updated, so those same signatures arguments that were taken can no longer be used, so the proper transaction that got frontran will be reverted in the same part of the code where the nonce got updated:


**contracts/src/core/BatcherPaymentService.sol:L248\-L249**



```
require(user_data.nonce == signatureData.nonce, "Invalid Nonce");
user_data.nonce++;

```
* The `feePerProof` argument is given directly in `checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures()`, so a malicious user can simply pick a large number to subtract all funds from user balances. Just as a note \- in `createNewTask()` the `feePerProof` argument is constructed from arguments by an authenticated called which is the batcher, so, while the resulting `feePerProof` could still be unfairly large, this is at least less possible from an authenticated called which has access to other admin\-like functionality on the contract.


The impact of this function’s visibility is that users may lose all their funds, and proper transactions can be reverted.


#### Recommendation


Adjust visibility and other argument checks on the `checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures()` function.
summary: The bug report discusses an issue with the `checkMerkleRootAndVerifySignatures()` function in the `BatcherPaymentService` contract. This function is publicly accessible and does not have any restrictions for the user calling it. This means that anyone can call this function and manipulate the contract by validating signatures and deducting funds from user accounts. This can lead to users losing all their funds and legitimate transactions being reverted. The recommendation is to change the function's visibility and add checks for arguments to prevent this issue. This bug has been addressed in a recent update by changing the function name and visibility, and redeploying the contracts.

title: Draining the protocol fully
summary: The bug report describes a vulnerability in a protocol where an attacker can exploit the system and drain a large amount of funds. The attacker deposits a large collateral and creates a series of orders that will increase the mark price and add unrealized profit to the collateral balance. This allows the attacker to create more orders and repeat the process until reaching the maximum allowed open interest. After the account is liquidated, the attacker can easily withdraw the remaining funds. The report includes a proof of concept that demonstrates how the attack can be carried out. The impact of this vulnerability is significant as it can result in a large amount of funds being stolen from the protocol. The report recommends investigating the issue and implementing measures to prevent similar attacks in the future.

title: Wrong parameter passed in `TradingAccount::deductAccountMargin` function that results in excess margin withdrawal
summary:
This bug report discusses an issue where the wrong parameter is passed in the `TradingAccount::deductAccountMargin` function, resulting in excess margin withdrawal. This is a high-risk issue that can have severe consequences. 

The problem occurs when a liquidation is executed, and the wrong parameter value for `pnlUsdX18` is passed in the `TradingAccount::deductAccountMargin` function. This causes the `marginBalanceUsdX18` to be inflated and the wrong tokens to be transferred. 

To demonstrate this issue, a Proof of Concept (POC) has been provided. This POC shows that a trader can receive 7,102 USDz as excess margin and 7,102 USDz less transferred to the `marginCollateralRecipient` upon liquidation. 

The impact of this bug is that the owner of the trading account can withdraw this excess margin. This can lead to a loss of funds for the platform and its users. 

To fix this issue, the absolute value of `accountTotalUnrealizedPnlUsdX18` should be passed as an argument for `pnlUsdX18` in the `TradingAccount::deductAccountMargin` function. This will prevent the inflation of `marginBalanceUsdX18` and ensure that the correct tokens are transferred. 

In conclusion, this bug can have severe consequences and should be fixed immediately to prevent any loss of funds.

title: `LiquidationBranch::checkLiquidatableAccounts()` executes `for` loop with wrong values, causing array out of bounds to be recovered, the program will not work as expected
summary: The program is experiencing a bug where a for loop is using incorrect values, causing the program to not work properly. This can be a medium risk issue. Even if the program conditions are not met, it will still store objects with a value of 0, which will affect how the program runs. This can be fixed by changing the code and testing it again to make sure it works properly.

title: Market Disruption and Financial Loss Post-Liquidation
summary: This report highlights a serious issue with the liquidation process of Zaros, which can result in a denial of service (DoS) and disrupt the market, potentially causing financial losses for traders. The root cause of this vulnerability is a mistake in the code that sets certain variables to zero instead of adding their values, which can lead to incorrect metrics and fees being calculated. This can also cause a DoS for positions that need to be updated, further impacting the market. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate the issue.

title: Incorrect logic for checking isFillPriceValid
summary: This report is about a bug in a program's code that checks if a trader has set a valid target price for their trade. The bug causes the program to always think the target price is invalid, so the trade cannot go through. This means traders cannot add take profit or stop loss to their trades. The bug can be fixed by changing the code to check if the target price is greater than or equal to the fill price for buy orders and less than or equal to the fill price for sell orders.

title: `SettlementBranch._fillOrder` does not guarantee the collateral of a position is enough to pay the future liquidation fee.
summary: The bug report is about a function called `SettlementBranch._fillOrder` that does not properly check if there is enough collateral to pay for future liquidation fees. This can be a problem because traders may not put enough collateral to cover the fees and exploit the system. The report suggests adding a check in the function to make sure the fees can be paid after opening a position. An alternative solution is also proposed, which involves estimating the total fees and comparing them to the available collateral.

title: Positive PnL is lost for all parties when liquidating an account, potentially causing that the MarginCollateralRecipient ends up receiving way less USD value than what it could have received.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue where when an account is liquidated, any positive PnL (profit) that it has is not properly transferred to the TradingAccount and MarginCollateralRecipient. This can result in the MarginCollateralRecipient receiving less USD value than they should have. The severity of this bug is considered high risk. The report provides details on how this bug occurs and how it affects the liquidation process. It also suggests a solution, which involves verifying if the account has positive PnL and minting it to the TradingAccount before deducting margin. This will ensure that the liquidated account receives the correct amount and the MarginCollateralRecipient receives the full USD value.

title: Inadequate Checking of `isIncreasing` when trader adjusts position size
summary: The report discusses a bug in the protocol that allows traders to increase their position size in the opposite direction, despite the market and settlement being disabled. This can lead to unexpected behaviors and make traders subject to liquidation. The bug is caused by inadequate checking of the `isIncreasing` function, which only checks if the `sizeDelta` direction is the same as the position size, but not the `self.size + sizeDelta` direction. The report recommends updating the `isIncreasing` function to also check the `self.size + sizeDelta` direction to prevent this bug.

title: [H-05] Swap of option profit to base token is not handled correctly
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `liquidate` and `exercise` functions in the `HegicModule.sol` file. These functions are used to exercise options and calculate profits. However, there is a problem with the code that converts profits from USDCe to USDC, which can cause the functions to fail or result in lower profits than expected. A proof of concept is provided, along with recommendations for fixing the issue.

title: [H-04] Accrued interest is not accounted for when withdrawing
summary: This bug report discusses a problem with the calculation of accrued interest in a `LiquidityPool` contract. When a user withdraws from the pool, the accrued interest is not taken into account, resulting in the user receiving less than their original deposit. This bug has a medium impact and a high likelihood of occurring. The report includes a proof of concept and recommendations for fixing the issue.

title: [H-03] Debt-free margin accounts can be liquidated
summary: The report describes a bug found in the `liquidate` method of the `MarginTrading` contract. This method allows anyone to liquidate an unhealthy account, but it does not properly check for debt-free accounts. This means that an attacker can maliciously liquidate a debt-free account, causing inconvenience and potentially causing financial harm to the account owner. The report provides a proof of concept for this attack and recommends adding an additional check to prevent it from happening.

title: [H-02] Potential swap failure in `UniswapModule`
summary: This bug report discusses an issue where the system fails to clear debts during liquidation. This is caused by a misconfiguration in the `UniswapModule` where the `swapOutput` function is not setting the `amountInMaximum` parameter correctly, resulting in the swap reverting and leaving the system unable to convert USDC into the needed `poolToken`. The recommendation is to adjust the `amountInMaximum` to reflect the actual maximum input expected for the swap, ensuring that the swap does not fail.

title: [H-01] Swaps are available for `MarginAccounts` undergoing liquidation
summary: This bug report addresses an issue with the `swap` function in the `MarginTrading` contract. This function is used to execute trades, but it does not properly check the liquidation status of a `MarginAccount` before executing the trade. This means that a malicious user could manipulate the trade and potentially cause asset loss. The report recommends adding a check to ensure that only healthy `MarginAccounts` can use the `swap` function.

title: [C-04] Users could avoid liquidation by providing a large number of position NFTs
summary: This bug report describes a problem where users can provide an unlimited number of position NFTs to their margin account, which can cause issues during liquidation. This can be exploited by users to avoid liquidation by causing an out-of-gas error. The report recommends restricting the maximum number of NFTs that can be added to a margin account to prevent this issue.

title: [C-03] Users can borrow tokens without generating debt shares
summary: This bug report is about a problem in the `borrow` function of the `LiquidityPool` contract. The function calculates the amount of debt shares to credit to a borrower, but there is an issue with the calculation that can be exploited by a malicious user. This allows the user to borrow tokens without generating any debt shares, draining the pool and causing losses for other borrowers. The report includes a proof of concept and a recommendation to fix the issue by rounding up the amount of debt shares instead of rounding down.

title: [C-02] Option NFTs can be exercised by any account
summary: The severity and impact of this bug are high, and the likelihood of it occurring is also high. The `exercise` function in the code does not check if the margin account owns the token that is being exercised. This means that any account can exercise the options of another account and receive its profit. A proof of concept code is provided to demonstrate how this bug can be exploited. To fix this issue, a requirement should be added to check if the margin account has ownership of the token before it can be exercised.

title: [C-01] Using Uniswap spot price is subject to manipulation
summary: This bug report highlights a high severity issue in the protocol that uses the Uniswap V3 quoter contract. The quoter is used to get the current value of supported tokens in terms of a base token (USDC). However, these values can be easily manipulated, which could result in losses for other users. This is because the quote of tokens is used in critical parts of the protocol such as withdrawal, borrowing, repayment, and liquidation. Additionally, in some transactions, there are multiple swaps involved, which can further complicate the issue. The report provides a proof of concept that demonstrates how an attacker could manipulate the price of a token in their favor and cause losses to other users. To prevent this, the report recommends using Chainlink oracles to get the price of assets instead of relying on the quoter.

title: [H-02] The limit for jars minted can be exceeded
summary: This bug report is about a high severity and high likelihood bug in the `Beekeeper` smart contract. The contract has a function called `_canMintHoneyJar` that checks if the number of jars being minted exceeds a predefined limit. However, there is a possibility for an attacker to use a reentrancy attack to bypass this check and mint more jars than allowed. This can lead to incorrect token ids being stored and potentially breaking the contract. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate this vulnerability. It is recommended to add a reentrancy guard to all functions that mint jars to prevent this attack.

title: [H-01] Funds distribution can fail due to the rounding up
summary: This bug report describes an issue with a function called `distribute` in a contract called `BearPouch`. When a certain type of digital asset called an NFT is sold, the function is supposed to distribute the funds received to different people. However, the function uses a calculation method that rounds up the amounts to be transferred, which can cause the total amount transferred to be more than the total amount received. This makes the transaction fail and prevents the NFT sale from being completed. The report suggests using a different calculation method to fix the issue.

title: [C-01] The communication channel for `HoneyJarONFT` can be blocked
summary: The bug report is about a problem in a contract called `HoneyJarONFT` that manages the transfer of NFTs (non-fungible tokens) between different blockchains. The problem occurs when the contract receives a cross-chain message, which is supposed to trigger the transfer of NFTs. However, due to a mistake in the code, the contract can run out of gas and fail to complete the transfer, causing the message to be stored for later processing. This can lead to the loss of NFTs for the user and also block the contract from receiving any more messages. The report suggests a change in the code to fix this issue and prevent it from happening in the future.
