title: H-1: Malicious users can bypass the blacklist.
description:
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-05-midas-judging/issues/9 

The protocol has acknowledged this issue.

## Found by 
0xloscar01, Drynooo, PNS, blutorque, deepkin, den\_sosnovskyi, recursiveEth, wildflowerzx
## Summary
The protocol sets the blacklist through roles, and users can bypass the blacklist through the [renounceRole function](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/blob/f6febd79e2a3a17e26969dd0d450c6ebd64bf459/contracts/access/AccessControlUpgradeable.sol#L186-L190).

## Vulnerability Detail
[mTBILL does not allow blacklisted users to transfer funds.](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-05-midas/blob/a4a3cc23bb891913ce44665a4cdea9f5c1190f6c/midas-contracts/contracts/mTBILL.sol#L90-L102)
```solidity
    function _beforeTokenTransfer(
        address from,
        address to,
        uint256 amount
    )
        internal
        virtual
        override(ERC20PausableUpgradeable)
        onlyNotBlacklisted(from)
        onlyNotBlacklisted(to)
    {
        ERC20PausableUpgradeable._beforeTokenTransfer(from, to, amount);
    }
```

But it is implemented in the form of giving [BLACKLISTED_ROLE.](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-05-midas/blob/a4a3cc23bb891913ce44665a4cdea9f5c1190f6c/midas-contracts/contracts/access/Blacklistable.sol#L38-L42)
```solidity
    function _onlyNotBlacklisted(address account)
        private
        view
        onlyNotRole(BLACKLISTED_ROLE, account)
    {}
```

The AccessControlUpgradeable contract has a [renounceRole function](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts-upgradeable/blob/f6febd79e2a3a17e26969dd0d450c6ebd64bf459/contracts/access/AccessControlUpgradeable.sol#L186-L190), through which users can give up their BLACKLISTED_ROLE, thereby bypassing the blacklist.
```solidity
    function renounceRole(bytes32 role, address account) public virtual override {
        require(account == _msgSender(), "AccessControl: can only renounce roles for self");

        _revokeRole(role, account);
    }
```

## Impact
Malicious users can bypass the blacklist.

## Code Snippet
```solidity
    function _beforeTokenTransfer(
        address from,
        address to,
        uint256 amount
    )
        internal
        virtual
        override(ERC20PausableUpgradeable)
        onlyNotBlacklisted(from)
        onlyNotBlacklisted(to)
    {
        ERC20PausableUpgradeable._beforeTokenTransfer(from, to, amount);
    }
```

## Tool used

Manual Review

## Recommendation
It is recommended not to use roles to implement blacklists.



## Discussion

**pkqs90**

Nice issue. I missed the escalation period but still want to make a comment - should this therotically be medium instead of high, since it won't cause a direct loss of funds or non-material losses?

**amankakar**

> Nice issue. I missed the escalation period but still want to make a comment - should this therotically be medium instead of high, since it won't cause a direct loss of funds or non-material losses?

Although i have missed this finding But I think the High is appropriate because the user can easily bypass the blacklist status.

**blutorque**

I think this is more severe, considering the mTBill can immediately be traded in a secondary market(such as Morpho), which already hold ~[30%](https://etherscan.io/token/tokenholderchart/0xDD629E5241CbC5919847783e6C96B2De4754e438) of mTBill supply.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue where malicious users can bypass the blacklist in a protocol. The protocol sets the blacklist through roles, but users can bypass it by using the "renounceRole" function. This function allows users to give up their "BLACKLISTED_ROLE" and bypass the blacklist. This can have a severe impact as it allows malicious users to trade in a secondary market and potentially cause harm. The recommendation is to not use roles to implement blacklists. The report was found through a manual review and it was discussed whether the severity should be medium or high, with the conclusion being that high is appropriate due to the potential for harm.

title: Repeated Fee Deduction
summary: This report discusses a bug in a function called "claimSaleToken" that is responsible for charging a flat fee for claiming tokens. If this function is not designed carefully, it can introduce vulnerabilities, especially when it is called multiple times. The function "_chargeClaimFlatFee" checks for the correct fee and transfers it to the recipient, but this check only works correctly if the function is called exactly once per transaction. If it is called multiple times, subsequent calls will still see the original value sent with the transaction, potentially depleting the contract's funds. The recommended solution is to ensure that the function is only called once per transaction or to include state checks to prevent multiple deductions. This bug has been fixed in version 71216e4.

title: Claimer Fee Exploitation
summary: This bug report discusses an issue where a user can make a small purchase and then assign another user as the claimer. This results in the designated claimer being forced to pay a flat fee for each entry in the claimerToBuyers array, even for zero-value claims. This can lead to the claimer incurring fees for handling these zero-value claims. Additionally, an attacker can exploit this by creating multiple small purchases using different accounts, significantly increasing the gas cost of calling the claimSaleToken function and potentially making it too expensive or even impossible to execute within the block gas limit. The recommended solution is to set a minimum purchase amount to ensure that all purchases are substantial enough to warrant processing. This issue has been fixed in a recent update.

title: Signature Reuse Via Front-Running
summary:
The current signature scheme in NFTSimpleAuction may be vulnerable to front-running. This means that a legitimate user who completes the whitelist procedure and receives a valid signed code from the authorizedWLSigner can buy NFTs at a discounted price. However, if an attacker detects a whitelist purchase transaction, they can exploit the absence of ownership checks in the signature. The attacker can submit their own purchase transaction using the stolen signed code before the original user's transaction is confirmed. This allows them to purchase NFTs at the discounted price intended for the original user.

To fix this issue, a nonce mechanism should be introduced in the signed code. The whitelist server would generate a unique nonce for each user and include it in the signed data (extraData). The _checkAndSaveWL function would need to verify that the nonce has not been used before. This ensures that the signed code can only be used once, preventing attackers from re-using stolen codes.

This issue has been fixed in the adf0fe6 version.

title: Redeeming Does Not Discount Tokens of Removed Artists, Leading to Inflated Rewards
description:
**Update**
The client fixed the issue in commit `992783e5724f7ee97a84004f8d556960dfbc9e0f` and provided the following explanation:

> The onlyVerifiedArtist modifier has been added on each of the functions that manipulate the stake. A check on the status of the artist was added to the function, so if it is not verified it will not be able to accumulate tokens. The artist removal operation now does not delete the artist's artistCheckpoint and before the change in the Boolean associated with the artist's state claims the award for the artist. Since the artistCheckpoint is not deleted, re-verification of a previously removed artist is now handled separately, so that the lastRedeem parameter is changed and tokens do not accrue during the removal period.

**File(s) affected:**`FanToArtistStaking.sol`

**Description:** Function `FanToArtistStaking.redeem()` removes a given staked amount from the target artist:

```
if (_verifiedArtists[artist]) {
      _calcSinceLastPosition(artist, _stake[artist][user].amount, false);
   }
```

However, this is only applied for still actively verified artists, not to artists that have been removed from the contract owner via `removeArtist()`.

This leads to the removed artists gaining inflated accumulated rewards, compared to existing artists.

This issue is further exacerbated by the fact that stakers may increase or extend stakes to removed artists, or redirect existing stakes of existing artists to removed artists: existing stakes may still be increased or extended via `increaseAmountStaked()`, `changeArtistStaked()` and `extendStake()`, as those functions do no verify the artist to still be verified.

Finally, the removed artist (or anyone else) may call `getReward()`, minting the inflated accumulated value of `RECORD` tokens to that artist.

**Recommendation:** We recommend changing the logic to also deduct redeemed amounts of removed artists. Consider:

1.   Verifying that the artist is still active when calling:
    *   `increaseAmountStaked()`
    *   `extendStake()`
    *   for `newArtist` in `changeArtistStaked()`

2.   Update the staked amount of the artist when `redeem()` is executed, regardless of his status (active or not).
summary: This bug report is about an issue with the `FanToArtistStaking.sol` file, which is used for staking tokens in exchange for rewards from artists. The report explains that there was a problem with the `redeem()` function, which is used to remove a staked amount from an artist. The issue was that the function did not properly deduct redeemed amounts from artists who had been removed from the contract owner's list of verified artists. This meant that removed artists were receiving more rewards than they should have been. The report recommends making changes to the logic of the code to fix this issue. These changes include verifying the artist's status before allowing any stake increases or extensions, and updating the artist's staked amount when `redeem()` is called, regardless of their active status.

title: [H-01] Slashing isn't supported in the rebasing mechanism
description:
**Severity**

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** Medium

**Description**

The function `rebase()` has been used to increase the share price and apply staking rewards. The issue is that staking has its own risks and stake amounts can be slashed (In Commume or Bittensor network) and current logic doesn't support decreasing the share price. Also, some tokens can be stolen or lost when bridging so it would be necessary to have the ability to decrease the share price to adjust the share price according to those events.

**Recommendations**

Add the ability to decrease the share price too.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the function `rebase()` which is used to increase share prices and apply staking rewards. The problem is that staking carries its own risks and can result in a decrease in stake amounts. The current logic does not support decreasing the share price, which can lead to tokens being stolen or lost when bridging. The recommendation is to add the ability to decrease the share price in order to adjust for these events. This bug is considered high severity and has a medium likelihood of occurring.

title: [C-02] Function `rebase()` apply wrong APR in RivusTAO
description:
**Severity**

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

**Description**

The function `rebase()` is supposed to apply daily APR to the share price by decreasing the total share amount. The issue is that the code uses `totalSharesAmount * apr` to calculate `burnAmount` so the burned amount would be bigger than what it should be. This is the POC:

1. Suppose there are 100 shares and 100 tokens.
2. Admin wants to apply a 20% increase for one day.
3. Code would calculate the burn amount as `100 * 20% = 20` and the new total share would be 80.
4. Now the token to share price would be `100/80 = 1.25` and as you can see the ratio increases by 25%.
5. This would cause a wrong reward rate and those who withdraw sooner would steal others tokens.

**Recommendations**

Code should use `totalSharesAmount * apr / (1 +apr)` to calculate the burn amount.
summary: This bug report describes an issue with the `rebase()` function, which is supposed to apply a daily APR (Annual Percentage Rate) to the share price by decreasing the total share amount. However, the code currently uses an incorrect calculation for the `burnAmount`, resulting in a larger burned amount than intended. This can cause an incorrect reward rate and unfair distribution of tokens. The recommended solution is to use a different calculation for the burn amount.

title: [C-01] Unlimited token transfer
description:
**Severity**

**Impact:** High

**Likelihood:** High

**Description**

Function `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()` has been used to calculate amount of shares that corresponds to the RsTAO amount and it's been used in multiple functions like `_transfer()` and `_mintRsTAO()`. The issue is that the function `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()` returns 0 when the total minted amount is 0 while it should have returned the amount itself. This has multiple impacts like transferring unlimited tokens while the total mint is 0, this is the POC:

1. Suppose RivusTAO is recently deployed or for other reasons (upgrade or ...) the total amount is zero.
2. Now attacker can transfer unlimited tokens to 3rd party contracts like DEX or lending platforms and credit tokens for himself.
3. This is possible because when RivusTAO wants to transfer tokens in the `_transfer()` it would call `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()` to calculate the share amount and the share amount would be 0, so the code would have no problem transferring 0 shares.
4. In the end the 3rd party contract would charge the user account while in reality, it didn't receive any tokens. The `transferFrom()` call would return true and won't revert.

There are other impacts. Function `_mintRsTAO()` uses `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()` too and when the return amount is 0 then the code uses `amount` to mint shares. The issue is that the return amount of `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()` can be 0 because of the rounding error (small values of `amount`) and the code should have minted 0 shares while it would mint >0 shares. This can be used to extract value from contracts with small deposit amounts while the share price is high.

This issue exists for rsCOMAI and RivusCOMAI contracts too.

**Recommendations**

When the total minted tokens are 0 then the code should return `amount` in `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()`. The function `getMintedRsTAOByShares()` should be fixed too. Those fixes should be applied to COMAI contracts too.
summary: This bug report highlights a problem with the function `getSharesByMintedRsTAO()` in the RivusTAO contract. When the total amount of tokens minted is 0, the function returns 0 instead of the actual amount. This allows attackers to transfer unlimited tokens to other contracts and potentially extract value from small deposits. The report recommends fixing this issue in the RivusTAO and COMAI contracts.

title: [H-02] Arbitrary tokens and data can be bridged to `GnosisTargetDispenserL2` to manipulate staking incentives
description:
The [`GnosisTargetDispenserL2`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/GnosisTargetDispenserL2.sol) contract receives OLAS tokens and data from L1 to L2 via the Omnibridge, or just data via the AMB. When tokens are bridged, the `onTokenBridged()` callback is invoked on the contract. This callback processes the received tokens and associated data by calling the internal `_receiveMessage()` function.

However, the `onTokenBridged()` callback does not verify the sender of the message on the L1 side (or the token received).

This allows anyone to send any token to the `GnosisTargetDispenserL2` contract on L2 along with arbitrary data. The [`_receiveMessage()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/DefaultTargetDispenserL2.sol#L224) function in `DefaultTargetDispenserL2` will then process this data, assuming it represents valid staking targets and incentives.

### Impact

An attacker can bridge any tokens to the `GnosisTargetDispenserL2` contract on L2 with fake data for staking incentives. If the contract holds any withheld funds, these funds can be redistributed to arbitrary targets as long as they pass the [checks](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/DefaultTargetDispenserL2.sol#L160-L186) in `_processData()`.

Even if the contract doesn't hold any withheld funds, the attacker can cause the amounts to be [stored](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas/blob/3ce502ec8b475885b90668e617f3983cea3ae29f/tokenomics/contracts/staking/DefaultTargetDispenserL2.sol#L199) in `stakingQueueingNonces` and redeem them at a later point.

### Proof of Concept

1. Attacker calls `relayTokensAndCall()` on the Omnibridge on L1 to send any tokens to the `GnosisTargetDispenserL2` contract on L2.
2. Attacker includes malicious staking data in the `payload` parameter.
3. `onTokenBridged()` is called on `GnosisTargetDispenserL2`, which invokes `_receiveMessage()` to process the data.
4. Since the L1 sender is not validated, the malicious data is accepted and fake staking incentives are distributed.

### Recommended Mitigation Steps

The Omnibridge contracts do not seem to provide a way to access the original sender's address on L1 when [executing the receiver callback](https://github.com/omni/omnibridge/blob/master/contracts/upgradeable_contracts/BasicOmnibridge.sol#L471) upon receiving tokens. Hence, the most sensible mitigation may be to send the bridged tokens and associated staking data separately:

1. When bridging tokens, only send the token amount without any data via `relayTokens()`.
2. Always transmit the staking data through the AMB via `requireToPassMessage()`.
3. Remove the `onTokenBridged()` callback from  `GnosisTargetDispenserL2`.

This way, an attacker cannot send fake data along with the bridged tokens. The staking data will be validated to come from the authentic source on L1.

### Assessed type

Access Control

**[kupermind (Olas) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas-findings/issues/22#issuecomment-2188220224)**

**[0xA5DF (judge) commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas-findings/issues/22#issuecomment-2194772902):**
 > High severity seems appropriate, given that this can lead to the distribution of staking incentives to arbitrary targets.

**[Olas mitigated](https://github.com/valory-xyz/autonolas-tokenomics/pull/156)**

**[Varun_05 (warden) commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas-findings/issues/22#issuecomment-2254186575):**
> Fixed.

***
summary: The GnosisTargetDispenserL2 contract has a bug that allows anyone to send any token to the contract on L2 with fake data for staking incentives. This can result in the redistribution of withheld funds or manipulation of staking targets. The recommended mitigation is to send tokens and staking data separately through the AMB. This bug is classified as an access control issue and has been confirmed by the project team.

title: [H-01] `pointsSum.slope` Not Updated After Nominee Removal and Votes Revocation
description:
### Vulnerability details The `removeNominee` and `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` functions are part of the governance mechanism in the `VoteWeighting.sol` smart contract. - The `removeNominee` function removes a nominee from the voting system. - The `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` function revokes the voting power that a user has delegated to a nominee who has been removed. When a user votes for a nominee using the `voteForNomineeWeights` function, both `pointsSum.slope` and `pointsSum.bias` are updated to reflect the new voting weights: ```solidity pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias = _maxAndSub(_getWeight(account, chainId) + newBias, oldBias); pointsSum[nextTime].bias = _maxAndSub(_getSum() + newBias, oldBias); if (oldSlope.end > nextTime) { pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope = _maxAndSub(pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope + newSlope.slope, oldSlope.slope); pointsSum[nextTime].slope = _maxAndSub(pointsSum[nextTime].slope + newSlope.slope, oldSlope.slope); } else { pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope += newSlope.slope; pointsSum[nextTime].slope += newSlope.slope; } ``` However, when a nominee is removed by the owner through the `removeNominee` function, only `pointsSum.bias` is updated. `pointsSum.slope` is not updated, nor is it updated when users revoke their votes through the `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` function. As a result, the `pointsSum.slope` for the next timestamp will be incorrect as it still includes the removed nominee's slope. When the `_getSum()` function is called later to perform a checkpoint, the incorrect slope will be used for the calculation, causing the voting weight logic to become inaccurate: ```solidity function _getSum() internal returns (uint256) { // t is always > 0 as it is set in the constructor uint256 t = timeSum; Point memory pt = pointsSum[t]; for (uint256 i = 0; i < MAX_NUM_WEEKS; i++) { if (t > block.timestamp) { break; } t += WEEK; uint256 dBias = pt.slope * WEEK; if (pt.bias > dBias) { pt.bias -= dBias; uint256 dSlope = changesSum[t]; pt.slope -= dSlope; } else { pt.bias = 0; pt.slope = 0; } pointsSum[t] = pt; if (t > block.timestamp) { timeSum = t; } } return pt.bias; } ``` ### Impact The voting weight logic will be inaccurate after a nominee is removed, potentially compromising the integrity of the governance mechanism. ### Tools Used VS Code ### Recommended Mitigation To address this issue, ensure that `pointsSum.slope` is updated when a nominee is removed. This can be done in either the `removeNominee` or `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` functions to maintain correct accounting. ### Assessed type Error **[kupermind (Olas) confirmed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas-findings/issues/36#issuecomment-2191551133)** **[0xA5DF (judge) increased severity to High and commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas-findings/issues/36#issuecomment-2198226815):** > Marking as high, because this is going to break the core accounting of `VoteWeighting` every time a nominee is removed. The actual sum of the weights is going to be more than the declared sum. **[Olas mitigated](https://github.com/valory-xyz/autonolas-governance/pull/146)** **[Varun_05 (warden) commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-olas-findings/issues/36#issuecomment-2253868156):** > Partially fixed in revoke `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` but the issue still remains if all the users who voted for a removed nominee doesn't revoke their voting power. > > Elaborating the issues as follows. Nominee is removed due to which the following updation happens: > > ```solidity > uint256 oldWeight = _getWeight(account, chainId); > uint256 oldSum = _getSum(); > uint256 nextTime = (block.timestamp + WEEK) / WEEK * WEEK; > pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias = 0; > timeWeight[nomineeHash] = nextTime; > > // Account for the the sum weight change > uint256 newSum = oldSum - oldWeight; > pointsSum[nextTime].bias = newSum; > timeSum = nextTime; > ``` > > As seen, `pointsSum.bias` is updated by subtracted the left over weights of the removed nominee. Now, as `pointsSum.Slope` is not reduced by the amount contributed by the removed slope instantly. > > For mitigating this issue, the following changes were done in the `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower` function: > > ```solidity > if (oldSlope.end > nextTime) { > pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope = > _maxAndSub(pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope, oldSlope.slope); > pointsSum[nextTime].slope = _maxAndSub(pointsSum[nextTime].slope, oldSlope.slope); > } > ``` > > The issue is if there is even a delay of a week from when the nominee was removed to when the users who voted for the nominee then the `pointsSum.bias` would be reduced by wrong amount thus it will break the core accounting of vote weighting. > > Also, there is no loss of voting power for the user who voted for the removed nominee as he can call revoke removed nominee voting power any time and can get his voting power back thus they can even delay calling this function thus affecting vote accounting. > > One of the mitigation can be as follows: > >
> > ```solidity > function removeNominee(bytes32 account, uint256 chainId) external { > // Check for the contract ownership > if (msg.sender != owner) { > revert OwnerOnly(owner, msg.sender); > } > > // Get the nominee struct and hash > Nominee memory nominee = Nominee(account, chainId); > bytes32 nomineeHash = keccak256(abi.encode(nominee)); > > // Get the nominee id in the nominee set > uint256 id = mapNomineeIds[nomineeHash]; > if (id == 0) { > revert NomineeDoesNotExist(account, chainId); > } > > // Set nominee weight to zero > uint256 oldWeight = _getWeight(account, chainId); > uint256 oldSum = _getSum(); > uint256 nextTime = (block.timestamp + WEEK) / WEEK * WEEK; > pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].bias = 0; > ++ pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope = 0 > timeWeight[nomineeHash] = nextTime; > ++ uint256 totalSlope; > ++ for (uint256 i = 1; i =< MAX_NUM_WEEKS; i++) { > ++ uint256 time = nextTime + i * WEEK; > ++ if(changesWeight[nomineeHash][time]>0){ > ++ totalSlope += changesWeight[nomineeHash][time]; > ++ changesWeight[nomineeHash][time] = 0; > ++ changesSum[time] -= changesWeight[nomineeHash][time]; > } > > } > > // Account for the the sum weight change > uint256 newSum = oldSum - oldWeight; > pointsSum[nextTime].bias = newSum; > ++ pointsSum[nextTime].slope -= totalSlope; > timeSum = nextTime; > > // Add to the removed nominee map and set > mapRemovedNominees[nomineeHash] = setRemovedNominees.length; > setRemovedNominees.push(nominee); > > // Remove nominee from the map > mapNomineeIds[nomineeHash] = 0; > > // Shuffle the current last nominee id in the set to be placed to the removed one > nominee = setNominees[setNominees.length - 1]; > bytes32 replacedNomineeHash = keccak256(abi.encode(nominee)); > mapNomineeIds[replacedNomineeHash] = id; > setNominees[id] = nominee; > // Pop the last element from the set > setNominees.pop(); > > // Remove nominee in dispenser, if applicable > address localDispenser = dispenser; > if (localDispenser != address(0)) { > IDispenser(localDispenser).removeNominee(nomineeHash); > } > > emit RemoveNominee(account, chainId, newSum); > } > ``` > >
> > Then, there is no need of the following logic in revoke removed nominee voting power function. They can be omitted. > > ```solidity > uint256 nextTime = (block.timestamp + WEEK) / WEEK * WEEK; > // Adjust weight and sum slope changes > if (oldSlope.end > nextTime) { > pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope = > _maxAndSub(pointsWeight[nomineeHash][nextTime].slope, oldSlope.slope); > pointsSum[nextTime].slope = _maxAndSub(pointsSum[nextTime].slope, oldSlope.slope); > } > > // Cancel old slope changes if they still didn't happen > if (oldSlope.end > block.timestamp) { > changesWeight[nomineeHash][oldSlope.end] -= oldSlope.slope; > changesSum[oldSlope.end] -= oldSlope.slope; > } > ``` ***
summary: The `VoteWeighting.sol` smart contract has two functions, `removeNominee` and `revokeRemovedNomineeVotingPower`, that are used for the governance mechanism. However, when a nominee is removed, the `pointsSum.slope` is not updated, causing the voting weight logic to become inaccurate. This could potentially compromise the integrity of the governance mechanism. To fix this, the `pointsSum.slope` should be updated when a nominee is removed. This issue has been confirmed and marked as high severity, as it can break the core accounting of the `VoteWeighting` contract.

title: Insufficient Src Validation allows Malicious Users To Steal WSHIDO From Users With Zero Allowance
description:
**Severity**: Critical

**Status**: Resolved

**Description**

The WSHIDO token is forked from the WETH contract on the Ethereum Mainnet and is intended to allow users to wrap SHIDO to be used in the ecosystem. In the `transferFrom` function, there is a check which ensures that if src address is not equal to the `msg.sender` and the allowance is not equal to zero, deduct from allowance. After this check with no conditions, deduct from the src address and add to the dst address which both variables are user supplied and is where the issue lies. As a result, free token transfers can be made from users with zero allowance.

**Recommendation**: 

It’s recommended that the `transferFrom` method for the WSHIDO contract is refactored to include logic to account for the src address being the `msg.sender` and deduct amounts accordingly.
summary: The WSHIDO token, which allows users to wrap SHIDO for use in the ecosystem, has a critical bug that has been resolved. In the `transferFrom` function, there is a check to ensure that if the source address is not the same as the sender and the allowance is not zero, it will deduct from the allowance. However, the bug allows for free token transfers from users with zero allowance because there is no condition for this check. It is recommended that the `transferFrom` function is updated to account for this and deduct amounts accordingly.

title: [H-04] Liquidation incorrectly tries to transfer token from Market instead of liquidator if `remainingMargin` is negative
summary: This bug report describes an issue with the liquidation process in the PredyPool protocol. Liquidation is a process where a user's assets are sold to cover their debts in case of a margin call. However, if a user's position is entirely wiped out during liquidation, the code checks for remaining margin in the vault. If there is bad debt (negative margin value), the liquidator is responsible for paying it. However, the code tries to transfer tokens from the Market protocol instead of the liquidator, making it impossible to liquidate a vault with negative margin. This issue also leads to accumulating lending fees and increasing bad debt. The recommended solution is to transfer tokens from the liquidator instead of the Market protocol. The severity of this bug is high, and it has been confirmed by the project team.

title: [H-03] One pair can steal another pair's Uniswap liquidity during `reallocate()` call if both pairs operate on the same Uniswap pool and both have the same upper and lower tick during reallocation
summary: The Predy protocol has a bug where it does not properly check and allocate liquidity when a pair is being reallocated. This can cause issues when a trusted operator creates two pairs with the same Uniswap pool, but with different quote tokens. If a user trades gamma on the first pair and the price moves outside the threshold of the second pair, a reallocation on the second pair will take liquidity from the user's open gamma position in the first pair. This can lead to incorrect accounting and make it impossible to close or liquidate positions properly. A proof of concept test has been provided to demonstrate this issue. To mitigate this bug, it is recommended to perform internal accounting of the liquidity and collect fees proportionally from each pair. The severity of this bug is high and it has been confirmed by the Predy team.

title: [H-02] Liquidators can bypass remaining negative margin check and leave the loss to the protocol
summary: This bug report discusses a vulnerability in the Predy protocol that allows liquidators to profit from the protocol's insolvency. The protocol has a mechanism in place to protect against insolvency, but it only checks for negative margin if the position is fully closed. This means that liquidators can bypass this check by only partially closing a position and leaving the loss to the protocol. This can lead to value leaking from the protocol, but it only happens in certain situations. The suggested fix is to move the check for negative margin outside of the block that checks for an open position. The severity of this bug is rated as medium, as it only occurs in specific scenarios, but it can still have a negative impact on the protocol.

title: [H-01] Reallocation depends on the `slot0` price, which can be manipulated
summary: The `reallocate` function in the Perp.sol contract can be manipulated by anyone, potentially causing a loss of yield for the protocol. This is because the `slot0` price used to determine if reallocation is necessary can be manipulated. This can be exploited by forcing a reallocation to occur and then taking advantage of the re-allocated liquidity in an extreme tick range. The vulnerability is caused by using the spot square root price from the Uniswap V3 pair, which can be manipulated by external factors. It is recommended to use a TWAP price instead to mitigate this issue. The severity of this vulnerability has been increased to High and it is considered an Invalid Validation. The root cause is the same as another vulnerability (#157), but they have different impacts and cannot be mitigated in the same way. A potential re-design of the reallocation mechanism may be necessary to properly address this vulnerability.

title: H-2: Many cases `stEth::transferFrom` will transfer 1-2 less way, which would result in revert in consequent functions, because of not enough balance
description:
Source: https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-05-sophon-judging/issues/63 

The protocol has acknowledged this issue.

## Found by 
Bauchibred, EgisSecurity, zzykxx
## Summary
When user calls `depositStEth`, he passes `_amount` param, which is set to `IERC20(stETH).safeTransferFrom()` func and then the sam `_amount` is passed down the chain:
```solidity
        IERC20(stETH).safeTransferFrom(
            msg.sender,
            address(this),
            _amount
        );

        _depositPredefinedAsset(_amount, _amount, _boostAmount, PredefinedPool.wstETH);
 ```
## Vulnerability Detail
The probability of issue appearing is high and you can check in the following discussion. It has also been classified as a High severity on past contests:
https://github.com/lidofinance/lido-dao/issues/442

`stETH` is using shares for tracking balances and it is a known issue that due to rounding error, transferred shares may be 1-2 wei less than `_amount` passed.
This would revert on the following line as we have transferred `_amount - 1` and farming contract do not hold `stEth` funds:
```solidity
    function _stEthTOwstEth(uint256 _amount) internal returns (uint256) {
        // wrap returns exact amount of wstETH
        return IwstETH(wstETH).wrap(_amount);
    }
```
The impact may be bigger if the staking contract is implemented by 3rd party protocol and expect this the function to be always fine.
## Impact
- Contract functionality DoS 

## Code Snippet
https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-05-sophon/blob/05059e53755f24ae9e3a3bb2996de15df0289a6c/farming-contracts/contracts/farm/SophonFarming.sol#L474-L478
## Tool used

Manual Review

## Recommendation
Use lido recommendation to utilize `transferShares` function, so the `_amount` is realistic, or implement FoT approach, which compares the balance before and after the transfer. 



## Discussion

**sherlock-admin4**

1 comment(s) were left on this issue during the judging contest.

**0xmystery** commented:
>  valid because this parallels FOT as documented by Lido (best because the report is succinct and well documented)
summary: The report discusses a bug in a protocol where there is a possibility of transferring 1-2 less shares than the intended amount, resulting in a revert in subsequent functions. This can lead to a denial of service attack on the contract's functionality. The bug was found by three individuals and has been acknowledged by the protocol. The report suggests using lido's recommendation to fix the issue or implementing a FoT approach to prevent it.

title: H-1: The quantity is calculated incorrectly when depositing ETH to weETH.
summary: Bug report H-1 states that there is an issue with calculating the quantity when depositing ETH to weETH. The code treats the quantity of eETH shares as the actual quantity of eETH, but these two quantities are not equal. This is because the Etherfi `LiquidityPool.deposit` and `stETH.submit` functions both return shares instead of the actual token amount. While the protocol handles stETH correctly, it does not handle eETH correctly. This is due to a discrepancy in the code in the `weETH.wrap` function, where the parameter should be the actual amount of eETH instead of the amount of shares. This can lead to two potential scenarios: 1) if a user deposits 100 ETH and receives 100 eETH and 90 eETH shares, then tries to wrap 90 shares, they will lose 10 eETH, or 2) if a user deposits 100 ETH and receives 100 eETH and 110 eETH shares, then tries to wrap 110 shares, the transaction will fail and the user will not be able to deposit their assets. The report suggests returning the difference of eETH balance instead of directly returning the result of `LiquidityPool.deposit` to fix this issue. The protocol team has accepted and resolved this issue.

title: Signature replay during the release/deposit operations on the LiquidityManager.
description:
**Severity**: High

**Status**: Resolved 

**Description**

LiquidityManager.sol: preRelease(), depositToClosePreRelease()

1) In the preRelease() operation: nonce is not a part of the signature and is not validated to
be used, thus it can be re-used. And in that case the amount in `amountsPerNonce` is
overridden, making it unreliable in terms of the amount to return.

2) in the `depositToClosePreRelease()` operation: the nonce is not checked to be used
(isArbitrageNonceUsed is not validated), making its replay possible

3) Looks like nonces from preRelease() and depositToClose are mismatched:
- `amountsPerNonce` is only set in `preRelease()` and never validated/decreased in
depositToClose
- `isArbitrageNonceUsed` is set in `depositToClose`, but never validated and never related to
preRelease record bound to nonce.

The issue is marked as High, but not Critical, as despite the unreliable records and replayed
nonces, the total amount is still manually controlled by the Operator (in terms of how many
to release/deposit) and Authorities (in terms of liquidity withdraw from the manager).

**Recommendation**:

Match the nonce usage:
- include nonce into the signature in preRelease()
- in preRelease() validate amountsPerNonce against the nonce re-usage OR avoid the
overriding by increasing the amount
- in depositToClose validate nonce against the amountsPerNonce amount to decrease it OR
validate nonce against re-usage
- verify if release and deposit nonce are independent or they represent the same entity
opened in release and closed in deposit - and match both operations for it.
**Post-audit:**
The Chainport team provided necessary nonce validations and verified, as the nonce is an
identifier of the crosschain operation, the backend service monitors it to be used in that way
(deposited on one side and released on another side within the same nonce). Since
operations are on different sides of the bridge, nonce is validated offchain (in terms of
matching both ends). Still, auditors highly recommend to make a part of the signature.
summary: This bug report discusses issues found in the LiquidityManager.sol file, specifically in the preRelease() and depositToClosePreRelease() operations. The report notes that the nonce is not being properly validated, which can lead to unreliable records and the possibility of replaying nonces. This is marked as a high severity issue, but not critical, as the total amount is still manually controlled by the operator and authorities. The recommendation is to match the nonce usage by including it in the signature and validating it against the amountsPerNonce. After further investigation, the Chainport team has provided necessary validations and monitoring offchain, but the auditors still recommend making the nonce a part of the signature.

title: Restricted setter open for unauthorized users.
description:
**Severity**: High

**Status**: Resolved 

**Description**

ChainportMainBride.sol
ChainportSideBride.sol
`setAddressLength()` setter can be called by anyone. The `onlyClassifiedAuthority` modifier
was deleted durin the code uprade.

**Recommendation**:

Set the appropriate restricting modifier to the function.
summary: The bug report is about a code upgrade that resulted in the deletion of a restricting modifier, which allowed anyone to call a specific function. This poses a security risk and the recommendation is to set the appropriate restricting modifier to the function. The bug has been resolved.

title: Bridge can appear to be out of funds of tokens managed by the liquidity manager
description:
**Severity**: High

**Status**: Acknowledged 

**Description**

ChainportMainBridge.sol, deposit / release flow
In current iteration, the main bridge adopted the Liquidity+anger as an additional entity for
holding the liquidity. In case if the token project is considered as managed (is listed on the
Liquidity+anager), all deposited liquidity is transferred to the Liquidity+anager. &nd vice
versa - during the release it is requested from the Liquidity+anager. However, currently the
project has 2 scenarios, when the liquidity will become unavailable (or partly unavailable) for
the withdraw
1) Token project is manually stopped from being manage
     - it is possible in case if liquidity is withdrawn from the Liquidity+anger contract (by the authority or project owner) and the owner is removed
2) Liquidity is unavailable - in case of being borrowed by the arbitrageManager
In both cases, there is no trigger to return the necessary amount of tokens to the bridge.
&lso, since there is no track of the liquidity deposited from the bridge and validation of the
amount borrowed by the ArbitrageManager against this track, the moment of the balancing
liquidity back can be missed
**Recommendation**:
Verify the current logic and provide the necessary sanitizing actions:
- add tracking of funds deposited from the bridge
- add validation of the funds borrowed by the &rbitrage+anager against the deposited amount
- leave some liquidity on the manager contract for the release from the bridge
- add triggers for returning the liquidity for bridge depositors in case of its withdraw from the liquidity manager by the authority/ownex
- check that owner removal is impossible in case if liquidity was borrowed to the
ArbitrageManager



**Post-audit**:
The Hord team verified that all mentioned checks are performed by the protocol backend. It
tracks the balances and supplies sinatures to:
- track the amount of funds borrowed by the ArbitrageManager and ensure no more than
the allowed amount is being borrowed.
- validate the liquidity left on the manager contract aainst the minThreshold parameter
durin release/mint events and ensure that there always is available liquidity.
- ensure that both arbitrae operator and project owner cannot withdraw funds that are
currently in flux and should be delivered to a portin user.

The Hord team commented that all actions (token movements) are stored onchain toether
with appropriate sined action from the responsible backend service, thus the full history of
actions can be retrieved. The whole process of cross chain arbitrage is packed into the
atomic arbitrae executions, thus the liquidity cannot be resolved in a sinle contract, but
only at both ends toether with the appropriate sined action from the backend worker&
Still, the security team leaves a concern reardin hih dependency on the backend service
- in terms of deleation of most of the crucial checks.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the deposit and release flow in the ChainportMainBridge.sol contract. The report states that the liquidity for a token project is transferred to the Liquidity+anager contract, but there are two scenarios where the liquidity can become unavailable for withdrawal. The first is if the token project is manually stopped from being managed, and the second is if the liquidity is borrowed by the ArbitrageManager. The report recommends adding tracking and validation of funds deposited and borrowed, leaving some liquidity on the manager contract, and adding triggers for returning liquidity in case of withdrawal. The post-audit states that the Hord team has verified these checks are performed, but there is concern about the high dependency on the backend service.

title: `TokenBridge::bridgeToken` allows 1-way `ERC721` bridging causing users to permanently lose their nfts
summary:
This bug report is about an issue with the `TokenBridge` contract. The `TokenBridge::bridgeToken` function is supposed to only support `ERC20` tokens, but it also accepts `ERC721` tokens. This causes a problem when users try to bridge back to the L1, as it always reverts and the tokens are permanently stuck in the `TokenBridge` contract.

To demonstrate this issue, a new file called `contracts/tokenBridge/mocks/MockERC721.sol` was added and a test was added to the `test/tokenBridge/E2E.ts` file. This test shows that the `TokenBridge` contract accepts `ERC721` tokens and successfully bridges them to the L2, but when the user tries to bridge them back to the L1, it fails.

The recommended solution is to prevent the `TokenBridge` contract from accepting `ERC721` tokens. One way to do this is by changing the `TokenBridge::_safeDecimals` function to revert if the call fails, as `ERC20` tokens should always provide their decimals while `ERC721` tokens do not have decimals. Another option would be to use `ERC165` interface detection, but not all `ERC721` tokens support this.

The bug has been fixed in the Linea codebase and has been verified by Cyfrin. The fix can be found in the commit [35c7807](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/commit/35c7807756ccac2756be7da472f5e6ce0fd9b16a#diff-e5dcf44cdbba69f5a1f8fc58700577ce57caac0c15a5d5fb63e0620aeced62d4L435-R446) merged in [PR3249](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/pull/3249/files#diff-e5dcf44cdbba69f5a1f8fc58700577ce57caac0c15a5d5fb63e0620aeced62d4L435-R449).

title: Deprecated variable `L1MessageServiceV1::__messageSender` is still used making `TokenBridge::completeBridging` revert for older messages preventing users from receiving bridged tokens
description:
**Description:** In `L1MessageServiceV1`, this [comment](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/l1/v1/L1MessageServiceV1.sol#L27) indicates that `_messageSender` storage variable is deprecated in favor of transient storage.

However the deprecated `_messageSender` is [updated](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/l1/v1/L1MessageServiceV1.sol#L122) in `L1MessageServiceV1::claimMessage` and also [set](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/l1/L1MessageService.sol#L68) in `L1MessageService::__MessageService_init`. But `L1MessageService::claimMessageWithProof` does [use](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/l1/L1MessageService.sol#L142) the transient storage method.

`MessageServiceBase::onlyAuthorizedRemoteSender` [calls](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/MessageServiceBase.sol#L52-L57) `L1MessagingService::sender` to retrieve the message sender and this function always [fetches](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/l1/L1MessageService.sol#L166-L168) it from transient storage and not from the deprecated `_messageSender`.

`MessageServiceBase::onlyAuthorizedRemoteSender` in turn is used by `TokenBridge`::[setDeployed](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/tokenBridge/TokenBridge.sol#L302) and [`completeBridging`](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/tokenBridge/TokenBridge.sol#L241).

**Impact:** Older L2->L1 messages using `claimMessage` to call `TokenBridge::setDeployed` and `completeBridging` will always revert since:
* the message sender will be fetched from transient storage
* `claimMessage` never sets message sender in transient storage as it still updates the deprecated `_messageSender` storage variable

As `completeBridging` will always revert for these transactions, users will never receive their bridged tokens.

**Recommended Mitigation:** Change `L1MessageServiceV1::claimMessage` to store message sender in transient storage and remove all uses of deprecated `_messageSender`.

**Linea:**
Fixed in commit [55d936a](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/pull/3191/commits/55d936a47ca31952cc65cc9ee1c7629b919c6aa2#diff-e9f6a0c3577321e5aa88a9d7e12499c2c4819146062e33a99576971682396bb5R122-R144) merged in [PR3191](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/pull/3191/files#diff-e9f6a0c3577321e5aa88a9d7e12499c2c4819146062e33a99576971682396bb5R119-R141).

**Cyfrin:** Verified.
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `L1MessageServiceV1` contract that can cause transactions to fail and users to lose their tokens. The issue is related to the use of the deprecated `_messageSender` storage variable and the new transient storage method. This issue affects older L2->L1 messages that use `claimMessage` to call `TokenBridge::setDeployed` and `completeBridging`. The recommended mitigation is to update the `L1MessageServiceV1::claimMessage` function to store the message sender in transient storage and remove all uses of the deprecated variable. The bug has been fixed in commit `55d936a` and has been verified.

title: [H-02] Invalid validation allows users to unlock early
summary: The bug report describes a problem with the `setLockDuration` function in the `LockManager.sol` contract. This function allows users to set the duration of their token lock, but it has a flaw that allows them to reduce their lock time or even unlock their tokens instantly. This can be exploited by changing the lock duration multiple times, resulting in an incorrect unlock time. This issue has been confirmed and fixed by the developers, and it has been rated as a high-risk vulnerability.

title: [H-01] Malicious User can call `lockOnBehalf` repeatedly extend a users `unlockTime`, removing their ability to withdraw previously locked tokens
summary: The report discusses a bug in a protocol that allows users to donate ether and/or tokens to another user. The issue arises when the `lockOnBehalf` function is used, as it resets the receiver's `lockedToken.unlockTime` and delays their ability to withdraw their tokens. This can be exploited by a malicious user to repeatedly call the function and delay the unlock time even further. Additionally, the function has no minimum quantity requirement, making it easier for the attacker to execute the exploit. The report also suggests some tests to demonstrate this vulnerability and recommends mitigations, such as limiting the use of the `lockOnBehalf` function to only the MigrationManager contract. The submission has been selected as the best because it clearly outlines the risks and provides appropriate recommendations.

title: High Risk of Bugs Due to Limited Test Suite
description:
**Update**
Marked as "Acknowledged" by the client. The client provided the following explanation:

> for public sale and vesting contracts, code is very simple and audited. for Xintx, the complex part of the code have been heavily audited and test in other project and have been adapted.

**Description:** The current test suite provides very low coverage of the code branches, with 0% branch coverage for the `VestingXINTX` and `PublicSaleINTX` contracts and 50% coverage for `IntxUpgradeable` while `StakedINTX` has a coverage of 14.77%.

Contracts not extensively tested are at high risk of serious bugs impacting the protocol's proper functioning and security. While audits can help developers to find bugs, they are not a substitute for thorough unit and integration testing.

**Recommendation:** A test suite should be created, which:

*   Has at least `90%` branch coverage
*   Includes unit tests and integration tests with a mainnet fork
*   Includes a variety of test cases, including:
    *   All "happy path" scenarios
    *   Negative test cases
    *   Unexpected or edge cases
    *   All role permissions and access control for protected functions.

*   Verifies the following through assertions:
    *   All state changes
    *   Invariants
    *   Emission of events

*   May include fuzz testing
summary: The client has acknowledged an issue with the code for public sale and vesting contracts. The current test suite has very low coverage, with some contracts having 0% coverage. This puts the protocol at risk for serious bugs. The report recommends creating a test suite with at least 90% branch coverage, including a variety of test cases and assertions to verify state changes and invariants.

title: Incorrect Reward Updates upon xINTX Minting
description:
**Update**
Marked as "Fixed" by the client. Addressed in: `2a51fba4fcbba13c524b2b9ddbc736c8eadaf9ee`. The client provided the following explanation:

> Fixed using lastTokenId instead of _tokenId.

**File(s) affected:**`StakedINTX.sol`

**Description:** In the `_stake()` function, `_tokenId` is intended to serve as the unique identifier for the newly minted token. This ID is crucial for tracking and managing individual stakes within the smart contract. However, in the current implementation, `_tokenId` is not assigned any value before it is used in the `_updateReward(_tokenId)` call. This oversight leads to `_tokenId` being passed as 0 to the `_updateReward()` function, which is most likely not the intended behavior.

**Recommendation:** We assume the intended behavior was to pass `lastTokenId` to `_updateReward()`. This would fix the behavior.
summary: A recent update to the `StakedINTX.sol` file has been marked as "Fixed" by the client. The issue was addressed in a specific commit, `2a51fba4fcbba13c524b2b9ddbc736c8eadaf9ee`, and the client provided an explanation for the fix. The bug report highlights a problem with the `_stake()` function, where the `_tokenId` variable is not assigned a value before being used in the `_updateReward()` function. This results in `_tokenId` being passed as 0 to the function, which is not the intended behavior. The recommendation is to use `lastTokenId` instead, which would fix the issue.

title: User Pending Rewards Can Never Be Paid Out
description:
**Update**
Marked as "Fixed" by the client. Addressed in: `31182abb586743450bcfb4359b26b5eee34b7f4d`. The client provided the following explanation:

> Now, _msgSender is used for pendingRewards[].

**File(s) affected:**`StakedINTX.sol`

**Description:** The `claim()` function performs the following two lines of code:

```
address _owner;
uint _amountOut = pendingRewards[_owner];
```

As can be seen, the `_amountOut` initial value is set before the `_owner` address is set to the output of `_ownerOf(_tokenId)` later on in the function logic. This means that `_amountOut` will always be initialized to zero instead of the initial `pendingRewards` entry of the transaction sender.

After adding up the rewards of each `xINTX` token and the pending rewards (`0`), the caller's pending rewards are reset to zero, resulting in the user's pending rewards being lost forever.

**Recommendation:** Set the local variable, `_owner`, as the caller's address.
summary: The client reported a bug in the `StakedINTX.sol` file where the `claim()` function was not working properly. The issue was that the `_amountOut` variable was being set to zero instead of the correct value, causing the user's pending rewards to be lost. The recommendation is to set the `_owner` variable to the caller's address to fix the bug.

title: Users Can Sell CryptoPunks They Do Not Own
description:
**Update**
Marked as "Fixed" by the client. Addressed in: `7013b81820420d8e555d8edc6948ab55570170e0`.

The client provided the following explanation: "Renamed Item->SaleItem for better code readability as well"

This issue is now fixed as it is enforced that the seller owns the punk.

**File(s) affected:**`CyanPrivateSales.sol`

**Description:** Prior to a seller listing a CryptoPunk on the Cyan Marketplace, the Punk must be offered for sale in one of two ways supported by the CryptoPunk smart contract; either allowing anyone to purchase the punk, or by allowing a specific address to purchase the punk.

`CyanPrivateSales.transferItem()` makes two seperate calls to the CryptoPunk contract during a buy, when the token is transferred from the seller to the buyer. First, `cryptoPunkContract.buyPunk{ value: 0 }(item.tokenId);` is invoked, which transfers the token from the seller to the `CyanPrivateSales` contract, then `cryptoPunkContract.transferPunk(to, item.tokenId);` is called to transfer the token to the buyer. This makes clear, that prior to selling the Punk on Cyan, the seller must invoke `offerPunkForSaleToAddress()` with a price of zero, and specifying the `CyanPrivateSales` contract as the sole purchaser.

`CyanPrivateSales.transferItem()` lacks a crucial check to enforce that the Punk being purchased, is actually held by the seller address. Since anyone can create and sign the data necessary for listing an item on Cyan, the following exploit can occur.

**Exploit Scenario:**

1.   Alice is planning to sell her CryptoPunk to Bob. Alice signs data for a private sale to Bob for an 100 ETH price.
2.   In preparation for the sale through Cyan, Alice invokes `offerPunkForSaleToAddress()`, specifying `minSalePriceInWei` to be zero, and `toAddress` to be `CyanPrivateSales`, on the CryptoPunk smart contrac.
3.   Eve observes this transaction, and creates and signs her own data for private sale to another address she owns, for the CryptoPunk that is not hers. Except, her price is substationally lower at `0.000001 ETH`. 
4.   As there is no verification that the seller actually holds the CryptoPunk, Eve has successfully stolen this Punk from Alice.

**Recommendation:** In `CyanPrivateSales.transferItem()`, check that `cryptoPunkContract.punkIndexToAddress(tokenId) == item.sellerAddress`.
summary: The client reported a bug where a seller could potentially lose their CryptoPunk when using the Cyan Marketplace. This was caused by a missing check in the code that verifies if the seller actually owns the CryptoPunk they are trying to sell. This allowed for an exploit where someone else could create and sign their own data for a private sale at a lower price, and steal the CryptoPunk from the original seller. The bug has now been fixed by adding a check to verify the seller's ownership of the CryptoPunk before the sale is completed.

title: [H-01] Game fee locked in `earlyEndGame`
summary: This bug report discusses an issue with the `earlyEndGame` function in a game contract. The problem is that the game fee, which is deducted from a player's payout, is not being transferred to the designated treasury address. Instead, it remains in the contract, causing the funds to be locked without a way to transfer them to the treasury. The report recommends implementing a mechanism within the function to ensure that the game fee is transferred to the treasury after it is deducted from the player's payout. This can be achieved by adding a transfer call to the function.

title: [C-03] Incorrect logical check in `endGame` function
summary: The `endGame` function in the `Game` contract has a mistake that causes it to not work properly. This function is supposed to handle payouts at the end of a game, but it uses the wrong symbol when comparing game IDs. This means that it skips players who are actually in the game, and no payouts or updates are made. The players' money stays locked in the contract and they cannot withdraw it. To fix this, the comparison symbol should be changed from `==` to `!=` in the `endGame` function. This will allow the function to work correctly and update player balances and game status as intended.

title: [C-02] Winner's payout is incorrectly calculated
summary: The function that calculates the payout for the winner in a game is not working correctly, resulting in the winner receiving more money than they should. This happens when the admin ends the game and the player has won. The function is adding the wrong amount to the player's balance, causing them to receive more money than intended. To fix this, the function should be updated to only add the amount that the player has won, rather than the total payout. This will ensure that players receive the correct amount of money when they withdraw.

title: [C-01] Game fee handling is incorrect
summary: This report describes a bug in the `endGame` function of a game. The function is used by the admin to finish the game and distribute payouts to the participants. However, there is an issue with the `gameFee` variable that is used to take a fee from the winners' rewards. This fee is supposed to be accumulated and deducted from the total payout, but it is not reset for each new cycle. As a result, the `adjustedPlayerPayout` variable becomes incorrect and can cause the function to revert or distribute incorrect payouts. To fix this bug, the `gameFee` should be paid after all loop cycles and a new variable should be used to calculate the fee for each user.

title: Loss of precision while calculating claimable flux and Point
summary: The bug report is about a smart contract on GitHub that is not delivering the expected returns, but also not losing value. The issue is related to the precision of the contract's calculations, which is causing a loss of accuracy. The bug is caused by the `MULTIPLIER` and `iMULTIPLIER` variables being set to 2, which is not enough to preserve precision. This results in the contract not counting small amounts of locked funds in its calculations, leading to a loss of accuracy in determining the promised returns. The recommendation is to increase the precision of these variables from 2 to 1e18 for higher accuracy. The bug can be reproduced by running a test script on Foundry, which shows the difference in precision when using a higher `MULTIPLIER` value.

title: Loss Of Boosted Weight When Poking In The Same Boosted Vote Period
summary: This report discusses a bug in the `Voter` smart contract on GitHub that can permanently freeze unclaimed yield. The bug occurs when users "poke" their vote within the same boosted vote period, causing a loss of boosted voting power and potentially leaving unclaimed rewards frozen in the contract. The issue is caused by the `poke` function resetting the boost to zero when recalculating the vote, and the `pokeTokens` function also has the same issue. To fix this, the `poke` function should be updated to correctly account for the accumulated boost. A proof of concept test is provided in the report.

title: Infinite mint of FLUX using poke
summary: This report is about a vulnerability in the smart contract code for the FLUX token on the Alchemix Finance platform. The vulnerability allows for an unlimited amount of FLUX tokens to be created, which can impact the governance process and the market value of FLUX. The vulnerability can be exploited by anyone and can be done in one transaction. The report includes a proof of concept to demonstrate the attack.

title: `VotingEscrow.sol::checkpoint` is completely broken
summary: This bug report is about a problem in the code for a smart contract on GitHub. The contract is called "VotingEscrow.sol" and it is used in a protocol called Alchemix Finance. The bug can cause the protocol to become insolvent, which means it could run out of money. The problem is in a function called "_checkpoint" and it is caused by a mistake in how the contract updates the time. This mistake can break the whole protocol, including how rewards are distributed. The bug has been proven with a test, and it is important to fix it before the boost period ends. The code for the contract can be found on GitHub and the bug can be seen on lines 1170-1301.

title: Unfair Revenue Distribution in Non-Alchemix Revenue Tokens Leading to Theft of Unclaimed Revenues
summary: This report is about a bug found in a smart contract on the Alchemix Finance platform. The bug affects the `RevenueHandler` contract, which is responsible for distributing revenue to users who hold a certain type of token. The bug allows for the theft of unclaimed revenue, which can lead to unfair distribution of rewards and potential exploitation by malicious users. To fix this bug, the `checkpoint` function needs to be revised to accurately track and calculate revenue for each epoch. A proof of concept test has been provided to demonstrate the bug and its potential impact.

title: Certain small amount of tokens are not accounted for when deposited
summary: This report is about a bug found in a smart contract on GitHub. The contract is called "VotingEscrow.sol" and it is used to lock tokens for a certain period of time in exchange for rewards. The bug causes the contract to fail in delivering the promised returns and temporarily freezes the locked funds for 12 hours. This happens when a small amount of tokens is deposited and locked, and it is due to a miscalculation in the code. The bug does not result in any loss of value, but it affects the accuracy of the accounting. A proof of concept is provided in the report to show how the bug can be replicated.

title: FluxToken's unlimited mint and Exploitation of gauge voting results using it
summary: This report is about a bug found in the FluxToken smart contract on GitHub. The bug allows for the theft of unclaimed yield, direct theft of user funds, and manipulation of governance voting results. The vulnerability details include a function that can be called multiple times within an epoch, leading to the minting of an unlimited amount of flux tokens. This can also result in the attacker securing the majority of reward tokens. The recommendation is to modify the function to prevent this issue. A proof of concept is provided to demonstrate the bug.

title: No accounting for totalVoting in `Bribe.sol::withdraw` function leads to loss of Yield
summary: This is a report about a bug found in a smart contract called Bribe.sol, which is used by a platform called Alchemix Finance. The bug can be exploited by a malicious user to permanently decrease the amount of yield earned by other users. The bug occurs in the function called `withdraw` which is used when a user withdraws their vote. The function does not decrease a variable called `totalVoting` as it should, which can be exploited to increase the total supply and decrease the yield earned by users. This bug can be fixed by modifying the function to decrease `totalVoting` as well. The bug can be reproduced using a proof of concept code provided in the report.

title: A user is able to claim more bribes than they have earned
summary: This report is about a bug found in a smart contract on the GitHub website. The bug allows a user to claim more bribes than they have earned by claiming bribes for epochs they have not voted in. This means that the user can steal funds from other users and also prevent them from claiming their share of bribes. The bug is caused by a vulnerability in the code, where the balance of the user is not reset after claiming a bribe, allowing them to claim more bribes even for epochs they did not vote in. This breaks one of the rules set by the team that a user should not be able to claim more bribes than they have earned. A proof of concept has been provided to demonstrate how the bug can be exploited.

title: Rounding down in getClaimableFlux leads to less reward minting in nftClaim
description:
Report type: Smart Contract


Target: https://github.com/alchemix-finance/alchemix-v2-dao/blob/main/src/FluxToken.sol

Impacts:
- Permanent freezing of unclaimed yield

## Description
## Brief/Intro
```getClaimableFlux``` carried out multiplication on result of division leads to less amount minting  in ``` nftClaim``` function of ```FluxToken``` contract.

## Vulnerability Details
```getClaimableFlux``` function is called in ```nftClaim``` function to have the minting amount cached before ```mint``` is called.
```claimableFlux``` variable in ```getClaimableFlux``` function have mathematics operation which violates safe practice of carrying out multiplication before division that can lead to issue of rounding down.

## Impact Details
The rounding down issue in ```getClaimableFlux``` function will lead to minting less amount of ```FLUX``` tokens to be claimed against the ```eth``` deposited.
The minting of less token due to rounding down will cause depositor to have less reward for claiming causing direct loss.

## References
https://github.com/alchemix-finance/alchemix-v2-dao/blob/f1007439ad3a32e412468c4c42f62f676822dc1f/src/FluxToken.sol#L224

## Recommendation
The recommendation is made to carry out all division and multiplication separately to avoid loss of precision due to rounding down.
The recommended code will mint exact value that the depositor is eligible for claiming against the amount they deposited.
```diff
    function getClaimableFlux(uint256 _amount, address _nft) public view returns (uint256 claimableFlux) {
        uint256 bpt = calculateBPT(_amount);

        uint256 veMul = IVotingEscrow(veALCX).MULTIPLIER();
        uint256 veMax = IVotingEscrow(veALCX).MAXTIME();
        uint256 fluxPerVe = IVotingEscrow(veALCX).fluxPerVeALCX();
        uint256 fluxMul = IVotingEscrow(veALCX).fluxMultiplier();

        // Amount of flux earned in 1 yr from _amount assuming it was deposited for maxtime
-        claimableFlux = (((bpt * veMul) / veMax) * veMax * (fluxPerVe + BPS)) / BPS / fluxMul;

+	 claimableFlux_modified = (bpt * veMul * veMax * (fluxPerVe + BPS)) / (BPS * fluxMul * veMax); // all division after multiplication

        // Claimable flux for alchemechNFT is different than patronNFT
        if (_nft == alchemechNFT) {
            claimableFlux = (claimableFlux * alchemechMultiplier) / BPS;
        }
    }
```



## Proof of Concept
This simple test clearly demonstrates loss of rewards for user against amount deposited due to rounding down issue.

All the values are considered in default context as used in the ``` VotingEscrow``` contract that were passed in the calculation of ```claimableFlux``` variable in ```getClaimableFlux``` function.

The test have also modified code for ```claimableFlux``` variable named ```claimableFlux_modified``` to show the difference in result of mathematical operation carried out in normal code and modified code context.

Normal code as used by protocol carried out multiplication on result of division, while modified code group together multiplication and division to have more precise value.

```
    // forge t --mt test_rewardFlux -vv
    function test_rewardFlux() external view {
        uint256 bpt = 1000e18 * 40; // 1000 tokens passed as param to calculateBPT() of FluxToken
        uint256 BPS = 10_000; // value taken from VotingEscrow contract
        uint256 veMul = 2; // value taken from VotingEscrow contract
        uint256 veMax = 365 days; // value taken from VotingEscrow contract
        uint256 fluxPerVe = 5000;// value taken from VotingEscrow contract
        uint256 fluxMul = 4;// value taken from VotingEscrow contract
        uint256 alchemechNFT = 5;// value taken from VotingEscrow contract
        uint256 _nft = 5; // value assumed for VotingEscrow contract

        // Amount of flux earned in 1 yr from _amount assuming it was deposited for maxtime
        uint256 claimableFlux = (((bpt * veMul) / veMax) * veMax * (fluxPerVe + BPS)) / BPS / fluxMul;
        console.log("claimableFlux: %e", claimableFlux); // value on multiply result of division

        uint256 claimableFlux_modified = (bpt * veMul * veMax * (fluxPerVe + BPS)) / (BPS * fluxMul * veMax); // all division after multiplication
        console.log("claimableFlux_modified: %e", claimableFlux_modified); // value when all division is after multiply

        if (_nft == alchemechNFT) {
            claimableFlux = (claimableFlux * alchemechNFT) / BPS;
            console.log("Nft claimableFlux: %e", claimableFlux); // resultant value on default code

            claimableFlux_modified = (claimableFlux_modified * alchemechNFT) / BPS;
            console.log("Nft claimableFlux_modified: %e", claimableFlux_modified); // resultant value on modified code
        }
    }
```



The result clearly shows difference in amount claimed by user for normal code against the modified code.
The difference is due to loss of precision arising from rounding down causing direct loss.

title: Incorrect accounting of `totalVoting` leads to permanent freeze of funds in Bribe contract and incorrect bribe distribution.

title: [H-04] Multiple swap lack slippage protection
summary: This bug report discusses a problem with the current protocol, which involves swapping tokens in multiple places.
