title: Unlocking offers does not return any funds
description:
## Description

When a user unlocks (i.e., cancels) an offer, the offer is deleted from the protocol, but the purchase tokens are not returned to the user.

On line [235] of `TermAuctionOfferLocker.sol`, a call to `termRepoServicer.unlockOfferAmount()` should return the purchase tokens for an offer to the offerer. However, it is called with the argument `offerToUnlock.amount`. `offerToUnlock` is declared on line [228] as a variable of type `storage`. Storage variables are simply pointers or references to existing storage locations. Therefore, when the variable that `offerToUnlock` points to is deleted on line [230], the contents of `offerToUnlock` are deleted too. This means that `offerToUnlock.amount` will be zero, and so no tokens will be returned.

## Recommendations

Use a memory variable to copy values that are about to be deleted from storage. The variable type on line [228] could be changed to `memory`, but gas could be saved by instead copying only the information required:

```solidity
uint256 amountToUnlock = offers[id].amount;
```

Note that `uint256` variables inside functions are automatically of type `memory`.

## Resolution

Based on a retest of commit `e883f0e`, the issue has been resolved - `amountToUnlock` is now set to `offers[id].amount`.
summary:
This bug report is about an issue in the Term Auction Offer Locker.sol file. When a user unlocks an offer, the offer is deleted from the protocol, but the purchase tokens are not returned to the user. This is because on Line 235 of the file, the call to termRepoServicer.unlockOfferAmount() is called with the argument offerToUnlock.amount. OfferToUnlock is declared on Line 228 as a storage variable, and when the variable is deleted on Line 230, the contents of offerToUnlock are deleted too. This means that offerToUnlock.amount will be zero and no tokens will be returned. 

The recommendation is to use a memory variable to copy values that are about to be deleted from storage. The variable type on Line 228 could be changed to memory, but gas could be saved by instead copying only the information required: uint256 amountToUnlock = offers[id].amount. 

Based on a retest of commit e883f0e, the issue has been resolved - amountToUnlock is now set to offers[id].amount.

title: Bids only transfer collateral for the first token type
description:
## Description

When a bid is submitted, its validity is assessed against all the different collateral tokens in the bid added together. However, only the first collateral token is actually transferred. 

A user could submit a large bid with collateral in two tokens: A and B. The amount of token A could be tiny and the amount of token B could be very large. The system would accept the submitted bid and potentially allow this user to borrow a large amount of the purchase token whilst only making the small token A collateral payment.

The function which assesses whether a bid has sufficient collateral is `TermAuctionBidLocker._isInInitialCollateralShortFall()`. On line [434], this function loops through the array `collateralTokens_`, calculates their cumulative value, and on line [450] compares this to the bid’s repurchase price.

The code which stores an accepted bid only processes the first collateral token, however. This code is on line [231] to line [272] and it consistently assesses only `bidSubmission.collateralTokens[0]` and `bidSubmission.collateralAmounts[0]` including, crucially, in the calls to `termRepoCollateralManager.auctionLockCollateral()` where the collateral tokens are transferred.

## Recommendations

- If multiple collateral tokens are allowed in a bid, modify the code of `_lock()` to process multiple tokens at each step.
- If only one collateral token is to be allowed per bid, review and modify the code of `TermAuctionBidLocker.sol`.
- Consider that the system may be significantly simplified by limiting bids to only one kind of collateral token. Multiple collateral bids may be rare, and yet they add significant system complexity which results in higher gas costs and the potential for further security issues. A user could still submit multiple separate bids in the same auction using different collateral tokens.

## Resolution

Based on a retest of commit `e883f0e`, the issue has been resolved - multiple collaterals are now correctly supported.
summary:
This bug report is about a problem in the code of TermAuctionBidLocker.sol, which is part of the system that assesses whether a bid has sufficient collateral. When a bid is submitted, the system only processes the first collateral token, while it should process all of them. This could lead to a user submitting a large bid with two tokens, A and B, where the amount of token A is tiny and the amount of token B is large. The system would accept the bid and potentially allow the user to borrow a large amount of the purchase token, while only making a small token A collateral payment.

To resolve this issue, the code of TermAuctionBidLocker.sol was modified to process multiple tokens at each step. Alternatively, the system could be simplified by limiting bids to one kind of collateral token, as multiple collateral bids are rare and add complexity. After a retest of commit e883f0e, the issue was resolved and multiple collaterals are now correctly supported.

title: The beneficiaryWithdrawable Function Can Be Called by Anyone ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report covers a security issue with the `beneficiaryWithdrawable` function in the AgentPolice.sol and Agent.sol files. The function is supposed to be called by the Agent when a beneficiary is trying to withdraw funds, but the issue is that anyone can call this function directly, and the quota will be reduced without funds being transferred. To fix this, the recommendation is to ensure only the Agent can call this function. The bug was resolved by removing the beneficiary logic completely.

title: Wrong Accounting for totalBorrowed in the InfinityPool.pay Function ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report is about a problem with the InfinityPool.sol file, which is part of the GLIF Confidential Pool project. The issue is that if an Agent pays more than the current interest debt, the remaining payment is being accounted as repayment of the principal debt. This is due to two mistakes in the calculation, which should be fixed. The first mistake is that the calculation should be done using the `totalBorrowed` value instead of `0`. The second mistake is that the `principalPaid` cannot be larger than the `account.principal` in that calculation. The resolution is addressed as recommended in two pull requests.

title: Wrong Accounting for totalBorrowed in the InfinityPool.writeOff Function ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report concerns the `InfinityPool.writeOff` function in the `src/Pool/InfinityPool.sol` file. It involves a calculation of the amount of funds lost by the pool. The `totalBorrowed` value is decreased by the `lostAmt` value instead of the original `account.principal` value, which fails to acknowledge the loss. The resolution for this bug was to fix the code, which was done by [pulling a file](https://github.com/glif-confidential/pools/pull/440/files).

title: Agent Data Oracle Signed Credential Front-Running Attack ✓ Fixed
description:
#### Resolution



[Mitigated](https://github.com/glif-confidential/pools/pull/464) by allowing only the `Agent` to request credentials.


#### Description


For almost every action as an `Agent`, the owner of the `Agent` is supposed to request `SignedCredential` data that contains all the relevant current info about the “off-chain” state of the `Agent`. New credentials can only be requested when the old one for this `Agent` is used or expired. Anyone can request these credentials, containing all the data about the call. So if the attacker consistently requests the credentials with the function and parameters that the actual `Agent` wouldn’t want to call, the `Agent` won’t be able to generate the credentials that are needed.


#### Recommendation


Ensure an `Agent` can always have new credentials that are needed. One solution would be to allow only an Agent’s owner to request the credentials. The problem is that the beneficiary is also supposed to do that, but the beneficiary may also be a contract.
summary: This bug report is about an issue with requesting credentials for an Agent. The issue is that anyone can request these credentials, containing all the data about the call, which could lead to the Agent not being able to generate the credentials that are needed. The recommendation is to ensure an Agent can always have new credentials that are needed by allowing only the Agent's owner to request the credentials. This was mitigated by allowing only the Agent to request credentials. The problem is that the beneficiary is also supposed to do that, but the beneficiary may also be a contract. To solve this, the owner of the Agent needs to be able to request the credentials, while also allowing the beneficiary, which may be a contract, to do the same.

title: InfinityPool Contract Authorization Bypass Attack ✓ Fixed
summary:
This bug report is about an attack that could be used to bypass the `subjectIsAgentCaller` modifier to borrow funds from the pool, draining any available liquidity. The attacker could create their own credential and set the Agent ID to `0`, which would allow them to call the `borrow` function with any `msg.sender` and an arbitrary `vc.value` as the parameter. This would allow the attacker to steal all the funds from the pool.

The resolution to this bug is to not allow the `vc.subject` to be zero. This would ensure that only an `Agent` can call the `borrow` function and pass the `subjectIsAgentCaller` modifier. The resolution was addressed by a pull request on GitHub.

title: The beneficiaryWithdrawable function can be called by anyone ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report is about an issue with the `beneficiaryWithdrawable` function in the AgentPolice.sol file. The function is supposed to be called by the Agent when a beneficiary is trying to withdraw funds, however anyone can call this function directly and the quota will be reduced without funds being transferred. The resolution for this bug is to remove the beneficiary logic completely, which has been done in the pull request. To prevent this issue from occurring again, it is recommended that only the Agent can call this function.

title: Wrong accounting for totalBorrowed in the InfinityPool.pay function ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report is about an issue found in the code of the InfinityPool.sol file. The code in question is located at lines 382-401. It is intended that when an Agent pays more than the current interest debt, the remaining payment should be accounted as repayment of the principal debt. However, there are two mistakes in the calculation. Firstly, the value of totalBorrowed should be decreased by the principal that is repaid, but the code currently sets it to 0. Secondly, the principalPaid should not be larger than the account.principal in that calculation. To address the issue, two pull requests have been implemented.

title: Wrong accounting for totalBorrowed in the InfinityPool.writeOff function ✓ Fixed
summary: This bug report is about the `InfinityPool.writeOff` function in the `code/src/Pool/InfinityPool.sol` file. The part of the code in question is from line 271 to 287. The issue is that when the `totalBorrowed` is decreased, it is decreased by the `lostAmt` value instead of the original `account.principal` value. This does not acknowledge the loss, and needs to be changed. The resolution to this bug is that the `totalBorrowed` should be decreased by the original `account.principal` value. This has been fixed in the pull request at the following link: https://github.com/glif-confidential/pools/pull/440/files.

#### Resolution



[Mitigated](https://github.com/glif-confidential/pools/pull/464) by allowing only the `Agent` to request credentials.


#### Description


For almost every action as an `Agent`, the owner of the `Agent` is supposed to request `SignedCredential` data that contains all the relevant current info about the “off-chain” state of the `Agent`. New credentials can only be requested when the old one for this `Agent` is used or expired. Anyone can request these credentials, containing all the data about the call. So if the attacker consistently requests the credentials with the function and parameters that the actual `Agent` wouldn’t want to call, the `Agent` won’t be able to generate the credentials that are needed.


#### Recommendation
